Jatan Markets Cloud: The Kaveri Pod

Mumbai, Sunday, 27 September 2026

1. Opening

At twenty minutes to midnight, Ananya Raghunathan was still at the dining table in her flat in Prabhadevi, with two versions of the same slide open side by side. The board of Jatan Markets Cloud met at ten the next morning at the company's Lower Parel office, and the fourth item on the agenda was hers: Engineering operating model, FY27. One version of the slide said the company would move all nine engineering pods to the shape the Kaveri pod had invented in April — two engineers, a product manager reading code, coding agents doing most of the typing, no separate quality gate. The other version said Jatan would hold that shape to one pod for another quarter while it worked out what had gone wrong in July.

Both slides were defensible. That was the problem. The Kaveri pod had delivered a rebuilt margin-call notifier in six weeks against a comparable module that had taken fourteen, at less than a third of the labour cost, and then produced seven escaped defects in ninety days, two of which had reached clients. Ananya's CFO wanted the cost line; her head of engineering wanted a hiring plan he had not been allowed to publish. Her largest client, in Dubai, wanted a written answer by 15 October about how Jatan's software was now being written, and her regulatory assurance head wanted her to be very careful about what that written answer said.

2. Company history

Jatan Markets Cloud was founded in Pune in 2016 by two former exchange technologists to sell risk and post-trade software to Indian broking firms. Its product, Jatan RiskDesk, computed intraday margin obligations and pushed margin calls to clients. By September 2026 the company employed 372 people, 143 of them engineers, served 41 broking and wealth-management clients across India, Singapore and the Gulf, and reported annual recurring revenue of about ₹112 crore, growing 38 percent year on year. Headquarters moved to Mumbai in 2020; engineering stayed in Pune, with a second centre in Bengaluru from 2021.

One decision from 2021 shaped everything that followed. Jatan's third-largest client at the time, a full-service broker in Chennai, refused a shared multi-tenant deployment on the grounds that its own SEBI system audit would then depend on another firm's data hygiene. Jatan's founders, chasing a large contract in a year when growth mattered more than architecture, agreed to single-tenant deployments — a separate instance of RiskDesk per client, version-pinned, released on the client's schedule. By 2026 there were 41 such instances. Every material change to the margin engine had to be regression-tested and re-certified against each one; the release engineering team of nine existed almost entirely for this reason, and the certification pack for a margin-logic change ran to 2,400 automated tests and roughly eleven working days of human sign-off. Ananya had inherited a company that could write code quickly and could not, structurally, ship it quickly. Whatever the Kaveri pod had proved about writing, it had proved nothing about the eleven days.

3. The industry

The Indian broking market that Jatan sold into had been reshaped twice in five years. The discount-broking wave led by Zerodha and Groww, followed by Angel One and Upstox, had pushed per-trade revenue down and volumes up: a firm processing two lakh orders a day in 2019 was processing twenty lakh in 2026, with margin obligations computed intraday. SEBI's peak-margin regime and the T+1 and then optional T+0 settlement cycles had each forced Jatan's clients to re-plumb their risk systems, and each such change arrived as a dated circular with a compliance deadline rather than as an opportunity to be prioritised.

That regulatory cadence was Jatan's moat and its ceiling. Clients bought RiskDesk because Jatan shipped circular-compliance changes faster than TCS BaNCS or an in-house team could, and because Jatan's certification packs were accepted by the CERT-In empanelled auditors who signed off client system audits. SEBI's Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework had, since 2025, required regulated entities to evidence change management and software supply-chain controls — which meant an auditor could, and at one Ahmedabad client in August had, asked who wrote a given block of code and who reviewed it. Jatan's principal rival, Jaladhi Post-Trade Systems of Hyderabad, was privately funded, half Jatan's size, and had spent the year advertising an "AI-assisted delivery guarantee" to prospects. Beyond India, Jatan earned about 19 percent of revenue outside the country: wealth platforms in Singapore, and a Dubai-based cross-border wealth manager, Jawaher Wealth Advisory DMCC, which served non-resident Indian investors and was Jatan's single largest contract.

4. The situation in detail

In March 2026, Devika Pillai, who led the Kaveri pod in Bengaluru, asked for four months and a frontier-tier agent licence budget to rebuild the margin-call notifier — a ten-year-old service that fanned out margin calls by SMS, email and webhook, and that nobody wanted to touch. Ananya approved it as a contained experiment on a component with no direct effect on the margin computation itself.

What Devika actually did went further than the brief. By the second week she had taken the pod from four engineers to two, moving the other two onto a different pod; the remaining pair wrote specifications and reviewed diffs rather than typing code. Daily stand-ups stopped. The pod's product manager, Vikrant Shah, began reading pull requests himself, which he had never done in six years at Jatan, and stopped writing the weekly status note because, he said, the merge log said it better. The separate QA pass was folded into the pod: the agents generated tests, the engineers reviewed them, and the release went to the certification pack directly.

The first sign of trouble came on 9 July, when a Pune-based client reported that four hundred and twelve margin calls had gone out with the correct amount but the wrong deadline timestamp — 5.00 p.m. instead of the client's contracted 3.30 p.m. cut-off. Ishaan Chowdhury, Jatan's data scientist in Toronto, found the cause in two days: the rebuilt notifier read the cut-off from a configuration field that, for four of the 41 deployments, had never been populated, and the generated code defaulted silently to the platform default rather than failing loudly, as the old service had. The behaviour was covered by a generated test — and the generated test asserted the default.

The second incident, on 2 August, was smaller and worse. A retry path introduced during the rebuild re-sent 1,900 margin calls to one client's investors after a webhook timeout, some of them to investors whose positions had since been squared off. The client escalated to its compliance officer. Jatan issued a credit note of ₹18 lakh and a written root-cause report. On 21 August, the auditor conducting that client's system audit asked Jatan's release engineering lead a question nobody had prepared for: what proportion of the changed lines in the June release had been authored by a coding agent, and what evidence existed of independent human review of those lines. The honest answer was that Jatan did not record it.

By September the picture had become genuinely contradictory. Two other pods — Bhima in Pune and Sharavati in Bengaluru — had adopted agents informally over the monsoon and reported throughput gains comparable to Kaveri's, with, so far, no escaped defects at all. But Bhima had shipped only internal tooling in that window, and Sharavati's numbers turned out to include an automated dependency-upgrade bot. Meanwhile Devika had, without telling Ananya, quietly reinstated a nightly human review of every merged change in Kaveri from the third week of July, and two of her original four engineers had asked to be moved to pods that still wrote code.

5. The people

Devika Pillai — Engineering Lead, Kaveri pod, Bengaluru
Position: roll the model out to all nine pods from 1 October; the July and August defects were a review gap, not an argument against agents. Incentive: she is the internal candidate for Director of Engineering, a role created in the FY27 plan and contingent on the operating-model decision. Not saying: she reinstated nightly human review in July, which means the six-week figure in Exhibit 1 describes a pod configuration that no longer exists.
Harish Ranganathan — VP Engineering, Pune
Position: extend to two more pods, not nine, and only on non-client-facing surfaces. Incentive: the board's FY27 cost brief asks him to take ₹10 crore out of a ₹58 crore engineering payroll; a throughput story that does not translate into headcount reduction leaves him exposed. Not saying: he has already modelled which eleven roles disappear under a full rollout, has shared the model with the CFO, and has not shared it with Devika or with the pod leads whose engineers are in it.
Katrin Vogel — Design Lead, Berlin
Position: a design and interaction review must be restored as a blocking gate on anything a client or a client's investor sees, however the code was produced. Incentive: her team of five is the smallest and most visible cost line outside India and has no pod of its own. Not saying: she was not consulted on the notifier at all, considers the message copy in the August incident partly her responsibility, and is interviewing elsewhere.
Ishaan Chowdhury — Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: no agent-authored change should reach the margin surface until an evaluation suite exists that tests generated logic against recorded production traffic; he estimates ten weeks to build it. Incentive: the suite would be his; it is also the most interesting work available to him. Not saying: he believes about a third of Jatan's existing hand-written margin code would fail the same suite, which would raise questions nobody has asked yet.
Wei Ling Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Position: freeze the model until the Jawaher renewal closes in December; her accounts cannot absorb another incident. Incentive: her variable pay is weighted to gross retention across eleven APAC and Gulf accounts. Not saying: Jawaher's technology head has already asked her, informally, whether Jatan would accept a contractual clause requiring disclosure of AI-generated code, and she has not yet reported the question to Ananya in writing.
Ramesh Kulkarni — Head of Regulatory Assurance, Mumbai
Position: Jatan must be able to answer the auditor's August question before it changes anything else; provenance logging first, rollout second. Incentive: he signs the certification packs personally. Not saying: he thinks the single-tenant architecture, not the agents, is the real constraint, and that saying so out loud would reopen a 2021 decision the founders do not wish reopened.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the comparison that started the argument, and the one Devika puts on the first slide of every deck.

7. Voices

"Six weeks. Fourteen before. We can argue about the rework line, but nobody in this room has shipped a rewrite of that service in a decade and we did it with two people. If we hold this to one pod because two things broke, we are telling ninety engineers that the safe thing is to be slow."Devika Pillai, engineering review, 15 September
"The auditor's question was not hostile and it is not going away. He asked who wrote the change and who reviewed it. Today I can answer the second half. I cannot answer the first half for any release since April, and I will not sign a pack that implies I can."Ramesh Kulkarni, regulatory assurance note, 18 September
"Small point. My whole July was diffs. I am better at the product than I was — I have read more of our system in three months than in six years. I also missed both discovery calls for the surveillance roadmap and I could not tell you today what our Singapore clients want next quarter."Vikrant Shah, pod channel, 19 September
"Jawaher asked if we would sign a disclosure clause on AI-generated code. Not a demand — a question. What may I say by 15 October?"Wei Ling Tan, message to Ananya, 22 September

8. The options as Ananya sees them

Option A — Rollout to all nine pods from 1 October. Every pod moves to the Kaveri shape, with pod leads free to set their own review rhythm, and Harish's headcount model executed in January once the gain is proven. It also generalises a configuration that, as of the third week of July, Kaveri itself no longer runs, and it does so across the 29 backlog items that touch margin computation with no evaluation suite and no provenance record.

Option B — Split the backlog by blast radius. Agent-led pods take the 38 internal and back-office items immediately; the 29 margin items keep the old cadence until Ishaan's suite exists. This is the option Ananya finds most reasonable and least defensible, because the tagging that the split depends on is self-reported by pod leads with a known 12 percent error rate, and because a notifier is exactly the kind of component that gets tagged back-office until the morning it sends 1,900 messages to investors.

Option C — Provenance before rollout. Nothing expands until every change carries an author-and-reviewer record that satisfies Ramesh, which release engineering estimates at five to seven weeks. It answers the auditor, protects the Jawaher renewal, and forfeits the quarter Marcus says he cannot forfeit.

Option D — Change the constraint instead. Leave the pod question open and spend FY27 collapsing the eleven-day certification path and the 41 single-tenant deployments that make it necessary. This is the option nobody has asked for. It reopens the 2021 decision, requires client consent Ananya cannot assume, and would mean telling the board that the bottleneck the whole argument is about was never in the writing of the code.

What troubles Ananya at the dining table is not which option to pick but whether the four are the right four. Every one of them treats the question as "how much agent-written code, and where" — and Exhibit 1 measures a pod, Exhibit 2 measures pull requests, Exhibit 3 measures defects, and none of the three measures the eleven days in Figure 1, or what Vikrant stopped doing in July, or what happens to a company's product judgement when the person closest to the customer spends sixty percent of his time reading diffs.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday 28 September and expects a recommendation, not options. The FY27 cost brief requires ₹10 crore out of a ₹58 crore engineering payroll, and the finance draft already assumes some of it; Harish's model naming eleven roles exists and the CFO has seen it. Wei Ling needs an answer for Jawaher by 15 October, ahead of a ₹4.4 crore renewal in December, and the question on the table is contractual disclosure, not reassurance. Ramesh will not sign a certification pack that asserts review provenance Jatan cannot evidence, and the next margin-surface release is scheduled for 20 October across all 41 deployments, seven of which carry a 45-day notice clause that has already been triggered. Ishaan's evaluation suite is ten weeks away at best and he has not been given the headcount. Katrin has one designer of five allocated to client-facing surfaces and no pod, on a Berlin band of ₹94 lakh loaded against ₹28 lakh in Pune. Of 96 open backlog items, 29 touch margin computation and 38 are internal or back-office, on tags that pod leads apply themselves and that the 2025 tagging audit found 12 percent wrong. And the Kaveri pod, whose six weeks are the entire evidentiary basis for the decision, currently has two engineers, one of whom has asked to move.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3 both describe the Kaveri pod. What is each one actually measuring, and what would you need to know before treating either as evidence about the other pods?
  2. Exhibit 2 was the number quoted at the all-hands. Given its footnote, what would you have to do to the table before it could support a company-wide decision — and is any corrected version of it still worth having?
  3. Devika removed stand-ups, the separate QA pass and two engineers at the same time, and later restored nightly review without saying so. Which of those four changes caused the six weeks, and which caused the seven defects? What would have told you the difference at the time?
  4. Vikrant's job changed more than any engineer's. Describe precisely what he gained and what he gave up, and say whether the trade is one a product organisation should institutionalise or contain.
  5. Figure 1 shows a certification path that neither pod shape touched. If that path is the binding constraint, what does the throughput gain in Exhibit 2 buy Jatan — and what does that imply about Options A, B and C?
  6. It is Monday morning. What do you do first, what do you say to the board, and what do you tell Wei Ling to write to Jawaher on 15 October — knowing that Ramesh, Devika and Marcus will each read the same words differently?

Closing

At a quarter past midnight Ananya wrote a third slide, with no title on it, listing the four things she was fairly sure of: that the code had been written faster, that nobody could yet say by how much once certification was counted, that two clients had been affected and one auditor had asked a question she could not answer, and that the pod everyone wanted to copy had already changed shape twice without anyone recording it. She left the two versions of the fourth slide open, both of them, and went to bed.

AI-Native Teams: Verification as the Binding Constraint

A near-expert reading on how vibe coding and coding agents change team shape, cadence, and the product manager's actual ownership.

1. Two Decisions, Six Weeks Apart

On 18 August 2026, Meera Raghunathan, vice-president of product at Barsaat Play, a Mumbai consumer entertainment app with 41 million monthly actives, sat with a spreadsheet that made her uncomfortable. Barsaat's four feature squads had been running coding agents since February. Merged pull requests per engineer-week had gone from 2.1 to 7.4. Experiments launched per quarter had gone from 63 to 71. The first number had tripled; the second had moved 13 per cent. Her staff engineer in Berlin, Anton Reiss, had a blunt reading: "We made the cheap part cheaper." Meera's decision, due before the October planning cycle, was whether to move from one PM per squad of six engineers to one per squad of eleven — a change her CTO wanted, on the grounds that engineers now needed less direction, and that Meera suspected was exactly backwards.

Six weeks later and 150 kilometres away, Iqbal Siddiqui, chief product officer at Bandobast Systems in Pune, faced the mirror image. Bandobast sells claims adjudication software to eleven Indian general insurers; its core rules engine, first written in 2013, adjudicates roughly ₹4,200 crore of motor and health claims a year. Iqbal's engineering lead had piloted agents on the reporting module and reported a 4.1x implementation speed-up, and the board asked why Bandobast should not adopt the same model platform-wide. Iqbal's problem was that on the claims path, implementation was only 22 per cent of cycle time. The rest was insurer user-acceptance testing, IRDAI-facing change control, and interpretive decisions no test suite could adjudicate. Making 22 per cent of the work four times faster would compress a nine-week cycle to about seven and a half, while adding a new class of plausible-but-wrong change to a system where being wrong is a regulatory event.

Both were asking one question from opposite ends: when the fastest way to produce a first draft of software stops being a person typing, what changes about team shape, cadence and PM ownership? The argument here is that almost nothing changes about deciding what is worth building, and almost everything changes about establishing that what came back is right. The redesign that matters is a redesign around verification.

2. The Idea, and Who Disagrees About It

Define terms precisely. An AI-native team is one in which the unit of work handed between people is no longer a task but a specification paired with an acceptance oracle — a statement of intent plus a means of establishing that a candidate implementation satisfies it — and in which roles, review points and cadence have been redrawn on the assumption that implementation capacity is elastic and verification capacity is not. A team that buys agent licences and changes nothing else is AI-assisted: it has made one station faster. A team is AI-native only once it has re-allocated people and time to the station the speed-up exposed.

The intellectual lineage is older than the tooling. Fred Brooks, in The Mythical Man-Month (1975) and more sharply in "No Silver Bullet" (1986), split software difficulty into accidental complexity — the friction of expressing an idea in a language and toolchain — and essential complexity, the difficulty of working out what the thing should do. Brooks predicted no tool would give an order of magnitude against the essential kind. Coding agents are the largest assault on accidental complexity yet built, and Brooks's split is the cleanest available explanation of why Barsaat's pull requests tripled while its experiments barely moved. Conway's law (1968) supplies the second thread: organisations ship systems shaped like their communication structures, which raises an open question once part of the "organisation" is non-human. Goldratt's theory of constraints (1984) and Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) supply the third: speeding a non-bottleneck station yields nothing but inventory. And Andrej Karpathy's February 2025 coinage of vibe coding — stating intent in natural language and accepting the result largely on faith — named the practice that makes the question urgent, because faith is precisely what verification capacity has to replace.

Four schools now disagree, and about specific propositions rather than mood. Setting out what each would and would not sign is the fastest way to referee an argument between two competent practitioners.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Flow / constraint (Reinertsen, Goldratt)Agents change one station's service time; measure the queue network and rebalance until the new bottleneck is visible.That roles or team shape must change at all. Rebalance capacity, keep the pod.
Thin team (generalist product engineers)The PM / designer / engineer split was an artefact of skill scarcity; agents collapse it, so three broad owners beat a pod of eight specialists.Adding a verification specialist — that re-creates the handoff they are deleting.
Assurance (verification-first)Trust is the binding constraint; rebuild the org around evaluation infrastructure with named owners and budget.Widening the PM-to-engineer ratio before verification capacity is shown to be elastic.
Continuity (Brooks lineage)Agents attack accidental complexity only; specification and judgement always were the job, so cadence should barely move.Any claim that team shape changes by an order of magnitude, or that sprints are obsolete.
Table 1 — The four positions. Meera's CTO is arguing thin-team; Meera's instinct is assurance; Iqbal's regulated context pushes him towards continuity; Anton Reiss is a flow purist.

3. Mechanics: Working the Queue

Experts reason about this as a queueing network, because the central phenomenon — arrival rate into review rises sharply, service rate does not — is exactly what queueing theory describes. Take review as a single station. Let λ be the arrival rate of changes per day, S the mean service time in days per change, and ρ = λS the utilisation. For a single-server queue with variable arrivals, mean wait before service is approximately W = S · ρ / (1 − ρ). What matters is that W is not linear in ρ: modest up to about 0.7, then explosive.

Run Barsaat's numbers. Before agents, a squad generated about 4 changes per day, a reviewer took 0.2 days per change, and one reviewer's worth of attention was available. ρ = 0.8, so W = 0.2 × 0.8 / 0.2 = 0.8 days of waiting on top of 0.2 days of reviewing — a day in review, which nobody noticed. After agents, the same squad generated 12 changes per day at the same service time: ρ = 2.4. That is not a slower queue but an unstable one, where the backlog grows without bound and the symptom is not "review takes longer" but "the queue never empties and the oldest item is three weeks old."

The instructive part is what does not fix it. Doubling reviewers takes ρ to 1.2 — still unstable. Tripling them reaches 0.8 and restores the original one-day wait, at three times the senior-engineer attention, which is the resource nobody has. The other lever is S. Barsaat's harness — scripted checks derived from each specification's acceptance criteria, run before any human opens the diff — cut mean human service time from 0.2 days to 0.07, because reviewers stopped re-deriving whether the code matched the specification and adjudicated only judgement calls. With one reviewer, ρ = 12 × 0.07 = 0.84 and W = 0.07 × 0.84 / 0.16 = 0.37 days. Review latency falls from three weeks of queue to under half a day, at the same headcount.

Fig. 1 — Why adding reviewers is the weaker lever. Moving left along the curve by cutting service time buys far more than raising capacity, because the curve is convex near ρ = 1.

Three second-order effects follow, and they are the steps most teams leave implicit. The first is trust tiering: once implementation is cheap, the design choice that matters is which code paths an agent may merge behind automated gates alone, which it may only draft for review, and which a human must author. Barsaat put feed-ranking experiments and internal tooling in tier 0, player and payments UI in tier 1, billing reconciliation in tier 2. Most teams operate an implicit tiering nobody wrote down, so it is unenforced and silently renegotiated under deadline pressure.

The second is context ownership. Agent output quality is dominated by how well the repository states its own invariants — conventions, boundaries, the reasons behind odd-looking code. That document becomes a maintained artefact with a named owner. Teams that skip it find the dominant defect class is not code that fails but code that is locally correct and violates an invariant nobody wrote down.

The third is architectural erosion, a genuine inversion of Conway's law. Humans respect module boundaries partly because crossing them is laborious; an agent crosses fourteen files as cheaply as two. Barsaat's mean files-touched-per-merged-change drifted from 3.1 to 8.4 over two quarters, and the coupling that produced took nine months to unwind. The architecture stopped mirroring the org chart and drifted toward a monolith no team owned.

Fig. 2 — Routing by blast radius rather than by difficulty is the move competent teams miss. Difficulty is what agents changed; blast radius is not.

The cadence consequence follows from the queue, not from taste: when batch size collapses and arrival rate rises, a two-week planning ceremony is no longer a scheduling device. It is a scheduled opportunity for humans to make the decisions no oracle can make.

Expert teams therefore split cadence in two. Shipping goes continuous, governed by trust tiers and a published review service-level commitment. Judgement keeps a rhythm — a standing checkpoint whose only agenda is irreversible choices, ambiguous requirements and sequencing bets. Estimation splits the same way: estimating implementation effort becomes nearly worthless, while estimating verification effort becomes the number that predicts delivery. A team still T-shirt sizing build effort is measuring the variable that stopped mattering.

4. When the Redesign Applies, and When It Misleads

The conditions can be stated as four testable claims, each answerable with data a team already has. Applied to Meera and Iqbal, they explain why the same evidence supports opposite decisions.

Testable claimBarsaat PlayBandobast Systems
C1. Implementation is at least 40% of current cycle time.Yes — 55% before agents.No — 22%. UAT and change control dominate.
C2. At least 60% of work has acceptance expressible as a machine-checkable oracle.Yes — feature flags, metric guardrails, contract tests.Partly — adjudication rules yes; regulatory interpretation no.
C3. The codebase is legible: modular, tested, conventions written down.Mostly — three years old, 71% line coverage.No — 2013 rules engine, 340 undocumented invariants found in audit.
C4. A plausible-but-wrong change is recoverable within one release.Yes — flag off, roll forward.No — a mis-adjudicated claim is a customer and regulatory event.
Table 2 — The same four questions, opposite answers. Barsaat passes all four; Bandobast passes none cleanly.

The idea is actively misleading where the real constraint was never build. If a company's binding limit is distribution, regulatory approval, certification or the sales cycle, restructuring the product organisation around agents is expensive theatre: it consumes the scarce senior attention that might have addressed the real constraint and makes the organisation feel modern while the calendar does not move. The second misleading case is the greenfield inference — a team that shipped a new service in four days concludes the same multiple applies to the legacy core. It does not, and C3 is why.

5. Hard Edge Cases and the Organisational Seams

Single-team analysis hides most of the difficulty; the interesting failures happen at seams. In multi-product companies, the platform team becomes the bottleneck nobody budgeted for: five product teams triple their change rate into shared infrastructure, and the platform review queue goes from ρ = 0.6 to ρ = 1.8 without anyone deciding anything. The tell is product teams forking shared libraries rather than waiting, converting a queueing problem into a permanent maintenance problem.

In two-sided marketplaces, supply-side and demand-side teams rarely adopt agents at the same rate, and the matching layer between them holds invariants both must respect. When one side ships four times faster, violations appear as matching anomalies neither team's tests catch, because each side's tests are locally correct. Mature marketplaces answer with cross-side contract tests owned by neither team — an organisational answer to a technical symptom.

In regulated contexts — Iqbal's world — the unresolved question is authorship. Change-control regimes assume a named human is accountable. Assigning a human owner to every agent-authored merge restores exactly the bottleneck the agent was meant to remove, and firms claiming otherwise usually mean a human clicks approve without reading. Honest structures reduce the number of changes touching regulated paths rather than the scrutiny per change: agent work goes to adjacent modules and the core stays deliberately slow.

Hardware-plus-software produces a cadence mismatch rather than a queue. Mahavat Robotics, a Chennai warehouse-automation firm, found its fleet app shipping weekly against firmware on an eleven-week cycle bounded by BIS certification and board revisions. Agents widened the gap from three-to-one to eight-to-one, and the app team began shipping features depending on firmware behaviour not yet in the field. The fix was a capability contract: the app may assume only firmware capabilities present in the oldest supported build. In AI-native products the burden doubles: the product itself is non-deterministic, so "the tests pass" is a weaker signal, and the team needs evaluation of model behaviour and verification of the code wrapping it. Two systems, two owners, twice the constraint.

What mature companies do, as opposed to what they announce, is run two regimes and decline to say so. A small greenfield team gets real autonomy, tier-0 defaults and a relaxed gate; the revenue-bearing core keeps the old process almost unchanged. The reliable diagnostic is an organisation operating two review service levels that no document acknowledges, with transfers flowing one way.

6. Nine Distinctions That Separate Expert From Competent

The bottleneck moves, but not to where the slides say. The common claim is that it moves "to product." The expert's tell is asking where the queue physically is: in most teams it is in review and integration, not specification. A PM with a backlog of unwritten specs is a symptom; a reviewer with fourteen open diffs is the constraint. Treating the former as the cause produces more PM hiring and no change in cycle time — Barsaat's exact situation in August.

Throughput gains do not translate into ratio changes. The obvious reading — engineers are three times as productive, so one PM can support three times as many — fails because the PM's load per unit of shipped work went up, not down, as specification became the interface to the agent. The tell is measuring PM hours per shipped feature before proposing any ratio change. Where that number rose, widening guarantees a specification-quality collapse two quarters later.

Agent confidence is uncorrelated with agent correctness. Code review evolved around a useful signal: hesitant code looks hesitant. Agent output is uniformly fluent whether right or wrong, so reviewers lose the heuristic that told them where to look hardest. The tell is a reviewer reporting that everything looks fine and nothing looks interesting. The counter is routing attention by blast radius rather than by apparent risk, because apparent risk is no longer informative.

Velocity metrics invert their meaning. Pull-request count, commits and lines changed were proxies for effort, and effort a proxy for progress. Agents break the second link, not the first, so the metrics still measure something real — they simply stopped measuring what anyone cared about. The tell is a dashboard where throughput and outcome metrics have diverged for two consecutive quarters and nobody has renamed it.

The apprenticeship pipeline breaks silently and late. Juniors historically learned system behaviour by writing the boilerplate agents now write. Removing the work removes the learning without removing the job title, and the effect surfaces two to three years later as a shortage of engineers who review well. The tell is rising median tenure among people trusted to approve tier-2 changes. Cheap to address now, nearly impossible once the gap has opened.

Specification debt compounds faster than code debt. An under-specified feature used to cost one rework cycle. Now it produces a confidently wrong implementation that passes its own generated tests, ships, and becomes the reference the next agent reads. The tell is an agent producing output consistent with a previous mistake. The obvious reading — that the agent is unreliable — is wrong; it is faithfully reproducing an invariant the team taught it.

Cadence redesign is not cadence removal. Teams that read "sprints are obsolete" abolish the checkpoint and find six weeks later that no irreversible decision has been consciously made in a month; the decisions were made incidentally, by whoever's change landed first. The tell is architectural choices nobody remembers making. Rhythm is no longer a batching device, but it remains the only reliable forcing function for judgement.

Review is a scarce, high-status skill being treated as low-status work. Reading agent diffs all day is cognitively heavy and organisationally invisible, so the best reviewers rotate away. The tell is senior engineers requesting transfers to greenfield work, or review quietly delegated to the most junior person available. Left alone, the organisation loses exactly the capacity its new operating model depends on, and the loss looks like ordinary attrition.

The PM's deliverable changes shape, not size. The artefact is no longer a document a human reads and interprets generously; it is a specification whose acceptance criteria are precise enough to be mechanically checkable, which means the PM owns the definition of done operationally. The tell is whether a PM can state, for a feature shipped last month, the check that would have failed had the implementation been wrong. Most cannot — which is why their harnesses test the code's behaviour rather than the product's intent.

7. Product Type and Company Stage

The differences are real in some places and imaginary in others, and it is worth saying which. In consumer products, where changes are small, reversible and measurable within days, the redesign leans hardest into agent speed: the PM's scarce output becomes experiment design and metric guardrails, and tier 0 can be genuinely wide. In B2B and enterprise, releases are larger, customers hold uptime commitments, and a regression appears not in an A/B test but in a support ticket; the PM's time goes into exhaustive edge-case specification, because an agent builds the happy path flawlessly and omits the exception nobody named. Platform and marketplace products differ mainly at the seam above: internal consumers of a platform are themselves accelerating, so platform teams must shift from serving requests to publishing contracts.

In hardware, the constraint is certification and physical revision cycles, which agents do not touch at all; AI-native design applies to the software layer and creates a management problem at the boundary, nothing more. In AI products, verification doubles as described. Across company stage the difference is mostly about who reviews: at seed and Series A the founder prompts and reviews their own output, and a wrong shortcut costs a rewrite next year; beyond roughly 150 engineers, agent-authored code passes the same gates as human code and the binding constraint becomes senior engineers' willingness to trust a diff they did not watch being written — a cultural transition slower than the technical one, and not accelerable by policy.

8. Three Worked Cases, Including One That Failed

Barsaat Play (worked). Meera's pilot squad held at six engineers and one PM, seconded one engineer half-time to own the harness, and moved review from a per-diff human read to a harness-first flow. Cycle time from approved specification to production fell from 9.4 days to 5.1, and experiments launched per quarter rose from 17 to 29 for that squad — because the constraint on experiments had been review latency, not implementation. Cost: half an engineer and four weeks of harness construction.

Mahavat Robotics (partial). Mahavat's app layer achieved a 3.2x implementation speed-up and a 40 per cent cycle-time reduction, but time-to-customer-value moved 11 per cent, because value required firmware on an eleven-week certification cycle. The correct response was to stop optimising the app layer and negotiate the capability contract with the firmware group — a decision that looked like slowing down and was the only lever available.

Haazri Workforce Cloud (failed). Haazri, a Hyderabad deskless-workforce SaaS with 1,900 enterprise customers, read its own 3.4x rise in merged changes as evidence of capacity and widened PM coverage from one per six engineers to one per eleven in a single quarter, cutting two PM roles. Specification quality degraded within six weeks; the harness that would have caught it was never built, because the freed budget went to more engineers.

Two enterprise accounts worth ₹11 crore of annual recurring revenue escalated; one did not renew. Recovery took seven months in three parts: re-narrowing to one PM per seven engineers and rehiring one cut role; eleven weeks of specification-debt remediation, writing acceptance oracles retroactively for the forty highest-traffic flows; and a standing rule that no ratio change may precede a demonstrated reduction in review service time. The chief product officer's later summary was that the company had treated an implementation speed-up as an organisational mandate when it was only evidence about one station.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Diagnostics

Mistaking inventory for throughput. Early sign: change volume up sharply, cycle time flat. Diagnostic: which stage absorbed the time build gave up? Cost late: a planning cycle spent hiring against the wrong constraint, plus the credibility loss when the promised speed-up never appears.

Widening spans on build-speed evidence. Early sign: a ratio proposal citing pull-request counts. Diagnostic: have PM hours per shipped feature fallen? Cost late: Haazri's numbers — two quarters of degraded specification quality, a churned account, a seven-month recovery.

Unwritten trust tiers. Early sign: engineers disagree about whether a change needs human review. Diagnostic: asked separately, do two engineers name the same tier for the same module? Cost late: the first incident on a path everyone assumed someone else was watching, then a blanket policy that slows everything.

Architectural erosion. Early sign: rising mean files touched per change, falling ownership clarity. Diagnostic: has the ratio of cross-module to within-module changes moved this quarter? Cost late: Barsaat's nine months of unwinding, during which agent effectiveness itself degrades as the codebase becomes less legible.

Reviewer attrition. Early sign: transfer requests from senior engineers, or review concentrating in fewer people. Diagnostic: what share of tier-2 approvals came from the top three reviewers last month? Cost late: the constraint becomes a named individual, and their notice period becomes the delivery risk.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Does the sustainable PM-to-engineer ratio widen? The thin-team position at its strongest: implementation time freed from engineers converts into engineers doing their own specification work, which is the historical division of labour in high-performing small teams anyway; the evidence is that three-person startups now ship what eight-person teams shipped in 2022. It would be wrong if verification load scales with change volume and cannot be automated below some floor, in which case widening only relocates the failure. The assurance position holds precisely that, citing organisations like Haazri; it would be wrong if harness construction is a one-time cost rather than a per-domain cost — which some teams report and others emphatically do not.

Is the apprenticeship problem real? One camp argues the loss of boilerplate work destroys the mechanism by which engineers learned to review, and that the shortage surfaces around 2029. The other argues this is the complaint made about compilers, garbage collection and Stack Overflow, and that juniors trained on agent output learn faster because they see more systems sooner. The disagreement is empirically resolvable and unresolved; it turns on whether the skill being lost is writing or judging, and nobody measures the second cleanly.

Automate verification, or socialise it? The harness school says trust must be mechanised or it will not scale. The craft school, well represented among staff engineers, says a harness encodes only failures you anticipated, and the defects that matter are the unanticipated ones a skilled human notices; investing in harnesses at the expense of review culture buys false confidence. The steel version is that Barsaat's harness caught the two regression classes it was built for and would not have caught a third. For the harness school to be wrong, the marginal defect in agent-authored code would have to be predominantly novel rather than recurrent. Evidence is mixed and domain-dependent, which is a more honest conclusion than either camp usually offers.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in observable ways. Presented with a speed-up claim, they ask for the stage decomposition before the headline number, and treat a throughput metric that has decoupled from an outcome metric as a fact requiring explanation rather than a success requiring celebration. They design the verification system before widening any span, and can name the specific check that would catch the error class they most fear. They route work by blast radius rather than difficulty, because agents changed the second and not the first. They keep a rhythm for judgement while shipping goes continuous, and can say which decisions belong in it. Asked whether their team is AI-native, they answer with the review service time rather than the tool list.

12. What Meera and Iqbal Decided

Meera declined the ratio change and told her CTO why in one sentence: the evidence for widening was build-speed evidence, and build was no longer the constraint. She funded one harness owner per two squads, published a review service-level commitment, wrote down trust tiers, and added a mandatory machine-checkable acceptance section to the specification template. She would revisit the ratio only after squad review service time had held below 0.1 days for a full quarter — making it a consequence of a measurement rather than a bet.

Iqbal took the narrower path his conditions demanded. Agents went to reporting, integration and internal tooling, where C1 through C4 largely hold; the adjudication core stayed at tier 2 with a named accountable engineer per change. He told the board plainly that cycle time would improve by roughly a sixth, not fourfold, because 78 per cent of the cycle was never implementation. He also started the work with the longest lead time — documenting the 2013 engine's invariants — on the reasoning that C3 is the only one of the four conditions a company can deliberately change.

  1. Barsaat's experiments per quarter rose 13 per cent while merged changes tripled. What are the three most plausible explanations, and what single measurement would distinguish between them in a week?
  2. Haazri's chief product officer had the same data Meera had. What in the two organisations' decision processes — not their data — produced opposite conclusions?
  3. Iqbal cannot change C1, C2 or C4 in the short term, but he can change C3. If invariant documentation is the highest-leverage investment available to a regulated incumbent, why do so few fund it, and what would you say to a board that calls it maintenance?

13. Going Deeper

  • Agile in practice — the cadence this topic modifies; you cannot redesign a rhythm you cannot describe.
  • AI-assisted building — the tool mechanics producing the team-shape pressure described here.
  • How AI is reshaping the PM role — the individual counterpart to this organisational argument.
  • The AI-era PM skillset — what a PM must do personally, including writing checkable acceptance criteria.
  • Dividing work between PMs, engineers and agents — the allocation question this page raises and leaves open.
  • AI-era product operating model — the company-wide version: funding, planning, incentives.
  • Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved — the discipline that would have saved Haazri.
  • Team shape as the PM-design-engineering gap narrows — the thin-team position on its own terms.
  • The software development lifecycle — the stage decomposition every diagnostic here depends on.
  • Kanban and flow — the queueing intuitions of section three, developed properly.
  • The execution rhythm — keeping a judgement cadence once shipping goes continuous.
  • Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing — why estimating verification now predicts delivery.
  • Backlog management and refinement — where specification debt accumulates before it shows.
  • Definition of done — the artefact that quietly became the PM's most operational deliverable.

AI-Native Teams: When the Agent Is the Fastest Typist in the Room

A reading on how vibe coding and coding agents change team shape, cadence, and what the product manager owns.

1. A Wednesday in Bengaluru

On the second Wednesday of September 2026, Kabir Anand, director of product at Dastak Systems, a Bengaluru-based B2B software company selling dispatch and fleet-visibility software to mid-sized Indian trucking operators, opened a dashboard he had built himself and did not like what it showed. Dastak's engineering org had spent the summer adopting AI coding agents — tools that write, test, and often submit working code from a written brief rather than from a human typing line by line — and leadership had expected this to make the company faster. Pull requests were indeed up: 340 opened in August, against 118 a year earlier, a threefold jump. But the metric Kabir actually cared about — days from an approved spec to a feature live in front of a paying fleet operator — had barely moved, from 11 working days to 8.5. Meanwhile his three PMs, each nominally responsible for one squad of five engineers, were each burning 30-plus hours a week just writing and clarifying specs, and two had asked, independently, whether the pod structure still made sense at all.

Dastak's board meeting was six weeks away, and the CEO wanted an answer: should the company restructure its sixteen product squads around AI coding agents — changing how many engineers report into each PM, how sprints run, and what a PM is accountable for — or was the current wave of agent enthusiasm producing more code without producing more value, making restructuring premature. Kabir's answer would set the operating model for the next eighteen months of hiring. Getting the shape wrong either way was costly: over-restructure, and Dastak would burn scarce senior-PM time on process redesign while rivals shipped into the same accounts; under-restructure, and burnt-out PMs would leave, taking specification discipline — the thing that actually made the agents useful — with them.

2. The Idea

An AI-native team is a product-and-engineering team whose roles, review points, and rhythm have been deliberately redesigned around the fact that a coding agent, not a person at a keyboard, is now usually the fastest way to turn a written specification into a working first draft of software. This is narrower than "a team that uses AI tools." Plenty of teams bolt an AI coding assistant onto an unchanged workflow — same sprint length, same reviewer-per-engineer ratio, same PM job description — and simply get a faster typist. That is an AI-assisted team. An AI-native team goes further: it treats the agent as a team member whose output has to be specified, reviewed, and integrated by someone, and redraws the org chart, cadence, and PM job description around that fact.

The term crystallised out of two developments that arrived together in 2024 and 2025. First, "vibe coding," a phrase the AI researcher Andrej Karpathy popularised in February 2025 to describe writing software by stating intent in natural language and accepting the agent's output largely on faith, made it obvious that the bottleneck in delivery was shifting away from typing speed. Second, agentic coding tools — capable of reading a codebase, making multi-file changes, writing their own tests, and opening a pull request unattended — moved from novelty to daily use over that same stretch. Engineering organisations that had spent a decade tuning the "two-pizza team" (Amazon's Jeff Bezos, mid-1990s) and the squad model (Spotify, popularised by Henrik Kniberg around 2012) around human coding throughput found that throughput assumption no longer held, and had to decide what to keep.

The sentence Kabir could say in a board meeting without sounding glib: "An AI-native team isn't a team that uses AI — it's a team that has moved its bottleneck, on purpose, from writing code to deciding what code is worth writing and trusting what came back."

3. How It Actually Works

Redesigning a team around agents is a sequence of four steps, and teams that skip one usually end up exactly where Dastak had: more pull requests, no faster delivery. The first is an honest inventory of what agents currently do reliably — scaffolding a new service, writing boilerplate endpoints, generating unit tests against an existing spec, mechanical refactors — against what still needs a human's judgment: an ambiguous requirement, an irreversible architectural choice, whether a workaround is acceptable debt or a landmine, and taste about what the product should feel like. Step two, which most teams underweight, is recognising that agent output raises rather than lowers the demand on specification quality: an agent executes a vague brief literally and confidently, producing code that compiles, passes its own generated tests, and does the wrong thing. The PM's spec becomes the actual interface to the agent, which is why Kabir's PMs were suddenly spending more hours per feature, not fewer.

Step three is redrawing where review sits in the cadence. Before agents, review was a light gate because code volume was bounded by typing speed; after agents, volume is bounded by how fast the team can specify work, which is much faster, so review becomes the new constraint and needs its own owner, time budget, and quality bar. Step four is redefining cadence itself: a two-week sprint built around "how much can five engineers type in ten days" stops being meaningful when a well-specified feature can go from brief to draft pull request in an afternoon. Teams that get this right do not abolish rhythm; they replace sprint-as-batch-size with sprint-as-checkpoint-for-judgment — a standing cadence for decisions only humans can make, layered over continuous shipping of agent-executable work.

Fig. 1 — Cycle time does not compress just because build time did. Left unmanaged, review absorbs the time build gave up.

4. A Worked Example

Kabir ran the arithmetic on one of his own squads, the one building trip-scheduling for fleet dispatchers, to see where the 11-to-8.5-day change had come from and whether a further change was available. Before agents, a typical feature moved through four stages: two days to write and align a spec, six days of engineering build, two days of review and testing, one day of release — eleven days total. After the squad adopted an agent for scaffolding and test generation, build time fell to about one and a half days, since the agent produced a working first draft, tests included, within hours of a clear spec. But review time rose from two days to four: reviewers were reading roughly three times the code volume, and two production incidents in July had made them more cautious. Spec and release were untouched. Total: 2 + 1.5 + 4 + 1 = 8.5 days — a real but disappointing 23% improvement against a build stage that individually got four times faster.

The second pass changed one input: instead of asking reviewers to read more code more carefully, the squad built an automated evaluation harness — scripted checks against the spec's acceptance criteria, run before a human opens the diff — that caught the two classes of regression the July incidents came from. With the harness doing the first pass, human review time fell from four days to one and a half, since reviewers were now checking judgment calls, not re-deriving whether code matched the spec. New total: 2 + 1.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 6 days, a 45% reduction from the original eleven. The lesson Kabir drew was that the win did not come from the agent typing faster; it came from moving the review bottleneck to where humans add the most value, which required building the harness — a deliberate investment, not a byproduct of buying agent licenses.

5. The Nuances

AI-native is a redesign, not a tool purchase

The distinction between AI-assisted and AI-native is the single most common thing leaders blur. Buying agent licenses changes nothing about cadence or ownership by itself; it only changes build speed, and as Kabir's numbers showed, build speed alone barely moves the metric that matters.

Vibe coding has a domain, and it is not production

Accepting agent output largely on faith is reasonable for a throwaway prototype. Carrying that same trust into a production pull request touching billing or fleet safety data is a category error, and teams that get burned usually never explicitly decided which mode they were in.

Throughput does not scale the ratio linearly

It is tempting to assume that if agents make engineers three times faster, one PM can support three times as many. In practice the constraint moves to review and integration, which do not get three times faster just because code arrives three times as fast, so the sustainable ratio shift is smaller than the raw speed-up suggests.

Cadence redesign is not cadence removal

Moving away from two-week sprints does not mean abandoning rhythm. It means separating the checkpoint humans need for judgment calls from the shipping cycle for agent-executable work, and keeping the former on a schedule even as the latter goes continuous.

An AI-native team cannot tell you if the feature was worth building

However well a team redesigns around agents, the redesign only accelerates execution of a decision; it says nothing about whether the decision was right. Shipping the wrong feature in six days instead of eleven just means finding out it was wrong five days sooner.

Codebase maturity changes the answer

Agents perform well against clean, loosely coupled code and considerably worse against a decade-old, tightly coupled legacy system, where a plausible-looking but wrong change is riskier. Design around the codebase a team actually has, not the one vendors demo against.

"AI-native" is often confused with "smaller"

The goal is reshaping where a team's time goes, not shrinking headcount. Some AI-native teams stay the same size and ship more; others hold output flat and redeploy freed time to work previously starved, such as customer discovery or technical debt.

Questions worth asking before relying on any of this

Who reviews agent-authored code, against what explicit standard? What happens when an agent's output passes its own tests but is subtly wrong — is there a rollback plan? And is anyone tracking the debt that accumulates specifically from agent-generated code, which tends to be locally correct and globally inconsistent?

6. Consumer, B2B, and Marketplace — and Early-Stage versus Large

In a consumer product, features tend to be small, reversible, and testable within days, so AI-native teams there lean hardest into agent speed: a PM asks for three onboarding variants and A/B tests them within a week, and the PM's time shifts from writing exhaustive specs toward designing the experiment that judges the output. In B2B software like Dastak's, releases are fewer and larger, customers hold uptime commitments, and the review bar must be correspondingly higher, because an agent-introduced regression does not show up in an A/B test — it shows up as a support ticket from a fleet operator whose trucks are not dispatching. B2B PMs spend agent-era time not on experiment design but on making specs exhaustive about edge cases, since an agent will happily build the happy path and skip the exception nobody mentioned. Marketplace products sit between the two: agents accelerate matching and ranking experiments, but anything touching trust and safety between the two sides usually keeps a human gate regardless of agent speed, because an error there erodes trust built over years.

Company stage matters as much as product type. At an early-stage startup, the founder or an early PM often prompts the agent personally with no separate review layer, since the cost of a wrong shortcut is a rewrite next quarter, not an escalation against a signed contract. At a company Dastak's size and larger, agent-authored code passes through the same release gates, security review, and audit trail as human-authored code, and the redesign has to reckon with senior engineers who reasonably do not yet trust a diff they did not watch get written — a cultural transition slower than the technical one.

7. Common Mistakes

Mistaking pull-request volume for delivery speed. The symptom is a dashboard that looks great — PRs up threefold — while spec-to-shipped time is flat or worse. The underlying error is assuming the bottleneck was always typing speed. The cheapest diagnostic is what Kabir ran: break cycle time into spec, build, review, and release, and see which segment absorbed the time the others gave up.

Treating agents as a reason to skip the spec. The symptom is rework: an engineer accepts an agent's first draft, ships it, and a customer finds a case the spec never covered. The underlying error is believing the agent "just knows" what was meant. The diagnostic is to sample ten recent agent-authored pull requests and count how many needed a second clarifying message before they were mergeable.

Keeping sprint ceremonies as ritual after they stop producing decisions. The symptom is planning meetings and stand-ups that persist even though work now ships continuously, producing status theatre rather than coordination. The underlying error is treating cadence as sacred rather than as a tool for surfacing judgment calls. The diagnostic: for each recurring meeting, ask what decision it produced last month; cut any that produced none.

Leaving PM headcount untouched while PM workload triples. The symptom is Kabir's own PMs logging 30-plus hours a week on specs and eyeing other jobs. The underlying error is assuming team-shape questions are purely an engineering concern. The diagnostic is tracking spec-writing hours per PM against features shipped; if that line rises while engineer build-hours fall, the redesign is incomplete.

8. What Good Looks Like

Six months after a comparable inflection point, a peer company's payments-infrastructure team had settled into a shape worth naming: pod size held at one PM and five engineers, unchanged, but a sixth role, a rotating "quality owner" drawn from the engineering bench, took responsibility for the evaluation harness and the first pass of every pull request. Sprint planning dropped from every two weeks to a monthly checkpoint focused solely on judgment calls — architecture trade-offs, ambiguous requirements, sequencing bets — while shipping ran continuously against a published review SLA of same-day for routine changes and 48 hours for anything touching money movement. The PM's spec template grew a mandatory section of explicit acceptance criteria the harness could check automatically, and the PM's own week rebalanced from 70% writing requirements to roughly 40% requirements and 30% defining and reviewing "done." Cycle time on that team fell from ten days to five, and, more tellingly, production incidents traced to shipped features fell too, because the redesign put more scrutiny, not less, on the stage that mattered.

9. What Kabir Decided

Kabir's recommendation to Dastak's board was neither "restructure everything" nor "wait and see." He proposed keeping each pod at five engineers per PM for now, since the arithmetic did not support a larger ratio until review time was under control, and asking the board to fund one new role per three pods — an engineer seconded part-time to build and own evaluation harnesses — rather than more PM headcount. He proposed retiring the sprint planning ritual in favour of a weekly judgment-call checkpoint over continuous release with an explicit review SLA, and rewriting the PM job description to name acceptance-criteria design as a core deliverable. He was explicit that this would not, by itself, tell the board whether trip-scheduling was the right feature to build next quarter; that judgment remained exactly as human, and exactly as hard, as before. The next things worth learning are how work actually divides between a PM, an engineer, and an agent once the pod is redrawn, and how to tell a genuine velocity gain from a velocity illusion when the dashboard says one thing and the calendar says another.

Two questions worth sitting with: if your team's pull-request count doubled next quarter, would you know within a week whether delivery got faster, or would you find out the way Kabir did, three months later, from a resignation letter? And what is the one review gate in your own product you would not want an agent's confidence to substitute for a human's judgment — and have you written that down anywhere a new hire could find it?

Pravega Systems: Deciding on AI-Native Pods

Bengaluru, Monday, 14 September 2026

Opening

Rohan Mehta, Vice-President of Product at Pravega Systems, read the Pune pod's retrospective note a third time before closing his laptop. The note said, in effect, that three engineers with AI coding agents had shipped a reconciliation module in five weeks that the roadmap had budgeted at eleven. It also said the module had gone to production without a design review and had produced two client-facing errors within a month. Rohan had four days. On Friday, 18 September, he had to send the board deck for Tuesday's meeting, where the CEO wanted a recommendation on whether Pravega's engineering organisation would move to "AI-native pods" for the whole Diwali-quarter roadmap — October to December — or hold the model to Pune alone. Whatever he recommended would set how thirteen product managers and sixty-two engineers worked for the next two quarters, and it would land in the middle of a renewal conversation with Pravega's largest Gulf account.

Company background

Pravega Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 to sell one product: Pravega OneLedger, a spend-and-expense platform for Indian mid-market companies. OneLedger issued RuPay-linked corporate cards through a partnership with ICICI Bank, captured employee spend in real time, and reconciled every invoice against GST input-tax-credit records so a finance team did not have to chase receipts at month-end. By September 2026 it served 480 companies — manufacturers, IT-services firms, and retail chains with 200 to 5,000 employees — for an annual recurring revenue of about ₹38 crore, growing 42 percent year on year. Its rivals were Zoho Expense and Happay in the mid-market, Fyle among smaller firms, and SAP Concur at the enterprise end where Pravega was trying to move next. Two institutional investors, including a Bengaluru growth-stage fund, had backed a Series B in 2024 on the promise that Pravega could out-build larger rivals on product velocity. That promise was now the board's standing question every quarter: was engineering shipping fast enough to justify the multiple.

The situation

In May, Priya Deshmukh, who led the Pune platform pod, had asked to pilot agentic coding tools — GitHub Copilot Workspace and Claude Code running against Pravega's own codebase — on a backlog item nobody wanted: rebuilding the GST reconciliation engine to handle multi-GSTIN clients. Her three engineers wrote specifications and reviewed diffs rather than typing most of the code themselves. The module shipped in five weeks. Pune stopped holding daily stand-ups after the second week; Priya moved to a twice-weekly async review instead, and started reviewing pull requests herself rather than routing them through a separate QA gate.

The trouble surfaced in August. Two multi-GSTIN clients reported reconciliation totals that did not match their books. Meera Krishnan, Pravega's data scientist in Toronto, traced it to an edge case the agents had generalised from majority-pattern training data: a rounding rule that held for single-GSTIN clients but silently misapplied to composite ones. Lukas Weber, the design lead in Berlin, separately flagged that the new reconciliation screen had shipped with three different date-format conventions because no one had run it past him before release. Farah Osman, the Singapore-based customer-success lead, was fielding calls from Prapti Retail Group, a Dubai-based retail conglomerate renewing its ₹2.1 crore annual contract in November, whose finance controller had asked, pointedly, whether Pravega's engineering process had changed. From New Jersey, sales head Derek Coleman wanted the whole engineering organisation moving at Pune's new pace, not just one pod, to counter SAP Concur on delivery speed in two live enterprise deals.

The people

Priya Deshmukh — Engineering Lead, Platform Pod, Pune
Wants the AI-native model adopted company-wide immediately. Argues the bugs were a review-process gap, not an argument against agents, and that Pravega cannot out-build SAP Concur without the throughput gain.
Lukas Weber — Design Lead, Berlin
Wants a mandatory design-review gate restored before any client-facing screen ships, regardless of how it was coded. Worried that removing ceremonies removed the checkpoints that used to catch this.
Meera Krishnan — Data Scientist, Toronto
Wants an evaluation suite built before agents touch financial-calculation logic again — she can build it, but not by Friday. Sees the rounding bug as a correctness problem, not a one-off.
Farah Osman — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Manages the Prapti Retail Group relationship and eleven other Gulf and APAC accounts. Wants slower, gated releases on anything touching client money until trust is rebuilt, even if that costs speed elsewhere.

Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows what the Pune pilot actually produced against Pravega's usual delivery pattern for a comparable module.

Exhibit 1 is the number Priya leads with: less than half the cost, less than half the time. It is also the number Meera and Lukas lead with, from the other direction — the rework line nearly erased the labour saving. Exhibit 2 sets the pilot against what is actually at stake in the renewal Farah is managing.

Exhibit 2 — Prapti Retail Group account, and Pravega's Q3 backlog exposure
