A quarter of the open backlog sits exactly where Meera and Farah are most nervous — financial logic that touches client money. Exhibit 3 sketches how the pilot changed what Priya's pod actually did day to day, which is the change Rohan has to decide whether to generalise.

The options

Option 1 — Roll out AI-native pods company-wide for the Diwali quarter. Rohan tells the board Pravega adopts Priya's model across all pods from October, trusting each pod lead to set its own review rhythm. Upside: answers Derek's competitive pressure and could unlock the roughly 55 percent velocity gain Exhibit 2 estimates. Cost: applies an unproven pattern to the fourteen financial-logic items in the backlog just as Farah is trying to rebuild trust with Prapti Retail Group, with no evaluation suite to catch the next rounding error before a client does.

Option 2 — Split the backlog by risk; phase the rollout. Rohan recommends AI-native pods for the 21 back-office and internal-tooling items immediately, while financial-logic and client-facing items keep the traditional cadence — design review, an evaluation gate Meera builds over six weeks, and QA sign-off — until that gate exists. Upside: captures most of the velocity gain where an error's downside is smallest, while protecting the accounts most exposed. Cost: a slower story for Derek's deals, and two visibly different ways of working inside one organisation.

Option 3 — Pause the wider rollout; keep the pilot contained to Pune. Rohan asks the board for one quarter to build the evaluation suite and a design-review checkpoint that fits an agent-assisted workflow, before extending the model further. Upside: no further exposure on financial-logic work while trust is rebuilt. Cost: forfeits most of the velocity gain this quarter, when Derek's deals are live now, and reads to engineering as proof that the pilot's cost outweighed its speed gain — which may not be the lesson Rohan believes is true.

Questions for discussion

  1. What did removing daily stand-ups and the separate QA gate actually change about what the Pune pod's PM owned — and was that change the cause of the defects, or a coincidence?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, is the pilot's net saving (labour minus rework) still positive? Does that answer change if the two defects had reached Prapti Retail Group's books instead of two smaller clients?
  3. Whose objection — Lukas's on design review, Meera's on evaluation, or Farah's on account risk — points at a gate that AI-native teams still need, and whose points at a ceremony that AI-native teams can safely drop?
  4. Which option best matches the backlog split in Exhibit 2, and what would Rohan need to tell Derek and the board to make that option sound like discipline rather than delay?

A note for the learner

The topic here is not whether agentic tools make engineers faster — Exhibit 1 already answers that. The topic is what changes in team shape and PM ownership once they do, and which of those changes a PM should accept versus resist. Vibe coding compresses the distance between a specification and working code, which is why Pune's stand-ups stopped mattering and why Priya, as PM-adjacent lead, ended up reading pull requests herself. That is a legitimate and probably permanent shift in what a PM owns: less status-reporting, more direct engagement with what the agent produced. But compressing that distance does not compress the need for a human check on correctness and design coherence — it relocates it. The mistake in the Pune pilot was not adopting agents; it was removing the design-review and QA gates at the same time, as if faster code generation also meant the judgment calls around it had become unnecessary.

A well-reasoned answer treats the backlog, not the organisation, as the unit of decision: where an error is low-cost and reversible, agent-assisted pods with light-touch review are the right shape, and the old ceremonies genuinely are waste. Where an error reaches a client's financial statements, as it did for Prapti Retail Group, the review gate is not agile theatre — it is the control keeping the speed gain from turning into a renewal risk. Option 2 is the defensible path: it extends the productivity case to most of the backlog now, keeps the traditional cadence exactly where Exhibit 2 shows the exposure concentrated, and gives Meera's evaluation work a real deadline. It costs Rohan a cleaner story for the board, but it is the story that survives the next reconciliation error.
case40v1-agile.kanban:
Tarazu Compliance Systems: The Queue Nobody Was Measuring

A teaching case on delivery process, demand and the shape of engineering work

1. Sunday night, Lower Parel

At a quarter past ten on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Devika Sundaram was still in the seventh-floor office of Tarazu Compliance Systems on Senapati Bapat Marg, Mumbai, with the monsoon's last rain on the glass and three browser windows open that refused to agree with each other. In the first was the Alerts and Surveillance squad's delivery record: sixty-two per cent of committed work delivered across eight sprints. In the second, a six-week experiment the same squad had run over Ganesh Chaturthi, which appeared to show cycle time halved. In the third, a spreadsheet Farhan Qureshi had sent at 9.40 p.m., counting regulatory circulars over thirty months, the notice period shrinking in every row.

At 9.30 the next morning Devika chaired the fortnightly delivery review. On 22 October she was due before the board with the FY27 second-half roadmap, and its newest member, a partner from the fund that led the Series B, had asked for something specific: dates, and the reason to believe them. Devika, forty-one and eleven years into shipping regulated software, could construct a defensible argument for three different answers, and had spent the evening noticing that each required her to disbelieve a different exhibit.

2. Tarazu Compliance Systems

Tarazu was founded in 2016 by Rohit Marathe, nine years a builder of trade-monitoring systems at a market infrastructure institution, and Chandrakant Pai, a chartered accountant who had run inspections for a broking house. Their thesis was simple: every SEBI-registered intermediary had to watch its own order flow for manipulation, report to the exchanges and depositories on a punishing calendar, and prove to an auditor that it had done so — and almost all were doing it with spreadsheets and a clerk. Tarazu sold a hosted surveillance engine that ingested order and trade feeds, raised alerts, managed the case file, and produced the regulatory submissions. By FY26 it had 43 Indian clients and seven in the Gulf, ARR of ₹71 crore, and 264 employees, 96 of them engineers across Mumbai, Pune and Bengaluru.

Two old decisions shaped everything Devika could now consider. The first was commercial. In 2021, to win a contested account against a larger incumbent, Pai had put a regulatory currency clause into the master agreement: any circular requiring a platform change would be delivered production-ready at least fifteen calendar days before the compliance date, failing which the client received a fee credit of four per cent of the quarterly licence fee per week of delay, capped at twenty-five per cent. The clause closed the deal, then became standard because it closed every deal, and by 2026 sat in 31 of 43 Indian contracts. The second was internal. In 2022, after a bad quarter of missed dates, the company standardised: every squad on two-week sprints, a quarterly planning day, and a roadmap published from it. The Jira configuration built for that decision now also produced the change-management evidence pack client auditors asked for at annual due diligence — each release traced to a sprint, an approval and a ticket. Nobody had designed that dependency; it had grown.

3. The industry

Indian capital markets had grown faster than the machinery that watched them. Demat accounts had multiplied, discount brokers such as Zerodha and Groww had brought in a generation of first-time traders, and SEBI and the exchanges had responded with a widening stream of obligations — surveillance thresholds, client-level risk disclosures, cyber-resilience audits. For a broker none of this was optional and none of it was revenue; it was the cost of a licence. That made Tarazu's category defensible and unforgiving at once: clients did not ask whether the product was delightful, but whether it would be ready before the compliance date, and whether the auditor would accept the evidence.

Competition came from three directions. Large services firms bid the same work as a managed engagement; two well-funded RegTech start-ups sold narrower, cheaper modules; and the exchanges and depositories periodically released utilities that absorbed a slice of what vendors charged for. Meanwhile the DPDP Act's consent and retention rules had begun to reach into how long Tarazu could hold client order data, a workstream nobody had priced.

The Gulf had been the growth story. In 2024 Tarazu opened a two-person desk in Dubai and won Lujain Capital Markets DMCC, a brokerage across the UAE and Saudi markets, on a ₹5.6 crore annual contract with its own reporting calendar and a separate incident SLA. Lujain was now the reference every prospect asked for, and renewed on 15 January 2027.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The platform group held three squads. Regulatory Reporting, seven engineers under a manager in Pune, built the submission engines against dates set by regulators. Client Integrations, six engineers, onboarded new feeds. Alerts and Surveillance, nine engineers in Bengaluru under Anjali Kulkarni, owned the detection engine, the case-management workflow, and — since a reorganisation in April 2025 nobody had revisited — first-line support for all fifty client environments.

Through FY26, Devika had believed three things: that the Alerts squad's miss rate was an estimation problem curable by better sizing; that regulatory work was the plannable part of the portfolio, since circulars carried compliance dates; and that the squads were comparable, so the healthy one showed what the sick one should do. Exhibit 1 had been read for a year as evidence for all three.

Each belief had since been damaged. In June 2026 Nikhil Menon, the analytics lead in Toronto, instrumented the board properly and produced Exhibit 2, which showed four kinds of work with wildly different natural durations moving through one two-week container — and, in its footnote, something Devika had not known: the clock everyone quoted began only when a card entered Analysis. In August, Farhan Qureshi's count of circulars (Exhibit 3) showed regulatory demand nearly doubling in thirty months while median notice fell from 57 days to 16. Plannable work with a shrinking planning horizon is a contradiction the sprint calendar had been quietly absorbing. And in September, Anjali's flow experiment (Exhibit 4) produced numbers so good that Devika distrusted them on sight — correctly, as its footnote suggests.

The fourth discovery arrived last and was the most awkward. On 2 October, preparing the board pack, Devika asked why two regulatory releases had slipped past the fifteen-day buffer. The answer had nothing to do with sprints. Every change touching order-feed handling had to pass exchange conformance certification in a mock-trading environment available only on Saturdays, and just two engineers — one in Pune, one in Bengaluru — held the credentials to run it. One had been on leave for three weeks in August.

5. The people

Devika Sundaram, VP Product and Delivery, Mumbai. Owns the recommendation and the board slide. Measured on ARR delivered against roadmap and on fee credits, which pull in opposite directions. Not saying: she designed the 2022 sprint standard herself, and a reversal will be read as an admission.

Harsh Vardhan Sinha, Head of Engineering, Pune. Runs all three squads. Position: the Alerts squad's problem is demand, not method, and no policy fixes nine engineers doing the work of thirteen. Incentive: he has approved headcount for four hires and wants them, not a process experiment. Not saying: he thinks Anjali's pilot was run to produce a result.

Anjali Kulkarni, Engineering Manager, Alerts and Surveillance, Bengaluru. Ran the pilot. Position: WIP limits and an expedite lane made her squad visibly faster and measurably calmer. Incentive: three of her nine engineers resigned in twelve months and she is trying to keep the remaining six. Not saying: she knows the pilot overlapped a feature freeze, and left that out of the summary she circulated.

Farhan Qureshi, Head of Compliance Solutions, Mumbai. Former exchange inspector; classifies every circular and owns the regulatory-currency promise in practice. Position: unpredictable arrival is exactly why a fixed rhythm must be protected — the cadence is the only thing that forces triage. Incentive: fee credits are reported against his function. Not saying: two FY27 items in his own Exhibit 3 turned out not to affect the platform, and he has not reissued the count.

Katarina Brandt, Product Designer, Berlin. Supports both squads. Position: she needs to know when a design will reach a client, because compliance officers are trained on screens weeks in advance. Not saying: she has stopped starting Alerts work until an engineer is already free, which quietly removes design from the measured cycle time.

Nikhil Menon, Analytics Lead, Toronto. Built the instrumentation behind Exhibits 2 and 4. Position: neither sprints nor flow is the question; the group is not measuring the segment of the queue where the time goes. Not saying: the intake queue he discovered is largely populated by Farhan's team, and he has not said so in front of Farhan.

Wei-Lin Chua, Customer Success Lead, APAC and Gulf, Singapore. Owns Lujain day to day. Position: incidents must move the hour they arrive; the rest is engineering preference. Incentive: a ₹5.6 crore renewal sits on her number. Not saying: she has been granting Lujain informal priority for months by messaging Anjali's engineers directly, which is part of why sprint commitments keep failing.

Gregory Marsh, Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Selling to two US broker-dealers. Position: the dated roadmap is his product; probabilistic forecasts are unsellable. Incentive: commission on deals worth ₹9.2 crore of first-year value. Not saying: he has already shown prospects a Q4 date for a feature in no squad's plan.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the record both camps quote. Harsh reads it as understaffing, Anjali as work-mix, Devika as estimation.

8. The options as Devika currently frames them

Option A — Flow for Alerts, cadence for Reporting

Move the Alerts squad permanently to a pull system with stage-level work-in-progress limits and a capped expedite lane for P1 incidents and Lujain escalations; leave Regulatory Reporting on sprints, where dates are externally fixed. The argument: match the process to the arrival pattern of the work. The visible costs: the audit evidence pack is generated from sprint records, Gregory loses dated commitments for a third of the group, and Harsh will read a split as a verdict on his management. The cost she cannot see is whether two processes meeting at one interface simply create a new queue between them.

Option B — Keep the cadence, add a regulatory-response pod

Fund five engineers whose only job is circular-driven change and incidents, at ₹2.9 crore a year, and let the squads plan undisturbed. This preserves the audit trail and Gregory's roadmap, and answers Farhan directly. It also assumes arrival volume is roughly stable — which Exhibit 3 contradicts and Exhibit 6 complicates — and the board approved four heads, not five, against a break-even plan.

Option C — Flow across the whole platform group

Move all three squads to continuous flow, replace roadmap dates with percentile forecasts from throughput, and rebuild the evidence pack around releases rather than sprints. Internally coherent, and the only option that touches intake. It also asks the company to renegotiate how it proves compliance to auditors in the quarter of the Lujain renewal, and asks Gregory to sell differently while two deals are live.

Devika had written the three options on a page and then, at half past nine, added a fourth line and left it unanswered: none of these changes who can run a Saturday mock session, or who decides what enters the queue.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

  • Delivery review, 9.30 a.m., Monday 12 October 2026; board meeting, 22 October, with an FY27 H2 roadmap.
  • Next platform-affecting compliance date: 30 November 2026 — production-ready by 15 November under the clause, across 31 contracts.
  • Lujain renewal, 15 January 2027; two Indian renewals worth ₹3.1 crore in the same window, both citing the clause.
  • Client auditors have requested the change-management evidence pack for January due diligence; it is produced from sprint records.
  • Approved headcount: four engineers, ₹1.6 crore. FY27 plan requires ARR of ₹78 crore at break-even.
  • Exchange conformance certification runs in Saturday mock sessions; two credentialled engineers; training a third takes an estimated eleven weeks.
  • Time zones: Singapore opens the day, Bengaluru and Pune hold the middle, Berlin overlaps four hours, Toronto and New Jersey close it. Lujain's heaviest settlement activity falls on Sunday.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What does Exhibit 1 actually measure, and what would you need to know before treating the gap between the two squads as evidence about process?
2. Exhibits 2 and 6 both describe the same squad's work. Where do they disagree, and which footnote changes your reading the most?
3. Anjali's pilot (Exhibit 4) is confounded in at least three ways. Can any part of it still serve as evidence, and for what claim?
4. Farhan argues that unpredictable arrival is an argument for a fixed cadence, not against it. Build the strongest version of that case, then the strongest rebuttal.
5. If the binding constraint is the two certified engineers and the Saturday mock session, what happens to each of the three options — and is the option set itself the wrong frame?
6. What should Devika do at 9.30 on Monday, and what should she tell the board on 22 October — including what she will stop promising, and what evidence by January would prove she chose wrongly?

11. Sunday night, continued

At eleven Devika typed a message to Anjali, deleted it, and typed one to Nikhil instead, asking how long it would take to measure the intake queue properly. The reply came from Toronto within a minute — mid-afternoon there — and said: three weeks, but you are deciding in one. She looked again at the two exhibits she trusted least, and at the one nobody argued with: ₹41 lakh of credits in six months against ₹19 lakh in the whole year before. Outside, the traffic on Senapati Bapat Marg had thinned. The meeting was in ten and a half hours, and she still did not know whether she was being asked to change a process, buy capacity, or admit the company had sold a promise it never engineered the ability to keep.
case20v1-agile.kanban:
Unmesh Systems: When Sprints Stop Fitting the Work

A teaching case on Kanban, flow and the limits of sprint planning

1. The Monday morning problem

It was 8:40 a.m. on Monday, 21 September 2026, and Aniket Ghosh, VP of Engineering at Unmesh Systems, stood before a whiteboard at Prestige Tech Park on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road. On it, from that morning's retrospective, was a single number: 47%. That was the share of committed work the Dispatch Engine squad had delivered in the sprint just ended — the third sub-50% sprint in four. By Friday, 25 September, Aniket owed the CEO a recommendation on the squad's process, ahead of the company's Q4 planning offsite on 1 October. Q4 carried Diwali order surges and the November renewal of its first international contract, with a quick-commerce operator in Dubai. Aniket had run engineering teams on two-week sprints for a decade. He was no longer sure sprints fit the team in front of him.

2. Unmesh Systems

Unmesh Systems was founded in 2019 in Bengaluru by two IIT Bombay classmates who had watched quick-commerce grow without most operators building their own delivery logic. Giants like Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart owned their routing stacks end to end; the long tail of regional grocery and pharmacy challengers did not. Unmesh sold them a real-time driver-allocation and routing engine, an API plugged into a client's own app, so a client could offer ten-minute delivery without building the optimisation itself. By FY26 Unmesh had about 30 clients, roughly 46 engineers, and ₹42 crore in annual recurring revenue. It competed for the buy-versus-build decision against LoadShare's platform arm and Shadowfax's enterprise APIs, and increasingly against ONDC-network logistics participants, which lowered client switching costs. In FY25 Unmesh closed its first contract outside India — Mirsal Quick Commerce, a Dubai-headquartered operator expanding across the UAE and Saudi Arabia — which Robert Klein, the company's New Jersey-based sales head, was using as his reference story for two U.S. prospects.

3. What had changed under the squad's feet

The eight-engineer Dispatch Engine squad, led by engineering manager Priyanka Deshmukh out of Pune, had run two-week Scrum sprints since the company's earliest days, and for years that had worked: a stable backlog, planned ahead, delivered on a predictable cadence. Over FY26 the squad's job quietly changed without its process changing with it. It still built routing features, but had also become first responder for production incidents across all 30 client integrations, and primary technical contact for Mirsal's service-level agreement. Sprint reliability collapsed, and Exhibit 1 shows the pattern: committed-to-completed delivery swinging between 47% and 91%, driven almost entirely by how many unplanned "interrupt" tickets got pulled into a sprint already planned around feature work.

Meera Iyer, the Toronto-based data scientist supporting the squad part-time, had pulled a cycle-time breakdown by work type for August (Exhibit 2), showing three different kinds of work forced through one box: routine features that could wait weeks, incidents needing hours, and Mirsal's escalations between the two. Sarah Tan, Singapore-based customer success lead for Unmesh's APAC and Gulf accounts, had fielded three escalation calls from Mirsal's operations head in six weeks, each about a P1 bug past the contract's 24-hour target because its owner was mid-sprint and mid-cycle reprioritising was awkward. Robert Klein, watching from New Jersey, wanted nothing to disturb Mirsal before its November renewal. Lukas Weber, the Berlin-based designer handing off UI work, had a quieter complaint: he could no longer predict when a design would ship.

4. The people around the decision

Priyanka Deshmukh, Engineering Manager, Pune. Priyanka led the eight engineers and ran the retrospective behind the 47% number. She was tired of a ritual that manufactured disappointment: her team planned honestly, got interrupted constantly, then sat through a ceremony that framed the interruption as a failure to estimate. She wanted a process that admitted interrupts were normal, but worried about losing the discipline sprints gave her newer engineers.

Meera Iyer, Data Scientist, Toronto. Meera cared about the numbers, not the ideology. She was quietly convinced a two-week box was the wrong unit for work whose true durations ranged from ninety minutes to eleven days, and wanted whatever Aniket chose to keep producing measurable flow data, not trade one unmeasured ritual for another.

Sarah Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Sarah owned the Mirsal relationship day to day and absorbed its frustration first. She wanted a guarantee that P1 issues would move immediately, without waiting for a sprint boundary to make room. She cared less about engineering ritual than about never making another apology call.

Robert Klein, Sales Head, New Jersey. Robert needed two things in tension: a bullet-proof Mirsal renewal, and a roadmap he could show two U.S. prospects with dates he could stand behind. He was wary of any change engineering called "experimental" this close to renewal, which pulled him toward keeping something sprint-shaped.

5. The evidence

Exhibit 1 shows the squad's last eight sprints. Only twice did the team clear 90% of its commitment; in the other six, interrupt volume explains almost all of the shortfall.

Domestic contracts carry no penalty clause; Mirsal's contract, worth ₹3.4 crore annually and up for renewal in November 2026, penalises 2% of the monthly fee per hour a P1 breach runs past target, capped at 20%.

Exhibit 3 sketches Priyanka's alternative: a continuous flow board with a capped WIP limit at each stage and a separate expedite lane for P1 incidents and Mirsal escalations, able to jump the queue without a planning ceremony.

Exhibit 3 — the board format Priyanka circulated at the retrospective, adapted from her own reading of the squad's cycle-time data.

6. Aniket's options

Option A — Move the Dispatch Engine squad to Kanban, with an expedite lane

Aniket could approve Priyanka's board for her squad alone: no sprint boundaries, WIP limits at each stage, a capped expedite lane letting P1 incidents and Mirsal escalations jump the queue without a planning meeting. Upside: the squad's real bottleneck becomes visible and capped, and Sarah gets a standing answer for Mirsal — incidents move now. Cost: Robert loses sprint-shaped dates for this squad, and Aniket needs a throughput-based forecast sales has never used.

Option B — Keep sprints, add a protected "firefighting" capacity buffer

Aniket could leave Scrum in place but have Priyanka reserve a fixed share of each sprint — say 30% of points — for unplanned work. Least disruptive, and it kept Robert's cadence intact. But interrupt load already swung between two and eleven tickets a sprint; a buffer sized for the average still blows through in bad sprints, and does nothing for Sarah's problem — a mid-sprint P1 still waits for the next planning slot.

Option C — Roll Kanban out to all of engineering immediately

Aniket could treat this as company-wide and move all of engineering — including squads delivering client integrations on fixed dates — onto flow boards at once, for consistency. This solves Dispatch Engine's problem, but applies an interrupt-driven fix to squads whose real problem is coordinated, date-committed delivery — and means retraining the whole organisation under deadline pressure with no evidence the change works anywhere at Unmesh.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What does Exhibit 1 tell you about the source of the squad's problem — estimation, capacity, or work-mix?
2. Using Exhibit 2, which work type genuinely suits sprint planning, and which does not — why does forcing all three through one two-week box produce Exhibit 1's pattern?
3. For Priyanka, Sarah, Robert and Meera, would Option A, B or C serve their interest best? Where do those interests conflict, and where do they align?
4. Should the recommendation apply to Dispatch Engine alone, or to all of engineering? What evidence would justify extending it?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on one distinction: sprints fit work arriving in plannable batches, protected from interruption; Kanban's flow model — WIP limits, cycle time, throughput — fits work arriving unpredictably, needing to move faster than a sprint boundary allows. Exhibit 2 is the diagnostic tool: three work types, three natural cycle times, one forced-fit process. A well-reasoned answer starts from that mismatch, not a general preference for one methodology.

The defensible path is Option A, scoped to Dispatch Engine only. The squad's own data justifies it: interrupt volume, not poor estimation, explains Exhibit 1's collapse, and an expedite lane with a hard WIP limit directly answers Sarah's and Mirsal's complaint — urgent work waiting for a ceremony. Meera's flow metrics replace sprint velocity like for like, so losing a sprint-shaped date is a reporting change, not an information loss. Option C should wait: no evidence shows Kanban fits squads doing scheduled, batchable work, and forcing one mechanic on every team repeats Dispatch Engine's error in reverse. Option B fails because it treats a structural mismatch as a sizing problem: no buffer survives a sprint with eleven interrupts. The discipline Priyanka fears losing does not vanish under Kanban — it moves from protecting a sprint boundary to protecting WIP limits, a different rigour, not less of one.

Kanban and Flow: Queues, Batches and the Limits of the Board

Delivery & Technology — Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration · near-expert depth

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On Thursday 6 February 2025, Tanvi Deshpande, Director of Product for the Merchant Platform group at Odhani Commerce Cloud in Bengaluru, was asked a question she could answer three ways and defend all three. Odhani ran a multi-tenant storefront and checkout platform for about 900 direct-to-consumer brands; its largest new logo, Nagara Foods, had signed a ₹3.4 crore contract conditional on migrating off a legacy stack before Diwali. Her chief revenue officer wanted a date in writing that afternoon.

Tanvi's checkout squad had abandoned sprints fourteen months earlier. Over the previous ninety days it had completed 142 items with a median cycle time of four days. She could have said "four days an item, thirty-four left, done in five weeks" and been applauded. She did not, because the eighty-fifth percentile of the same distribution was nineteen days and the ninety-fifth forty-one, and the average was 9.6 days — above the seventieth percentile. That is the signature of a strongly right-skewed distribution: the number everyone quoted described almost none of the actual work.

Six weeks later, Devika Menon, VP Product at Mrinal Imaging Devices in Hyderabad, argued the opposite case. Mrinal built portable ultrasound carts for diagnostic chains — its anchor account, Onkaar Diagnostics, ran ninety centres across Tamil Nadu and Kerala — plus a cloud reporting layer for remote reads. The cloud layer shipped every Tuesday; the firmware did not. As safety-classified code inside a licensed medical device, every release triggered a verification cycle costing eleven days of Mrinal's regulatory and QA pair and about ₹6 lakh. Her engineering director wanted "one-piece flow end to end." She thought that right for half her system and expensively wrong for the rest.

Both decisions turn on one claim, and it is not about boards. It is a proposition about queues: where work arrives irregularly through shared capacity, the dominant cost is not how fast anyone works but how long things wait, and waiting is governed by utilisation, variability and batch size, steeply non-linearly. The board is kanban's cheapest instrument, not its content.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Precisely stated: a kanban system is a pull system in which a downstream step signals upstream capacity, the work permitted inside is explicitly bounded, and that bound — not a calendar or a manager's allocation — determines when new work starts. Everything else filed under "kanban" is measurement the bound makes possible, or policy that makes it survivable.

The lineage has three trunks. Taiichi Ohno's work at Toyota from the late 1940s produced the card system, but the more transferable insight was Shigeo Shingo's on setup reduction: Toyota did not simply choose smaller batches, it spent years driving down changeover cost until small batches became economic. The second trunk is queueing theory, supplying Little's Law and Kingman's approximation. The third is the translation into knowledge work: the Poppendiecks' Lean Software Development (2003), David J. Anderson's Kanban Method (2010), Donald Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009), and the flow-metrics school around Daniel Vacanti. A PM who cannot tell these apart referees delivery arguments badly.

SchoolWill signWill not sign
Anderson / Kanban MethodStart with what you do now; change evolves under a WIP constraint. Classes of service and explicit policies are the mechanism.Reorganising teams or imposing cadence before the data justifies it.
Reinertsen / flow economicsEvery queue has a quantified cost of delay; batch size and utilisation are the high-leverage variables.Any practice, WIP limits included, justified by itself rather than by economics.
Vacanti / flow metricsForecast probabilistically from throughput history; percentiles and aging WIP are the instruments.That velocity or story points carry forecasting information worth the effort.
Scrum / cadence campA timebox is a forcing function: closure, a fixed feedback interval, a social contract flow dissolves.That cadence is a symptom of transaction costs and should vanish as they fall.
Scaled-cadence campAcross many teams, synchronisation beats local optimisation.That teams should pull independently when their work is entangled.

Drawn to be mutually exclusive where the schools conflict. Most practitioners hold a mixture, few consciously.

The sharpest live disagreement is between the second and fourth rows. Reinertsen's position is that cadence is an artifact: you batch because a transaction costs something, and as that cost falls the optimal batch falls toward one, leaving the calendar nothing to do. The cadence camp answers that some transaction costs are irreducibly social, and a team without a heartbeat loses the ability to stop and change direction.

3. Mechanics in depth: what the instruments actually say

Tanvi's squad had a board. What it lacked until February was a cumulative flow diagram: for every day, the cumulative count of items entering each state. Three quantities read off its geometry.

Odhani's checkout squad. Vertical distance is work in progress; horizontal distance is approximate lead time; the lower curve's slope is throughput.

The vertical gap is the work inside the system that day; the horizontal gap is roughly how long an item entering then waited — roughly, because it assumes first-in-first-out, which real teams violate. Little's Law — average work in progress equals average throughput times average cycle time — states only that these readings are not independent. Its assumptions are usually left implicit and matter: rough steady state, conservation of arrivals and departures, consistent units. Tanvi's squad held 28 items at 3.6 departures a week: an average cycle time of 7.8 weeks. The board said four days. Both were true.

The second instrument is the distribution itself, not its mean.

Odhani checkout squad, 142 items, 90 daysCycle time (days)
50th percentile (median)4
70th percentile8
85th percentile19
95th percentile41
Arithmetic mean9.6
Flow efficiency (active ÷ elapsed)18%

A mean above the 70th percentile is the signature of a long right tail; the mean is not a forecast.

Flow efficiency — the fraction of elapsed time in which anyone was touching the item — changes behaviour most: 18% means that if every engineer worked twice as fast, the median item would go from four days to about 3.6. Hiring does not touch the other four-fifths; removing a handoff does.

Why queues behave so violently is Kingman's approximation: waiting at a shared resource is three terms multiplied — utilisation, ρ ÷ (1 − ρ); variability, the average squared coefficient of variation of arrivals and service; and mean service time. Odhani's payments review was done by one pair, took two days, and had Poisson-like variability, so the middle term was about 1.

Kingman's approximation at Odhani's review pair, mean service two days: 80% to 95% loaded multiplies waiting nearly fivefold.

At 75% utilisation the wait was six days; at 85%, 11.3; at 95%, thirty-eight. That arithmetic explains why the managerial instinct to keep expensive specialists busy is the most reliable way to destroy delivery speed. It also exposes a second lever most teams never use: cutting the squared coefficient of service-time variation from 1.0 to 0.25 — done at Odhani by splitting reviews into a fast path for configuration changes and a slow one for anything touching money — multiplies waiting by 0.625, worth about as much as unloading the pair ten points.

The third instrument answers Tanvi's question: a Monte Carlo simulation samples weekly throughput history repeatedly to give a distribution of completion dates for the 34 remaining Nagara Foods items, from twenty-six observations averaging 3.8 a week.

The deterministic average and the fiftieth percentile coincide, which is the lesson: dividing remaining work by average throughput gives a date you miss half the time — a wager at even odds, presented as a plan.

4. When the claim holds, and when it misleads

"Flow beats sprints here" decomposes into four testable claims. First, work arrives in a pattern the team does not control — true for Tanvi's squad, roughly 40% merchant-triggered; false for firmware, planned quarters ahead. Second, items are small and independent enough that finishing one has value — true at Odhani, false for firmware, where no change reaches a customer without a verified release. Third, the transaction cost of delivering is low relative to an item's value: Odhani's minutes, Mrinal's ₹6 lakh. Fourth, the dominant cost is queueing rather than coordination — true for one squad, much less so across eleven with entangled dependencies.

The idea misleads where cycle time is dominated by learning rather than waiting. A discovery spike, a model-architecture experiment, a regulatory negotiation: their variance is irreducible, and placing them under the same WIP limit as ordinary delivery yields either a violated limit or a fiction in which the hard thing splits into small cards that flow beautifully while the question stays unanswered. Mrinal's verification cycle was not a queue to shorten but a process step with a floor; calling it waste was a category error.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Regulated software is the cleanest edge case because the constraint is legible. Mrinal's firmware sits under a CDSCO device licence and the IEC 62304 lifecycle standard; a change to safety-classified code requires verification evidence however small. The release transaction cost is genuinely fixed, and the right response is Shingo's — attack the setup cost — not shrinking batches while the cost stays put. Mrinal's automated verification suite cut per-release cost from ₹6 lakh to ₹3 lakh; only then did frequent releases become economic.

Hardware adds irreversibility: a printed-circuit revision has a fabrication lead time and a minimum order quantity, and no WIP limit changes that. Mature hardware-software companies run two coupled flow systems at different clock speeds, with a contract stating which software capabilities may assume which hardware revision. Companies claiming a single unified cadence are usually running software on hardware's clock and calling the idleness "alignment."

Marketplaces split by queue rather than by team. At Odhani, merchant onboarding, catalogue ingestion and trust-and-safety review are pure flow problems — a fraudulent listing cannot wait for a planning meeting — while ranking and pricing are experiment-gated, where flow metrics mean little because cycle time is set by the run length statistical power demands. AI-native products push further: training and evaluation runs are fixed-duration batches and "done" is a threshold on an eval suite, not a state transition, which strains the card model itself.

The seams are where mature companies differ most from what they publish. Cross-team dependency queues appear on no board; an item can show four days of squad cycle time and ninety of end-to-end lead time because it spent eighty-six in another group's intake. The honest handling is one measure of customer-visible lead time crossing every boundary, owned high enough that no team can define it away. The common one is flawless local metrics while the enterprise slows each quarter.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Percentiles, not averages, are the unit of promise. The tell is an expert who, asked how long something takes, answers with two numbers and a probability. The obvious reading — average as typical case — fails because software cycle times are almost universally right-skewed: the average sits above most of the mass and below the tail that causes escalations.

Aging work in progress beats completed cycle time as a signal. Cycle time is a post-mortem; by the time it is measured the damage is done. Experts look daily at how long each in-flight item has aged against the squad's percentile lines, because that is actionable now. The tell is a standup that takes the oldest card first, not person by person.

A WIP limit is a decision-forcing device, not a throughput lever. Its value is converting "should we start this?" from a private preference into a public, uncomfortable moment. The tell is whether anyone can name an occasion it stopped them; teams never stopped have a label, not a limit.

Blocked time must be measured separately or the data lies. An item showing nine days of cycle time, seven of them blocked on a vendor, teaches nothing about the team. Experts tag blockage the moment it starts; the diagnostic is whether the team can say what fraction of last month's elapsed time was blocked.

Classes of service are a pricing mechanism, not a courtesy. An expedite lane works only if using it is costly — it must displace something visible and named. The tell is a team that can point at the item pushed aside for the last expedite. Where expediting is free it becomes the default.

Batch size is usually a transaction-cost problem in disguise. Teams batch because releasing is painful. The expert response is to instrument that pain and reduce it rather than exhort people toward smaller batches; the reading that large batches mean weak discipline is wrong as often as right.

Utilisation and flow targets conflict, and one must be explicitly subordinate. A finance function measuring engineering by allocated utilisation defeats any WIP discipline, because the non-linearity in Kingman's formula is invisible on a cost line. The tell is whether the delivery leader has ever defended deliberate slack in a budget review and won.

Flow makes visible work fast and invisible work invisible. The most dangerous property of a well-running kanban system is that it optimises what is on cards. Architecture, deferred maintenance and unanswered discovery questions have no card, age silently, and surface eighteen months later as a rewrite. The tell is an expert who audits what is not on the board.

Aging work in progress at Odhani on 6 February: each dot an in-flight item, plotted by state and age against the squad's historical percentiles. Two had passed the 95th; neither had been discussed in a standup.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer software the difference is real and large: intake is dominated by experiment results and incident traffic, items are independent, deployment nearly free, so flow dominates and cadence survives only as a communication ritual. In B2B software serving a few large accounts, as at Odhani, the interrupt pattern is similar but promises are contractual, raising the value of probabilistic forecasting well above its consumer value — the point is not speed but saying a date and being right. In enterprise software with annual procurement, the external clock is so slow that internal cadence barely reaches the customer.

Hardware is where the difference is most often overstated: the software portion of a hardware company can and usually should flow, and the mistake is letting the hardware clock govern both. In AI products the unit of work is often a fixed-duration run, so throughput forecasting works while cycle-time reduction does not; forecast from completed evaluation cycles, not cards.

By stage: below roughly fifteen engineers, coordination happens by conversation and any explicit system is overhead. Between fifteen and a hundred, WIP discipline is the highest-return process investment available, because this is where everyone is nominally working on everything. Above a few hundred the binding constraint becomes between-team dependency, and the argument becomes whether synchronisation should be scheduled or pulled — genuinely unsettled.

8. Three worked cases

Odhani checkout: the limit was not the intervention

Tanvi's squad tightened its in-progress limit from an effective 28 items to 9 and required any item blocked over two days to be escalated by name at 10 a.m. Over the quarter, throughput rose from 3.6 to 4.1 items a week and eighty-fifth-percentile cycle time fell from 19 days to 8. Little's Law reconciles it: 28 ÷ 3.6 is 7.8 weeks, 9 ÷ 4.1 is 2.2. Tanvi's reading: a third of the gain from the limit, two-thirds from the blocked-item policy the limit had made impossible to ignore.

Mrinal firmware: the economics of the batch

Devika modelled release cadence as a batch-size problem. Mrinal generated about 48 firmware-affecting changes a year, each release cost ₹6 lakh in verification, and delay was costed at ₹40,000 per change per month from support load and deferred revenue on Onkaar's calibration fix. The economic batch quantity — the square root of twice annual demand times transaction cost, over annual holding cost — came to 11 changes, 4.4 releases a year, at ₹52.6 lakh.

The table carries the section's argument. Monthly releases without touching verification cost would have raised total cost 42% while feeling like progress. Halving setup cost first, and only then shortening the cycle, cut it 29%. Batch size is downstream of transaction cost; practitioners who reverse that order make things worse and cannot explain why.

Mausam Money: where it failed

Mausam Money, a Mumbai digital lender operating through an RBI-registered NBFC, moved nine squads off sprints onto kanban boards in early 2023. Within two quarters every squad reported an eighty-fifth-percentile cycle time under six days. Meanwhile the loan-origination rewrite, the year's one strategic commitment, slipped seven months and missed the co-lending launch window, at about ₹4.2 crore of engineering spend against no revenue.

Two mechanisms. First, the rewrite had been decomposed into sixty small cards that each flowed beautifully, so no artifact showed an aging item; the work was invisible because it was well-groomed. End-to-end lead time to anything customer-visible was 94 days and flow efficiency 7%, but nobody measured either, because every board measured only its own segment. Second, removing the sprint boundary removed the one moment at which nine squads looked at each other's dependencies; those did not disappear, they queued invisibly.

The recovery, eight months later, was not a return to sprints. Mausam kept flow inside squads, reintroduced a four-week cadence used only for cross-squad integration and dependency clearing — not for delivery commitments — and instituted one end-to-end lead-time measure owned by the CTO's office. The formula was "cadence for coordination, flow for delivery," which the organisation's flow purists never accepted.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Kanban theatre. Early sign: a column holding more items than the number above it, unremarked. Diagnostic: when was someone last refused permission to start? Caught late, the team has two years of flow data describing a push system, and every forecast built on it is worthless.

Local optimisation at the seams. Early sign: every team's metrics improve while customers report no change. Diagnostic: elapsed time from request to value, measured outside the teams. Caught late, this is Mausam's ₹4.2 crore.

Expedite inflation. Early sign: expedited items climb past one in seven completed. Diagnostic: name the item displaced by the most recent expedite. Caught late, the class-of-service system has quietly ceased to exist and reinstating it costs political capital.

Forecasting from averages. Early sign: dates quoted as single numbers with no confidence attached. Diagnostic: at what probability is this date? Caught late, missed commitments read as an engineering problem rather than a statistics problem, and the remedy applied is pressure.

Dropping the replenishment discipline. Early sign: the input queue grows unordered and pull goes to whoever shouts. Diagnostic: who ordered the next five items, on what basis? Caught late, the team flows the wrong work with admirable efficiency.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does cadence carry independent value? The flow position at its strongest: every benefit of a timebox belongs to some underlying practice — feedback, closure, stakeholder contact — obtainable on its own schedule; the timebox bundles them, and bundling is batching. The cadence position at its strongest: organisations reliably fail to do unscheduled things, and a heartbeat is the cheapest commitment device available. Each would be refuted by a clean finding the other cannot explain; the field has produced none, because the interventions are never isolated.

Are estimates worth producing once throughput data exists? The flow-metrics position is that counting items forecasts at least as well as sizing them, well supported for homogeneous work. The opposition concedes that and defends estimation on other grounds: estimating surfaces scope disagreements that otherwise stay hidden until implementation. Settling it needs evidence on rework rates, not forecast accuracy, and that evidence is thin.

Should WIP limits be set to pain or to economics? Anderson's tradition tightens until the system complains, treating discomfort as the signal. Reinertsen's objects that pain is not a currency and the limit should follow from the cost of delay and of idle capacity. The disagreement shows in how each reads a briefly idle team: one sees the system working, the other an untested limit.

Is evolutionary adoption humane or conservative? "Start with what you do now" is the Kanban Method's most contested commitment. Critics argue it preserves dysfunctional role structures by never confronting them; defenders reply that imposed reorganisations have a worse record, and the WIP limit forces the confrontation eventually anyway. Settling it needs longitudinal data three years after adoption, which almost nobody collects.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied flow installs a board, writes numbers above columns, and reports cycle time in a monthly deck. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They quote dates as percentiles and refuse to collapse them. They treat idle capacity as evidence the system is working, and can defend that in a budget conversation. They look first at the oldest item in flight, and ask what is not on the board at all. Most tellingly, they can name the parts of their own system the flow argument does not cover — the regulated release, the fixed-duration experiment, the irreducible learning problem — and manage those by different rules without apologising.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Tanvi took the eighty-fifth percentile — twelve weeks — to her CRO, with the fourteen-week figure and the statement that the nine-week number everyone used was a coin flip. She also proposed the fast-path review split, variability being cheaper to attack than load. Nagara Foods went live eleven weeks later. What persuaded the CRO was not the forecast's accuracy, unknowable in advance, but that it carried a probability and a named condition for cutting scope.

Devika declined one-piece flow for firmware, accepted it for the cloud layer, and reframed her engineering director's ambition as a setup-reduction programme: eighteen funded months of automated verification with requirement traceability, after which the economic cadence would fall from quarterly to every two months on its own arithmetic. She kept one end-to-end measure — days from a confirmed Onkaar field issue to the fix installed on a cart — the only number crossing both clocks.

For discussion

Tanvi's squad improved chiefly because of a blocked-item policy, not the WIP limit. If that is generally true, what is a WIP limit for, and how would you test your answer on your own team?

Devika treated the verification cost as a variable to attack rather than a constraint to accommodate. When is that the wrong instinct, and how would you recognise it before spending eighteen months?

Mausam Money's squads all had excellent local metrics while the strategic commitment slipped seven months. Who in your organisation owns a number that would have caught that, and what would creating one cost?

13. Going deeper

Agile in practice supplies the iteration model flow displaces; without it section 10 has one side. The software development lifecycle matters next because flow efficiency is set by the handoffs it defines. The execution rhythm turns cadence-versus-flow into a calendar decision. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing unlocks the estimation disagreement, including what sizing buys that counting does not. Backlog management and refinement governs the replenishment discipline whose absence is the fifth failure mode above. Definition of done fixes where the departure curve is drawn, and therefore every number here. The PM–engineering relationship is the precondition: WIP limits survive only where a PM can be told no and treat it as information.

Kanban and Flow

Delivery & Technology — Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

A director of engineering runs out of sprints

Kabir Rao, Director of Engineering at Drishya Systems, a 140-person Pune-based firm that built warehouse and inventory-management software for mid-sized manufacturers, was looking at the sprint burndown chart on a Tuesday in the second week of March 2024 and doing arithmetic he already knew the answer to. The team had committed to thirty-four story points at the start of the sprint. Twenty-three remained undone with four working days left. This was the fourth sprint in five where the team would close somewhere between sixty and seventy percent of what it had promised.

The gap was not effort. Kabir's nine engineers were, if anything, overworked. The gap was a production line: Drishya's largest customer, Ekavira Motors, an auto-components manufacturer in Aurangabad, was running Drishya's warehouse software through a difficult quarter-end, and every barcode-scanning failure or stock-mismatch alert from their factory floor landed on Kabir's team as an unplanned, same-day fix. Ekavira's ₹1.8 crore annual contract was up for renewal in April, and the renewal conversation increasingly turned on reliability, not features. Kabir's sprints had become a fiction the team performed every two weeks and then apologized for.

The idea

Kanban is a method for managing work by limiting how much of it is in progress at any moment, so that the rate at which work actually finishes — not a calendar — sets the pace of delivery. It did not begin in software. Taiichi Ohno, an engineer at Toyota, developed the kanban system on the factory floor in the late 1940s and through the 1950s: a physical card — kanban in Japanese literally means "signboard" or "visual card" — moved backward through the production line to signal that a station had capacity to pull more work forward, rather than upstream stations pushing parts downstream regardless of whether anyone was ready for them. Limiting work-in-progress reduced the inventory sitting idle between steps, shortened the time any single unit spent in the system, and exposed bottlenecks that a fully loaded line hides.

David J. Anderson, then leading a team inside Microsoft's engineering-services division, adapted the idea to knowledge work between 2004 and 2007 and published it as the Kanban Method in 2010.

Stop starting, start finishing — a team does better by limiting how many things it works on at once than by picking up everything the moment it becomes available.

How it actually works

Applying kanban to Kabir's team meant six deliberate moves, most of which practitioners skip past because they look too simple to need explaining.

First, visualize the actual workflow, not an idealized one. Kabir's team drew columns for the states work genuinely passed through — Backlog, Triage, In Progress, In Review, Awaiting Ekavira Sign-off, Done — rather than the three-column "To Do / Doing / Done" board that hides where things actually stall.

Kabir's redrawn board: six real states, per-column WIP limits, and "In Progress" shown at its cap of four — no card enters until one leaves.

Second, limit work in progress per column, not just overall. A WIP limit is a hard cap: if "In Progress" is capped at four cards and already holds four, nobody pulls a fifth, however urgent it looks, until one moves on. This is the step teams most often skip in spirit while keeping in appearance — they write "WIP: 4" atop a column and then wave a fifth card through anyway. The limit only does anything if breaching it is genuinely uncomfortable.

Third, manage flow rather than manage people. Instead of asking what each engineer did yesterday, Kabir's team asked which cards were stuck and why, using two measurements: cycle time, the elapsed time from when a card is pulled into "In Progress" until it reaches "Done," and throughput, the count of cards finished per week regardless of size. Fourth, make policies explicit — what "done" means, what qualifies for the single expedite slot reserved for genuine emergencies, and who may pull work versus only add it to the backlog. Fifth, run a short daily flow review that looks at the board for blocked or aging cards, not a status meeting. Sixth, improve collaboratively, using the data the board now produced rather than opinion.

A worked example: what tightening the limit actually does

Kabir needed to know, concretely, what changing his team's WIP limit would do to how fast a ticket got through the system. He used Little's Law, a result from queueing theory that predates kanban by decades and applies to any stable flow system: average cycle time equals average work-in-progress divided by average throughput.

Over the eight weeks before the change, the team had carried an average of six items in "In Progress" at any time and finished an average of three items per week. Cycle time was therefore six divided by three, two weeks — which matched what the team felt: a card pulled in on a Monday was rarely done before the Monday after next.

Kabir's proposal was to tighten the "In Progress" limit from six to four, forcing the team to finish work before starting more. If throughput held steady at three items per week — reasonable if the team was scattered rather than resource-constrained — cycle time would fall to four divided by three, roughly 1.3 weeks, about nine days. But he also ran the arithmetic for the case where tightening WIP exposed a real bottleneck: a single reviewer who approved every warehouse-integration change. If throughput dropped to two items per week because work piled up waiting on that one person, cycle time would be four divided by two, two weeks again — no better than before, and the limit alone would have accomplished nothing without also fixing the bottleneck it revealed.

Before the change632.0 weeks
WIP tightened, throughput holds431.3 weeks
WIP tightened, reviewer bottleneck422.0 weeks

The nuances a learner must become aware of

Kanban is not the absence of planning. Teams that drop sprints often drop planning with them, then blame kanban when the backlog turns into an unordered pile. The method still requires an ordered backlog and a replenishment cadence — a regular, lighter-weight meeting where the team pulls the next few items into the queue — it simply decouples that ordering from a fixed two-week clock.

A WIP limit is a discipline, not a display. The number at the top of a column is worthless if the team's habit, when someone is idle, is to start a new card rather than help finish one already in flight or genuinely wait. The tell is whether anyone has ever actually been refused permission to start something because the limit said no.

Cycle time and lead time are not the same measurement, and teams conflate them constantly. Lead time runs from the moment a request is logged to the moment it is delivered, including time sitting untouched in the backlog. Cycle time runs only from when work actually starts. A team can shrink cycle time while lead time stays terrible because the backlog itself is the bottleneck — a distinction that matters when Ekavira's account manager asks how long a ticket takes.

Little's Law describes a system in steady state — arrival and departure rates roughly matched, the mix of work not shifting wildly week to week. Applied to a team whose mix keeps changing, the same formula gives an average that no single week resembles, which is why Kabir tracked it over a rolling eight-week window rather than trusting any one week's number.

Not all work is the same class of service, and treating it as if it were is a common failure. An emergency production fix from Ekavira's floor and a minor cosmetic change do not deserve the same queue discipline; most kanban implementations reserve one expedite slot outside the normal WIP limit for genuine emergencies, and treat heavy use of that slot as a sign that "emergency" has stopped meaning anything.

Kanban does not tell you what to build. It manages the flow of work already judged worth doing; it says nothing about whether Ekavira's request deserved priority over three other customers' requests. Prioritization sits upstream of the board, and a beautifully flowing system can still be flowing the wrong work quickly.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and company stage

Flow tends to beat sprints where work arrives unpredictably and the unit of value is small and independent, which is why Kabir's situation — customer-driven support mixed with incremental fixes — was close to the textbook case. Consumer teams running rapid experimentation, such as a growth squad testing onboarding variants, often converge on kanban for the same reason: an experiment's next step depends on data that lands whenever it lands, not on a sprint calendar. B2B companies serving a handful of large accounts, like Drishya, see the same interrupt pattern multiplied by each account's own operational rhythm. Marketplace companies split more cleanly: catalog operations and trust-and-safety queues are almost always flow-based, because a fraudulent listing does not wait for sprint planning, while core matching-algorithm work is coordinated, roadmap-driven, and often still runs on iterations. Company stage matters too: an eight-person startup rarely needs the ceremony of sprints, because the whole team already coordinates by conversation; the discipline kanban imposes becomes valuable precisely at the size where informal coordination breaks down, which for Drishya had arrived around eighty engineers.

The same four cards sitting in the pipe move through faster only if the exit rate (throughput) does not fall when the pipe narrows.

Common mistakes

The first is mistaking the board for the method. A team that draws columns on a wall or in Jira and calls it kanban, without ever enforcing a WIP limit, is doing what practitioners call kanban theatre: the symptom is a board with more cards "in progress" than anyone can plausibly be working on. The underlying misunderstanding is treating visualization as the whole practice rather than its first step; the cheapest diagnostic is counting cards in the busiest column against the number written above it.

The second is letting every urgent request become an expedite item, because no one wants to be the person who tells an angry customer to wait. The symptom is an expedite lane holding as many cards as the regular lanes; the underlying error is a class-of-service policy enforced on paper but not in the moment it actually costs something. The diagnostic is a simple ratio — expedited items over total items closed — tracked monthly.

The third is ignoring blocked work instead of measuring it. A card can sit "in progress" for nine days while actually blocked for seven, and a team that tracks only cycle time never learns the real problem is a slow external dependency, not its own pace. The diagnostic is a blocked-time tag on every card, visible on the board itself.

What good looks like

Six weeks after Kabir made the change, the picture that mattered was not a chart but a Thursday-afternoon flow review. The team looked at eleven cards on the board, two of them tagged blocked, one waiting on the same integration reviewer Kabir had flagged in his second calculation — and instead of starting a twelfth card, two engineers picked up the review queue themselves for the afternoon. Ekavira's incident tickets, tracked separately with their own expedite discipline, were closing in under two days on average, down from nine. The roadmap feature Ekavira actually cared about, a batch-scanning mode, moved slower in absolute terms than the old sprint plan had promised, but moved at a pace the team could now state with a straight face three weeks in advance, because throughput had become steady enough to forecast from.

What Kabir decided

Kabir did not abandon planning; he abandoned the two-week box that forced planning and delivery onto the same clock as interrupts he could not schedule. He kept a lightweight monthly cadence for Ekavira's larger roadmap commitments, forecast now from throughput rather than story-point velocity, and ran the rest of the team's work as a continuously flowing kanban system with WIP limits he was willing to enforce even when it meant telling an anxious account manager that a ticket would wait one more day.

The renewal conversation with Ekavira in April went differently than Kabir had feared: what closed the deal was not a longer feature list but a delivery manager who could say, credibly, how long a ticket would take and be right. What Kabir still needed to learn was how to forecast a delivery date probabilistically from historical cycle-time data, rather than from a single average — the next tool past Little's Law.

Two questions worth sitting with:

What in your own team's work is actually interrupt-driven rather than plannable — and how much of your sprint calendar exists to manage that work, versus to manage the illusion that it doesn't happen?

What would you have to be willing to say no to, in the moment it actually mattered, for a WIP limit on your own board to mean anything at all?
case20v1-agile.backlog:
Chintan Payments Cloud: The Backlog Before Diwali

A teaching case for the ISB Product Management course — Delivery & Technology: Backlog Management and Refinement

1. Opening

Bengaluru, 8 October 2026, a Thursday evening. From her desk on the ninth floor of a building off Outer Ring Road, Kavya Rajan, Director of Product at Chintan Payments Cloud, has until Friday's 4 p.m. leadership review — less than twenty hours — to tell the founders how she intends to fix a Jira backlog that has swollen to 640 open items, and whether the company can still meet its Diwali-week go-live commitment to Majid Al Futtaim Retail. The Dubai-headquartered group's India franchise stores are Chintan's first marquee global logo, and the launch date, 4 November, is contractual. Kavya has spent the afternoon scrolling the backlog board, watching two-year-old tickets sit beside last week's escalations, and she knows that whatever she proposes tomorrow has to hold not just for one sprint but for how the company plans from here.

2. Company background

Chintan Payments Cloud was founded in 2019 by two former Flipkart payments engineers who wanted to give small and mid-sized retailers the reconciliation and checkout tooling that only large marketplaces had built in-house. The company sells a payment orchestration layer that sits above UPI, card networks and net-banking rails, handling settlement, GST-compliant invoicing and dispute management for direct-to-consumer brands and offline-to-online retail chains. It competes for the same SME wallet share as Razorpay, Cashfree Payments and Pine Labs, differentiating on same-day settlement and a reconciliation dashboard that finance teams like. By late 2026 it employs 140 people, serves roughly 3,200 merchants, and processes about ₹1,800 crore of monthly gross merchandise value. The Majid Al Futtaim deal, signed in June, requires Chintan's checkout stack to go live across 46 stores in time for the retailer's Diwali promotional calendar in India — the company's first test of whether it can deliver to a large enterprise customer's clock rather than its own.

3. The situation

The backlog problem did not arrive suddenly. Over eighteen months, as the team grew from nine engineers to twenty-six, everyone with access to Jira — product managers, support leads, sales, even a founder after customer calls — got into the habit of filing a ticket the moment an idea or complaint surfaced. Refinement, nominally a Tuesday ritual, had become a status read-out where engineers skimmed the newest items and the oldest ones were never opened. Of the 640 open tickets, 210 have no acceptance criteria, 84 are more than a year old, and nobody can say with confidence which are still wanted. Two sprints ago, carry-over — work planned but not finished — crossed 40 percent for the first time (Exhibit 2).

The distributed team sees the problem from different angles. Lena Voss, Chintan's lead product designer in Berlin, cannot find out which of forty candidate stories will actually be built, so half the stories reaching sprint planning arrive with no design attached. Daniel Osei, the data scientist in Toronto, wants his experimentation backlog — pricing tests, fraud-model tuning — ring-fenced from feature work, because it keeps getting bumped. In Singapore, customer-success lead Mei Lin Tan now files merchant escalations directly as Jira tickets, skipping Kavya so that nothing gets lost; this has added forty tickets in six weeks. Robert Alvarez, the sales head in New Jersey, has been promising US mid-market prospects that specific integrations will ship "next quarter," each promise landing as a new, oddly specific ticket bearing his name.

Kavya's engineering leads in Bengaluru and Pune say plainly that nobody can tell them, in planning, whether the top twenty items are the right twenty. The Majid Al Futtaim work itself is buried at position 340, tagged but not sequenced, while lighter items sit near the top simply because they were filed most recently.

4. The people

Kavya Rajan — Director of Product, Bengaluru
Protagonist. Owns the backlog and the Friday commitment to the founders; wants a fix that is credible to engineering, does not blow up the Diwali deadline, and does not require her to personally triage every ticket forever.
Lena Voss — Lead Product Designer, Berlin
Wants a shorter, stable list of "next up" stories with enough lead time to design against, rather than a moving target.
Daniel Osei — Data Scientist, Toronto
Wants his experimentation work protected from being reprioritised out of every sprint by louder, more recent tickets.
Mei Lin Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Wants merchant escalations to be seen and acted on quickly, and has lost faith that filing through Kavya achieves that.
Robert Alvarez — Head of Sales, New Jersey
Wants prospect-driven feature commitments honoured, and sees backlog "cleanup" as a threat to deals he has already promised.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1: Backlog composition, 8 October 2026

640 open Jira items by age and type

60 days – 6 months20432%Mix of feature stories, tech debt

Source: Jira export, compiled by the Pune engineering-operations analyst, 8 October 2026.

Exhibit 1 shows why Kavya's engineers stopped trusting the board: only a quarter of the backlog is recent enough to reflect what the business actually needs today, while 13 percent has sat untouched for over a year without anyone deciding to close it.

Exhibit 2: Sprint velocity and carry-over, last six sprints

Two-week sprints, story points committed vs. completed

S1 (Jul)867414%
S2 (Jul)907121%
