Source: engineering sprint reports; a ₹1 crore-a-quarter engineering payroll implies each committed-but-uncompleted point costs roughly ₹1.4 lakh in re-planning and context-switching, per Kavya's own estimate for the review deck.

Exhibit 2 is the number Kavya expects the founders to fix on: carry-over has risen every sprint for three months, and at 40 percent it means two of every five story points planned are now simply pushed to the next cycle — the clearest evidence that the team is planning against an unrefined list rather than a real one.

Exhibit 3: four weeks separate Friday's review from code freeze on the Majid Al Futtaim build; a single confused sprint of planning is most of the runway Chintan has left.

6. The options

Option A — A two-week backlog amnesty and re-baseline. Freeze new ticket intake for two weeks except for production incidents. Kavya, her two engineering leads and Lena jointly triage all 640 items against a simple DEEP standard — detailed appropriately, estimated, emergent, prioritised — closing anything without a clear owner, and sequencing the Majid Al Futtaim work to the top. Mei Lin's and Robert's new requests get one weekly intake slot instead of open Jira access. Upside: a trustworthy top-of-backlog within the four weeks available, at low tooling cost. Cost: two weeks of intake friction that sales and support will resist, and it needs the founders' visible backing to hold.

Option B — Replace the tool and automate triage. Migrate off Jira to a newer platform with automated staleness flags, AI-assisted duplicate detection and enforced templates, over three to four weeks. Upside: a more permanent structural fix. Cost: it consumes exactly the engineering time Chintan cannot spare before 4 November, and substitutes tooling for the habits that actually broke — the "too much agile mechanics" trap the company's own engineering partners warn against.

Option C — Hire a dedicated backlog owner in Pune. Bring on a business analyst whose sole job is grooming, estimation and intake gatekeeping, reporting to Kavya. Upside: lasting capacity, offloaded from a stretched Director of Product. Cost: recruiting and onboarding takes six to eight weeks — after the deadline — and a new hire lacks the context to make calls Mei Lin, Robert and Lena will contest in week one.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2's rising carry-over actually reveal about the backlog, as distinct from about the engineering team's effort or skill?
  2. Whose incentives currently push tickets into the backlog fastest, and what does each of the four stakeholders lose if intake is restricted?
  3. Which option gives Chintan a trustworthy top-of-backlog before 28 October code freeze, and which options only look attractive if that deadline is set aside?
  4. If Kavya chooses Option A, what would "small, ordered and understood" look like as an operating standard the team can sustain after the Diwali launch, not just during the crisis?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as one about the backlog's health as a working artefact, not about any single sprint's output. A backlog that is small, ordered and understood is a decision-support tool: it tells the team, at a glance, what matters most and why. Chintan's backlog had failed on all three counts — large (640 items), unordered (the highest-value work sat at position 340), and not understood (210 items lacked acceptance criteria). A well-reasoned answer starts from that diagnosis rather than urgency alone, then asks which option restores the property that broke, within the time available.

The defensible path is Option A. It is the only option whose timeline fits inside the four weeks before code freeze, and it treats the cause directly: an unrefined backlog, not an under-resourced or under-tooled one. A joint triage against DEEP criteria rebuilds the trust Exhibit 2 shows the team has lost, and a single weekly intake slot gives Mei Lin and Robert a legitimate channel instead of an unlimited one. Option B answers a real long-term need but is the wrong tool for a four-week runway, repeating the mistake the course cautions against — treating agile mechanics as the fix for a discipline problem. Option C is sound organisational design for 2027, not for a deadline in November. The reasoning that should generalise is that backlog refinement is a standing discipline to be reset and protected, not a one-time cleanup to be delegated away.
exp20v2-agile.backlog:
Delivery & Technology · Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

Backlog Management and Refinement

1. A Tuesday that used to take forty-five minutes

On the morning of September 8, 2026, Rohan Mehta walked into sprint planning at Aakar Systems, a Bengaluru-based maker of warehouse and order-operations software for roughly 140 direct-to-consumer brands, and did not leave for three hours. Eleven people sat through it: four engineers, two QA leads, a designer, engineering lead Deepak Suri, and three others who wandered in because, as one put it, "someone has to know what we're actually building." The meeting used to run forty-five minutes. It had grown in step with the backlog itself, which swelled from 120 open items in January to 340 by September — sales asks, half-written epics from a hackathon, untriaged support escalations, and a few items nobody in the room could explain.

The cost was visible in the numbers Rohan would present at the September 15 quarterly review: of fourteen stories committed the previous quarter, only six had shipped. Deepak's engineers were not idle — they were re-litigating scope on stories that, once read, turned out to be missing acceptance criteria, dependent on an unscoped API, or too large to estimate. Rohan's VP of product, Ananya Kapoor, had one instruction before the QBR: "Fix the backlog before you fix the roadmap." The decision facing Rohan was not which features to build, but how to keep an ever-growing queue small enough, ordered enough, and understood well enough that Tuesdays could go back to being about work, not archaeology.

2. The idea, precisely

Backlog management and refinement is the ongoing discipline of keeping a product backlog small enough to be understood, ordered so the next unit of work is obvious, and detailed only as far ahead as anyone can act on. It is a habit, not an event: a modest recurring slice of the team's time — the Scrum Guide's rule of thumb is no more than about ten percent of a sprint's capacity — spent looking two or three sprints ahead, splitting ideas into smaller ones, estimating roughly, and re-ordering as new information arrives. The term traces to Scrum practice in the early 2000s, where teams called it "backlog grooming"; Schwaber and Sutherland's Scrum Guide formally renamed it "refinement" in 2017. Roman Pichler, in his 2010 book on agile product management, gave the goal a memorable acronym: a healthy backlog is DEEP — Detailed appropriately, Estimated, Emergent, and Prioritized.

It was invented to solve a specific failure that Aakar Systems had just rediscovered: a backlog left unattended does not stay a helpful list, it becomes a junk drawer, and a junk drawer cannot be planned from. The sentence Rohan could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: a backlog earns its place at the top through evidence, not seniority — refinement is the recurring work that keeps that ordering honest.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run as a steady cycle, not a one-time cleanup, and Aakar's new version of it illustrates each step. First, intake: raw ideas — sales asks, support tickets, a hallway suggestion — land in a single unrefined tail, captured but not polished. Aakar routed these through one Slack channel into a Jira "Inbox" label, roughly forty items a month, so they stopped arriving as mid-sprint interruptions.

Second, a fixed cadence: Rohan, Deepak, and one rotating engineer met every Tuesday for forty-five minutes, looking only at the next two or three sprints, never the whole backlog. Third, splitting: large epics were broken into stories small enough to finish within one sprint, using the INVEST checklist (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable). A five-point epic, "multi-warehouse inventory sync," stuck for two months because no one could size it, became six stories once split — the largest finishable by one engineer in four days.

Fourth, estimating: the team sized stories in relative story points, chiefly to surface disagreement — when two engineers guess three points and one guesses thirteen, the conversation matters more than the number. Fifth, ordering: everything sat in one single list, not parallel lanes, so "what's next" always had one answer. Sixth, and easy to skip, a written Definition of Ready — acceptance criteria, flagged dependencies, a design link — before a story could enter planning. Seventh, the step most teams leave implicit: deliberate pruning. Anything untouched two full quarters was archived; Aakar archived ninety such items on its first pass. Eighth, a taper in depth — only the top dozen items were refined fully, everything further down left as a one-line placeholder, since most of it would change before its turn came.

4. A worked example

To decide what belonged at the top of the newly refined queue, Rohan's team scored five candidate stories on cost of delay — the sum of user value, time criticality, and risk reduction, each rated one to ten by the group — then divided by story-point size to get a rough priority score, a simplified version of the Weighted Shortest Job First method.

Table 1. Priority scoring, first pass (September 9, 2026)
StoryValueUrgencyRisk cutCost of delaySize (pts)Score
A. Multi-warehouse sync alerts8641882.25
B. Bulk SKU import via CSV5321033.33
C. GST e-invoice reconciliation7952154.20
D. Dashboard dark mode311522.50
E. Predictive stockout alerts94720131.54

Cost of delay for story C is 7 + 9 + 5 = 21, divided by a size of 5 points, giving 4.20 — the highest of the five, so it moved to the top, ahead of the bulk import tool despite lower raw value, because it was both small and urgent. Story E, predictive stockout alerts, scored lowest at 1.54 even though its raw value of 9 was the highest in the set: at thirteen points it was an unrefined epic wearing a story's clothing, and its size dragged it to the bottom.

That observation was itself a product of refinement. The following Tuesday, Deepak's team split story E, discovering a rules-based heuristic could ship stockout alerts without the machine-learning model originally assumed, cutting its size from 13 points to 5. Recomputed, its score rose to 20 ÷ 5 = 4.00 — close behind story C, now ahead of the CSV importer. The ranking changed not because anyone argued more persuasively, but because refinement replaced a guess with a smaller, truer estimate. That is the mechanism's real output: not a fixed order, but one that gets more honest each time the team looks again.

5. The nuances a learner must become aware of

Refinement is not planning

Refinement prepares work; planning commits capacity to work already prepared. Aakar's three-hour meetings ran long because refinement hadn't happened earlier in the week, so planning absorbed it — two activities blurred into one bad one.

Backlog is not roadmap

A backlog is an ordered execution queue for engineering; a roadmap is themes and outcomes communicated to stakeholders. Treating backlog position as a public delivery promise is a costly confusion — order should change weekly; a roadmap commitment should not.

Depth applies unevenly on purpose

Only the near-term slice deserves full detail. Deep-refining an item eight months out wastes effort, since most such items change or are abandoned before their turn — refinement debt paid too early is still debt.

Estimates surface disagreement, not hours

Story points reveal where two engineers see a task differently, not calendar time. Once a team converts points to hours for external commitments, the number stops doing its job and people start gaming it.

Scoring formalizes judgment, it does not replace it

WSJF-style scores are only as good as the value, urgency, and risk inputs feeding them, and those inputs remain human estimates. The score orders a debate; a low score is a reason to ask a question, not a verdict.

Refinement cannot tell you whether to build the thing at all

It optimizes the order among items already judged worth doing. Whether story E belongs on the backlog at all is a discovery question that refinement assumes has already been answered.

A Definition of Ready is a contract, not paperwork

An unenforced Definition of Ready quietly readmits the ambiguity refinement exists to remove — a story that "sort of" has acceptance criteria will still stall a sprint, just later than it would have.

Questions worth asking before relying on any of this

Who can reorder the backlog when stakeholders disagree? How much capacity does refinement itself cost, and is that spent deliberately? And, tellingly, when did this backlog last have something deleted rather than added?

6. Consumer, B2B, and marketplace, at different stages

The same discipline looks different depending on who is downstream. At a consumer product such as the imagined Chakor Retail Cloud, refinement leans on fast usage data, cadence is often weekly or faster, and the risk of neglect is a backlog stuffed with unvalidated requests from the loudest users. At a B2B company like Aakar Systems, refinement leans on named enterprise customers and contractual commitments, and the risk of neglect is a backlog silently reordered by whichever account executive shouted last. At a marketplace such as the imagined Batwara Exchange, refinement has to reconcile two backlogs — supply-side and demand-side — and the risk of neglect is optimizing one side while the other silently stalls.

Table 2. How refinement differs by product type and stage
ConsumerB2BMarketplace
Typical cadenceWeekly, data-ledWeekly–biweeklyWeekly per side
Who sets "ready"PM + data leadPM + solutions/CSPM per side, reconciled
Neglect riskLoudest-user biasSales-driven reorderingOne side starves

Company stage matters as much as product type. Early-stage teams can often keep the entire backlog in working memory and refine informally in a founder's head; that stops working somewhere around fifty to eighty open items, roughly where Aakar was in March. Larger organizations need the formal apparatus — DoR checklists, named refinement owners, archival rules — precisely because informal memory no longer covers the surface area, and because more people now have a reason to add to the queue than to prune it.

7. Common mistakes

Table 3. Mistakes, their cause, and how to catch them cheaply
SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheap diagnostic
Planning meetings run long and argumentativeRefinement is skipped, so planning absorbs itAsk what share of entering stories already had acceptance criteria attached
Backlog never shrinks despite steady shippingNothing is ever pruned, "just in case"Pull an age histogram of open items; flag anything untouched two-plus quarters
The top of the backlog changes every weekNo single owner has ordering authorityAsk who can move an item to position one, and check if two people answer differently
Sprint velocity swings wildlyStories are estimated before they are actually splitTrack what share of stories get re-estimated mid-sprint

Each of these is cheap to catch precisely because it leaves a visible trace in the tool the team already uses — a tag, a timestamp, an audit log — long before it shows up as a missed quarter.

8. What good looks like

By late February 2027, Aakar's backlog had settled near sixty open items, with the rest shipped, merged into tracked epics, or archived. Tuesday refinement ran forty-five minutes with three people. Sprint planning, once again, ran forty-five minutes with eleven, because every story entering it already had acceptance criteria, an owner, and a size the team trusted. Commitment reliability rose from 43 percent to 89 percent over two quarters, not because engineers worked faster but because the queue in front of them had stopped lying about what was ready.

9. What Rohan decided, and what comes next

Rohan's fix was not a new tool; it was a cadence, a checklist, and a willingness to delete things. He instituted weekly refinement capped near one-tenth of the team's time, adopted the cost-of-delay-over-size scoring as a starting order rather than a final verdict, enforced a written Definition of Ready before anything reached planning, and — hardest to defend to stakeholders — archived any item untouched for two quarters, trusting that anything that truly mattered would resurface on its own. His reasoning to Ananya was simple: the team's problem had never been engineering speed, it was that no one could tell, on any given Tuesday, what "next" meant.

The natural next topic for Rohan is prioritization itself in more depth — WSJF and RICE as full frameworks, and where each breaks down — since refinement only orders a queue that a prioritization method has to feed honestly. Two questions worth sitting with: how would you know, from outside, that a backlog has grown too large to manage honestly, not merely large? And who in your organization has both the authority and the standing to delete an item nobody has touched in a year?
case40v1-agile.backlog:
Kritarth Warehouse Cloud: Eleven Hundred Open Tickets

A teaching case for the ISB Product Management course — Delivery & Technology: Backlog Management and Refinement

1. The night before

Sunday, 15 November 2026. Rain had come late to Pune that year, and from the fourth-floor balcony of Kritarth Warehouse Cloud's office in Baner, Aparna Deshmukh could hear it on the parked cars below. It was 10:40 p.m. On her laptop were three documents. The first was a Jira export, 1,183 rows long, filtered to open items across the company's three product boards. The second was a one-page memo from the chief executive asking her to come to Monday's 9 a.m. board session with "a clear, dated plan to fix delivery." The third was a message from the company's lead investor, forwarded without comment, which described Kritarth's engineering output as "unpredictable at a stage where predictability is the whole valuation argument."

2. How Kritarth got here

Kritarth Warehouse Cloud was founded in 2019 by Harish Kamat, a former Infosys and Delhivery engineer, and Ravi Gokhale, who had run fulfilment operations for a large apparel brand and had spent years reconciling stock counts on spreadsheets. Their product was a warehouse management and order-fulfilment system for direct-to-consumer brands and third-party logistics operators: inbound receiving, bin-level inventory, wave picking, packing, carrier allocation, returns grading, and the GST and e-way bill documentation that Indian warehouse operations generate in volume. By November 2026 it had 310 employees, 61 of them engineers, ran 214 live warehouses, and had closed FY26 at ₹78 crore of annual recurring revenue.

The decision that constrained everything afterwards was made in August 2023. To win a competitive bid against Unicommerce and Increff for a fast-growing beauty retailer, Kritarth agreed to build a configurable rules engine that would let each customer define its own picking, allocation and returns logic without code. It won the deal. It also committed itself to a product where nearly every customer request was technically legitimate, because the architecture had promised that anything could be configured. There was no longer a clean line between "product" and "custom work." Seven of the top twelve accounts now ran on rule sets written specifically for them, and each of those rule sets generated its own stream of defects, enhancement requests and migration blockers, all of which landed in the same backlog as the roadmap.

3. The industry

Indian fulfilment software in 2026 was a crowded, thin-margin business. Kritarth sold against Unicommerce and Increff domestically, against Blue Yonder and Manhattan Associates at the enterprise end, and against the free tooling that Shiprocket and Delhivery bundled into their logistics contracts. Its customers were D2C brands scaling on Nykaa, Myntra, Amazon and Flipkart, quick-commerce operators managing dark stores, and 3PLs serving all of them. Volumes were savagely seasonal: the festive window from Navratri through Diwali could carry forty per cent of a customer's annual order count, and ONDC-driven order flow had added a second, less predictable spike.

Regulation shaped the roadmap more than any competitor did. The GST e-invoicing threshold had come down again in 2026, pulling several hundred mid-sized customers of Kritarth's customers into mandatory e-invoice generation. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent and erasure obligations had become live commitments, and Kritarth held consumer names, addresses and phone numbers for every shipment it processed. Both items sat in the backlog as epics with dates attached. Neither could be deprioritised, and neither won a single new deal.

The company's exposure was no longer only Indian. In March 2026 it had signed Kasturi Lifestyle DMCC, a Dubai-headquartered retail group operating 180 stores and three distribution centres across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman. The contract was worth ₹14.6 crore a year, roughly nineteen per cent of ARR, and carried a phased go-live: Dubai in October 2026, which had slipped to December, and Riyadh on 15 January 2027, which was contractual, with service credits of ₹22 lakh per week of delay capped at ₹2.6 crore. Kasturi's operations ran Sunday to Thursday; Kritarth's sprints ran Monday to Friday.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In April, after a ₹110 crore Series A extension, the company hired hard. Engineering reached 61 by August, organised into six squads. Believing that the bottleneck was capacity, leadership added no new planning discipline; the assumption stated openly at the April offsite was that a backlog that had worked for three squads would work for six. In June, engineering re-baselined story-point estimates because the new squads were sizing differently from the old ones. Everyone agreed this was housekeeping. It has since made every velocity comparison across the June boundary meaningless, a fact that was not written down anywhere and that Aparna discovered only in October, when she tried to build a trend line for the board.

In July, Kritarth split Jira into three boards — Core Platform, Rules & Configuration, and Integrations — to give squads cleaner queues. What it did not do was decide who owned ordering across the three. Each board grew its own priority scheme. An item marked P1 on Integrations was not comparable to a P1 on Core, and nobody could produce a single ordered list of what the company was doing next. Sales, support and solution architects all retained ticket-creation rights on all three.

In September the Kasturi Dubai go-live slipped. The stated reason was an Arabic-locale printing defect in packing documents. The actual cause, established in the October post-mortem, was that eleven of the fourteen stories required for the Dubai cutover had been filed in March, sized in May, and never re-examined; four of them described a warehouse layout Kasturi had since abandoned, and two duplicated work already shipped for an Indian customer. The team had built what the backlog said, and the backlog had been wrong for five months.

5. The people

Aparna Deshmukh — Vice President, Product, Pune
Protagonist. Position: the backlog must be cut to a single ordered list with an enforced definition of ready. Incentive: her credibility with the board rests on producing a February date that holds. Not saying: she has privately concluded that two of the six squads are working on items she cannot justify to anyone, and she does not yet know how to say so without appearing to blame the squads' managers.
Harish Kamat — Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Pune
Position: the problem is architectural debt in the rules engine, not process; refinement ceremonies will not fix a system where every change has unpredictable blast radius. Incentive: he built the rules engine and the 2023 bid was his commitment. Not saying: he has been quietly staffing a rewrite spike with three senior engineers whose time is booked against Kasturi delivery.
Ravi Gokhale — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune
Position: Kasturi's Riyadh date is non-negotiable and everything else is secondary until 15 January. Incentive: the Series B conversation depends on showing an ARR trajectory that includes Gulf expansion. Not saying: he has already told the investor that Riyadh will land on time, without checking with Aparna.
Shalini Vaidya — Engineering Manager, Core Platform, Bengaluru
Position: her squads will not commit to sprint scope until stories arrive with acceptance criteria and a named decision-maker. Incentive: her attrition ran at nineteen per cent last year and her engineers cite rework as the reason. Not saying: two of her four squads have started carrying an informal parallel list in a spreadsheet that reflects what they actually intend to build.
Frieda Lehmann — Principal Product Designer, Berlin
Position: design cannot work eight hours ahead of Pune against a queue that reorders nightly; she wants a frozen two-sprint horizon. Incentive: she is judged on shipped experience quality, not on throughput. Not saying: she has stopped designing for anything below the top fifteen items, so the apparent readiness of the rest of the backlog is an illusion.
Étienne Lapointe — Staff Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: the slotting and demand-forecast models he owns should be run as a separate, protected stream with its own cadence. Incentive: his roadmap is the one the investor memo praised by name. Not saying: his models have been retrained only twice this year because the data-pipeline tickets they depend on keep losing to customer escalations.
Serene Koh — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Position: escalation tickets must keep direct-to-board visibility; she has 38 open P1s across APAC accounts. Incentive: her renewal targets are gross, not net, so a churned account is unrecoverable for her year. Not saying: her team files an item for every customer complaint as a matter of policy, including ones they have already resolved by configuration, because open tickets are how she demonstrates workload in budget reviews.
Dale Pritchard — Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey
Position: the roadmap commitments register (Exhibit 3) represents contracted revenue and cannot be reopened. Incentive: his 2027 quota assumes four US 3PL logos closing on the strength of promised integrations. Not saying: roughly half the register's entries were verbal assurances in deal rooms, not contractual obligations, and he has never had to distinguish between the two.

7. Voices

"Every sprint we plan against a list that somebody reordered on Friday evening. Twice this quarter my squad started a story on Monday that had been deprioritised on Saturday and nobody told us. I am not asking for a better tool. I am asking for one list, and one person who owns the order of it."

Shalini Vaidya, engineering all-hands, Bengaluru, 4 November 2026

"With respect, the backlog is a symptom. We have 497 open items on the Rules board because we sold a system where every customer can have their own physics. Grooming that list will make it shorter. It will not make the rules engine safe to change. If we spend December in workshops instead of in the code, we will arrive at Riyadh with a tidy backlog and the same blast radius."

Harish Kamat, email to Aparna Deshmukh and Ravi Gokhale, 9 November 2026

"I want to be careful here. When we say 'archive anything older than 120 days', eleven of my 38 open P1s are older than that. Those are not stale ideas. Those are customers in Singapore and Sydney who have been waiting since June and who have stopped escalating because they have given up, not because it is fixed."

Serene Koh, delivery review call, 12 November 2026

"Can someone tell me which of the four US integrations is actually being built? I have told three prospects Q1. If the answer is none of them, I would rather know now and reset the conversations than find out in February. I am not the enemy of the cleanup. I am the person who will be standing in the room when it lands."

Dale Pritchard, message in the #revenue-product channel, 13 November 2026, 06:12 IST

8. The options as Aparna currently sees them

Option A — The single ordered list. Collapse the three boards into one queue with one owner — Aparna — and one ordering. Archive everything untouched for 120 days, publish a definition of ready that stories must meet before they can be planned, and restrict creation rights to seven named people with a weekly intake council. Estimated cost: three weeks of concentrated work across product and engineering management, during four of the sprints shown in Exhibit 6. It would make the backlog small, ordered and understood, and it assumes that someone can order 1,183 items against a strategy the company has not actually written down.

Option B — Federate the backlog to the squads. Give each of the six squads a named product owner, a customer segment and its own queue, and hold them accountable for outcomes rather than for a central order. Kritarth would stop pretending a single list is possible at its size. Shalini supports this; so, quietly, do the two squads already keeping a spreadsheet. It also multiplies the number of people who can say yes, and it is unclear who then decides between Riyadh and the DPDP module when both need the same three engineers.

Option C — Freeze and reconcile the commitments. Suspend all roadmap work except Kasturi and DPDP until 31 January, and use December to reconcile Exhibits 3 and 4 into one register that distinguishes contractual obligations from verbal assurances. Ravi would likely accept this; Dale would not. The register, once honest, might show that the ₹41.0 crore figure that has been driving prioritisation for eight months is closer to ₹12 crore, which changes what the backlog is for. It also does nothing about the 1,183 items themselves, and postpones the conversation to a February in which the same pressures will exist.

Aparna wrote all three on a page and then, underneath, a sentence she did not intend to show anyone: All three assume the problem is the list. She was no longer sure it was. The June re-baselining had been housekeeping until it destroyed her trend line. The 2023 rules-engine promise had been a deal-winner until it made every customer request legitimate. Refinement hours had nearly doubled and readiness had collapsed, which is not what happens when a team is merely undisciplined. It is possible, she thought, that Kritarth had no way of saying no, and that a backlog is what an organisation without a way of saying no looks like from the inside.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9 a.m. on Monday 16 November. Kritarth holds ₹62 crore in cash against a burn of ₹4.4 crore a month, giving fourteen months of runway. Hiring is frozen below director level until March. The Series B term sheet under discussion values the company at ₹720 crore and is conditional on exiting FY27 at ₹120 crore of ARR, which requires both the Kasturi Riyadh go-live and at least two of the four US logos in Dale's register.

Riyadh's 15 January date is contractual, with ₹22 lakh a week in service credits from 22 January, capped at ₹2.6 crore. The DPDP consent and erasure module is due to enterprise customers on 18 December and is a statutory obligation that cannot be traded against a customer date. Four sprints separate the board meeting from the Riyadh code freeze. Three senior engineers, the same three, are named on the Riyadh cutover plan, on the DPDP epic, and on Harish's unannounced rules-engine spike.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibits 1, 2 and 5, what can be said with confidence about Kritarth's delivery, and what cannot? Which of the three exhibits would you refuse to put in front of the board, and why?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 differ by roughly ₹29 crore. What is each measuring, who produced it, and what would a reconciled register have to define before the two could be compared at all?
  3. Each of the eight stakeholders has something they are not saying. Which unstated position, if it came out on Monday, would most change the shape of the decision?
  4. Aparna's three options all treat the backlog as the object to be fixed. State the problem in a way that makes none of the three the obvious answer. What evidence in the case supports your reframing, and what evidence cuts against it?
  5. Kritarth spends 68 hours a sprint on refinement and gets 24 per cent readiness. Is the correct response more refinement, less refinement, or different refinement — and what would you have to believe about the June re-baselining and the two auto-flagging squads to be confident in your answer?
  6. What should Aparna do on Monday morning — not in February, but in the first four hours? What, precisely, would she say to the board about the Riyadh date, given that Ravi has already told the investor it will hold, and what does she risk by saying it?

The rest of Sunday night

Her phone showed a message from Ravi, sent an hour earlier: Keep it simple tomorrow. They want to hear that we know what we are building. Below it, unsent, was her own draft reply, which began: That is the part I cannot promise. She did not send it. The rain had stopped. It was a quarter to midnight, and the board met in nine hours.

Backlog Management and Refinement: Queue, Inventory, or Illusion

For readers who know what refinement is and now need to referee arguments about it.

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

On 6 October 2026, in Pune, Vikram Sathe put one number on the screen and let the room sit with it. Sathe runs product at Kshipra Diagnostics Systems, maker of the KX-2 point-of-care haematology analyser, sold to some 900 small labs across India, and of the cloud console lab owners use to review results. The number was 412: open items across firmware, the on-device interface, and the console.

Kshipra ships on two clocks. The console releases every Thursday; firmware twice a year, in trains requiring regression testing against CDSCO registration and a change file for every altered behaviour. Sunita Rao, the engineering director, had spent September arguing that two clocks needed two backlogs. Farhan Qureshi, who owns quality and regulatory affairs, argued the opposite and harder: only a single ordered list let a firmware change and the console change depending on it be seen as one decision. Malini Desai, the chief executive, wanted the March 2027 train to carry the four items promised to the two largest lab chains, and to stop hearing that the team was still refining. Sathe's problem was not prioritisation but that nobody could say what 412 items cost.

Thirteen days later, Ira Bhatt faced a differently shaped version at Lakeer Money, a Mumbai app that reads users' bank and card statements and answers spending questions in natural language. Lakeer had 2.8 million monthly actives and shipped most weekdays. Its backlog was small — 168 items — but 61 percent were not features. They were evaluation failures: cases where the assistant answered wrongly, logged by Tanvi Iyer's applied-science group. Nikhil Warrier, the staff engineer on the assistant, objected on 19 October: "These aren't backlog items, they're measurements. Refine a measurement into a story and you'll ship a patch for each one and never fix the model." Bhatt had to decide whether a failure log belonged in the same queue as a roadmap, and if not, what governed it.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

Backlog management is holding pending work as an ordered list and keeping that order honest; refinement is the recurring work of making the near end executable — splitting, clarifying, sizing, deleting. The orthodox statement of the goal is Roman Pichler's DEEP. It descends from Scrum practice of the early 2000s, called grooming until the 2017 Scrum Guide renamed it and declined to make it an event, holding it to be continuous work.

The more interesting ancestry is from manufacturing. Donald Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) supplied the frame sophisticated practitioners argue inside: a backlog is not a list but a queue, and a queue is inventory. Factory inventory is visible and counted; a team's is invisible, apparently free to hold, and uncounted. Reinertsen insisted it still costs — in information decay, in re-reading and re-deciding, and in delay imposed on everything behind it. That reframing separates the modern schools.

Table 1. Five positions, as propositions each camp would sign and would refuse.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Scrum orthodoxy (Schwaber, Sutherland, Pichler, Cohn)One ordered list, refined continuously, makes the next move obvious most cheaply.That the backlog should be abolished.
Flow and queueing (Reinertsen; Anderson)A backlog is inventory; its size is a cost, to be capped like any work-in-progress limit.That a large backlog is optionality.
Fixed-cycle betting (Singer's Shape Up)Keep no backlog; important ideas resurface, and those that do not were not important.That ordering a long list is productive work.
Discovery and empowered teams (Cagan, Torres, Patton)The flat list is the defect; structure work as outcomes and order follows.That hygiene rescues a backlog of wrong items.
Scaled arithmetic (SAFe; weighted shortest job first)Order should be computed from cost of delay divided by duration.That team intuition scales.

The disagreement does not split the difference. Singer's claim that Basecamp keeps no backlog because good ideas come back is a claim that a long list has negative expected value once the labour of re-reading it is priced. Reinertsen agrees on the cost, rejects the remedy: cap the queue, because a capped queue keeps sequencing information a memoryless system discards. Cagan would say both argue about plumbing while the water is dirty.

3. Mechanics, with the arithmetic done

The central tool is Little's Law: in a stable system the number of items in a queue equals arrival rate times average time in it, L = λW, or W = L ÷ λ. Kshipra's 412 items at a throughput of 9 per two-week sprint give an average wait of 412 ÷ 9 ≈ 45.8 sprints, about 21 months. That is the number Sathe should have opened with: it turns an argument about tidiness into a fact — the median item will not be touched before late 2028.

The second calculation is the balance equation. Intake over two quarters averaged 14 items a sprint against 9 shipped — accumulation of 5 a sprint, roughly 130 a year. A queue with permanent positive drift is not a managed backlog but an unbounded buffer, and Little's Law does not strictly apply, the system being unstable. Most teams learn this only when someone plots it.

The third calculation is the one novices skip: what refinement costs and buys. Kshipra ran two 90-minute sessions a sprint with six attendees — 18 person-hours against a capacity near 720, a shade over 2 percent, well inside the customary ten percent ceiling. At about eight items brought to written readiness per session, the team refined roughly 16 a sprint against intake of 14. On paper, sufficient. It was not, because refinement went to the most recent arrivals rather than the likeliest to be built.

Table 2. Kshipra: return on refining an item, by rank. Written readiness costs about 1.1 person-hours of engineering, design and quality time per item.

Of 138.6 person-hours refining, 88.9 — 64 percent — went into items never built and, on this evidence, unlikely ever to be. Confined to the top forty ranks, the same hours would have returned a hit rate near 53 percent, with no change in how well any item was understood. This is the second-order effect the standard advice conceals: "refine ten percent of capacity" is a budget, silent on allocation, and allocation is where the waste sits.

Three steps are usually left implicit. Refinement has a direction: top down until the budget runs out, not inbox forward. Ordering and clarification are different activities on different rhythms; collapse them and the loudest arrival wins both attention and rank. And deletion is a first-class output: a session producing no removals has avoided its hardest judgements.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The practice rests on three testable claims. One: order changes the outcome. True when items differ in value and capacity is constrained. At Kshipra it holds emphatically: a reagent-calibration defect and a console export format are not interchangeable. At Lakeer it holds weakly, because 103 instances of one retrieval weakness are not 103 independent decisions, and ranking them against each other is theatre.

Two: holding an item costs less than re-deciding it later. This is the claim Shape Up denies. It holds where context is expensive to rebuild: Kshipra's regulatory items carry a test protocol and audit trail taking days to reconstruct. It fails where context is cheap and perishable — Lakeer's June 2026 ideas referenced a card-aggregation API since changed twice.

Three: detail added now will still be right when the item is built. The empirical check is the half-life of an item's acceptance criteria — how long before a refined item must be re-refined. Kshipra measured about 70 days for console items, closer to 200 for firmware. That difference is physical, and the strongest argument Rao had.

The idea actively misleads when cost of delay is not linear in time. Weighted shortest job first assumes smooth decay, so earlier is proportionally better. Regulatory work is not like that: a change required by a CDSCO submission deadline carries near-zero cost of delay until the date, then a step of several crore in blocked revenue. Scored smoothly it sits mid-list for months, then becomes an emergency. Experts keep such items out of the scored queue and schedule them backwards from the date.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Hardware-plus-software is the sharpest case. A firmware item and its dependent console item differ in reversibility: the console change can be withdrawn on Friday, the firmware change cannot be withdrawn from 900 instruments in the field. Mature hardware companies use one list for ordering plus a commitment horizon per surface — inside it items are frozen, outside they are ordered but uncommitted. Kshipra's were one sprint for cloud, fourteen weeks for firmware. Rao's two-backlog proposal was really a request for two horizons: a weaker and better change than she asked for.

Two-sided marketplaces present reconciliation. At Jhelum Transport Network, a Delhi freight-matching platform, supply-side and demand-side items were refined by separate pods with separate intakes and metrics. Eleven straight sprints improved shipper experience while operator liquidity on the Delhi–Nagpur corridor fell: each pod's backlog was healthy, the pair was not. Mature marketplaces order against a shared constraint metric rather than merging lists — harder than it sounds, because both pods must accept their own queue starving for a while.

Regulated finance inverts the usual advice on pruning. At Kusum Wealth Systems, a Chennai platform serving registered investment advisers, an item untouched for two quarters may be waiting on a regulatory clarification, and archiving it destroys the record that the firm knew of the gap. Such items move to a dated deferral register rather than being deleted — auditors care about the distinction; product managers do not.

The costliest seam runs between a platform team and its consumers. At Karigar Platform Cloud, an infrastructure group inside a Bengaluru commerce company, the backlog was ordered by platform value while eight consuming teams sat blocked in a sequence nobody held. Item 47 on the platform list was item 1 on three product teams' lists. The honest fix is a published queue position and a stated wait time, so consumers plan against a number rather than escalate at a person.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

Queue length is a decision, not a measurement. Competent practitioners report backlog size; experts set a cap and enforce it, because an uncapped queue converts prioritisation into first-in-first-out by exhaustion. The tell is a team that states velocity precisely and queue length approximately. The obvious reading — a long backlog shows healthy demand — is wrong: demand never to be served is noise, and costs as much to carry.

The depth taper is a budget allocation, not a rule of thumb. Everyone says refine the top; experts compute where the marginal hour stops paying, as in Table 2, and recompute when throughput changes. The tell is an agenda built from the inbox, not the order. "Refine the next two sprints" is right only if those sprints are drawn from the top of the list, which in escalation-heavy organisations they are not.

Deletion is cheaper than archiving, archiving cheaper than carrying. Experts treat removal as a primary output; Kshipra settled at about four a session. The obvious reading is that deleting risks losing a good idea. The correction: the marginal good idea returns, while the marginal carried item is re-read in perpetuity at minutes per reader per month — across 412 items, a fraction of a role.

Age predicts value better than any score. Age is observable, cheap and unglamorous. The tell is a team that can produce an age histogram in thirty seconds; those who cannot have never looked. The obvious reading — old items are unattended good ideas — fails empirically. At Lakeer, items older than 180 days shipped at 4 percent against 47 percent for items under 30 days, and priority does not explain the gap: the old items had scored highly when young.

Estimates are a conversation protocol whose output is disagreement, not duration. Competent teams estimate to forecast; experts estimate to detect divergence, then stop once it stops appearing. The tell is a team that abandons pointing for work that has become uniform. The obvious reading is that this loses predictability; in fact, for uniformly sliced work, counting throughput forecasts better than summing points — the hardest part of #NoEstimates to refute.

Ordering authority must be singular; ordering input plural. The tell is an organisation where several may argue for a position and exactly one may grant it, with a timestamp and a reason. The obvious reading is that consensus is fairer. It is wrong specifically: consensus produces an order nobody defends, so the queue is re-litigated rather than worked.

An unenforced definition of ready is worse than none. It teaches the team that written criteria are decorative, contaminating the definition of done. The tell is stories entering a sprint with acceptance criteria written inside the planning meeting. A partial standard looks like partial progress; it gives false assurance, and the ambiguity surfaces inside the sprint, where it costs several times more to resolve.

Refinement cannot repair a backlog of the wrong items, and experts tell the two problems apart within one session. The diagnostic is whether splitting makes the team more confident or less: split a good item and the pieces are individually defensible; split a bad one and each piece prompts the question of why anyone wants it. The obvious reading — a stalled backlog needs better process — is why teams install a cadence, feel briefly better, and return a quarter later with a tidier list of the wrong things.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the ordering signal is statistical and fast, so backlogs churn and staleness dominates. In B2B and enterprise it is contractual and named, so the risk is reordering by largest account rather than largest effect. In platforms the risk is invisible blocking, as at Karigar, and the remedy is published wait times. In marketplaces it is one-sided optimisation, as at Jhelum.

Hardware genuinely differs, though not as usually claimed: not that it is slower, but that it has an irreversible commitment point, so its backlog needs a freeze horizon and a late-change protocol software does not. AI products differ too: much of their queue is measurements rather than intentions, and measurements aggregate into classes where features do not.

The difference is overstated on cadence. Weekly refinement is not inherently better for consumer and worse for enterprise; cadence follows the half-life of the information, which at Kshipra varied more within the company than between the two firms. Stage matters more crudely: below fifty items a founder's memory beats any process; between fifty and three hundred the formal apparatus earns its cost; above that the binding constraint becomes intake governance — who may add.

8. Three worked examples

Kshipra, and the horizon fix. Sathe kept one list, rejected the second backlog, gave Rao the two freeze horizons her argument required, and capped the queue at 150. Getting from 412 to 150 was not a mass deletion but a four-week close-out: every item older than 300 days went to a named owner with five days to defend it in two sentences. Of 168 such items, 22 were kept, 39 moved to Qureshi's deferral register, 107 were removed. With an intake gate routing field escalations through weekly triage, arrivals fell from 14 to 8.5 a sprint against throughput of 9 — a small negative drift. By March 2027 the queue stood at 143 and the firmware train carried all four promised items.

Lakeer, and the decision not to refine. Bhatt accepted Warrier's objection in part. The 103 eval failures left the backlog for a taxonomy kept by Iyer's group, clustered into nine classes. Only a class, never an instance, could become a backlog item, and only above 2 percent of weekly sessions; two qualified in November. Arithmetically, 168 items became 65, of which 21 were roadmap. The effect on the work was larger: the biggest class, date-range misinterpretation, had generated 31 tickets — 31 patches under the old scheme; as one class it produced one retrieval change that closed 27 of them.

Latika Retail Systems, and the failure. Latika, a Hyderabad supplier of store-operations software to grocery chains, declared backlog bankruptcy in February 2026: 1,240 of 1,600 items closed in one afternoon under the note "bulk closure — recreate if needed." It looked like a triumph for eleven weeks. Then the recreations began — 180 by June, many duplicating work partly done, because the closures had erased provenance: who asked, when, and what had been investigated. Three items in the sweep were contractual commitments to a 240-store chain, whose July renewal was signed at reduced scope, costing about ₹2.1 crore in annual recurring revenue.

The fault was not the deletion but that deletion had been treated as an event rather than a practice, run without provenance or an owner-defence step. Recovery took two quarters: rebuild the commitment set from contracts, restore provenance for anything a customer had named, then institute the continuous, owner-defended close-out Kshipra later used. The final queue was barely larger than the one bankruptcy produced — but defensible, which the first was not.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Table 4. Each mode leaves a trace in the tracker long before it appears as a missed quarter.
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Unbounded queueArrivals beat throughput three sprints runningWhat is our net drift per sprint?Order becomes first-in-first-out
Refinement at the wrong endAgenda built from newest itemsWhat share of refined items shipped?The refinement budget buys nothing
Rank read as promiseSales quoting ticket numbersWho outside the team reads our order?Reordering turns political; the queue freezes
Instances instead of classesMany tickets, one root causeWhat share of defects sits in three classes?Patches that never move it
Deletion as an eventBulk closures, no per-item reasonWho asked for this, and when?Lost provenance, rework, broken commitments
Cross-team blockingEscalations rise; platform queue looks healthyWhose top item is our item 47?Consumers route around it

All six are cheap to detect — the tracker holds the evidence — and expensive to catch late, when the damage has left the tracker for contracts, architecture and trust.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Whether to keep a backlog at all. The abolitionist position rests on a real observation: at Basecamp, ideas that mattered returned unprompted, and the labour of maintaining a list was never recovered. It fails where re-decision cost is high and memory unreliable — Kshipra's case, where context took days to rebuild and nobody recalled a 2024 audit finding. It is strongest for small teams with stable membership, weakest at the organisations that quote it most.

Whether ordering should be computed. The scoring camp rests on evidence that unaided ordering is inconsistent: the same portfolio scored twice by one group yields different orders. Opponents rest on a sharper point — the inputs to weighted shortest job first are themselves estimates, so the formula launders judgement into arithmetic and makes it harder to challenge. Computation loses if input error swamps ordering error, and there is no settled evidence either way, because almost nobody measures it.

Whether a backlog should be flat. Patton's story mapping and Torres's opportunity trees hold that a one-dimensional list destroys structure: that items 19 and 74 serve one outcome is invisible in rank order. Defenders of flatness answer that structure shelters pet projects, since every item serves some outcome. The dispute is live at Lakeer, where class-versus-instance is a structural argument in disguise.

Whether refinement is the team's work or the product manager's. Orthodoxy says shared. The dissent, from senior engineers, is that a product manager who cannot bring an item to readiness alone is outsourcing homework at engineering rates — an 18-person-hour session a prepared PM could replace with three. It fails if refinement's value lies in surfacing engineering disagreement rather than producing documents, which is the orthodox claim and, as it happens, equally unmeasured.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this installs a cadence and a checklist. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They quote the queue as a number with a cap and a drift, as a finance manager quotes working capital. They can say what refinement cost last quarter and what share went to items that shipped. They remove things in public, with reasons, at a steady rate, willing to be wrong about single removals because they trust the policy. And they can tell within a session whether the list is disordered or wrong, and refuse to refine the second problem.

The negative tell is as clear. The student defends the backlog's contents item by item; the master defends the rules — cap, intake gate, horizon, removal rate — and treats any item's fate as a consequence of them rather than a matter for negotiation.

12. What each protagonist decided

Sathe refused Rao's second backlog and granted the two freeze horizons her argument required, reasoning that separate lists would hide the firmware-to-console dependencies Qureshi's audit trail rests on. He capped the queue at 150, made removal a standing output with an owner-defence step, and moved regulatory items into date-driven scheduling. His argument to Desai was arithmetic: at 412 items and 9 a sprint, the company had been promising from a queue whose median item was 21 months away.

Bhatt split the queue by kind rather than size. Measurements went to a taxonomy governed by thresholds; intentions stayed in the backlog. She conceded Warrier's central point and kept one thing he disliked: the two qualifying classes entered the same ordered list as features, because a parallel quality queue would let the team ship features while quality debt accumulated unranked beside them.

Discussion questions

  1. Kshipra's cap of 150 is arbitrary. What evidence would justify 90 instead, and what would the company lose at that level?
  2. Bhatt's rule promotes a failure class only above 2 percent of weekly sessions. What serious failures does a frequency threshold miss, and what second rule would catch them?
  3. Latika and Kshipra removed comparable proportions of their backlogs. Which procedural differences made one defensible and the other not, and which would you skip under time pressure?

13. Going deeper

Agile in practice supplies the cadence refinement lives inside. User stories and epics is the craft of the units; splitting quality decides whether Table 2's arithmetic is measurable. The software development lifecycle shows the other queues — review, test, release — where most delay accumulates. Kanban and flow continues this page's quantitative argument, treating queue caps and Little's Law properly. The execution rhythm covers how ordering is communicated between planning. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing takes up the divergence-versus-duration dispute above. Definition of done is the twin of the definition of ready; the two fail together. The PM–engineering relationship settles who owns readiness.
exp20v2-agile.quality.negotiation:
Negotiating Quality Bars and Cut Lines

What quality are we willing to ship this time, and who signs off?

1. Wednesday, 14 October, Pune

Pavitra Ambulkar had seven working days, since Tuesday 20 October, Dussehra, is a holiday in Maharashtra. Hindola Books, the Pune company where she managed the product, sold invoicing and tax-reconciliation software to 6,200 small traders who paid monthly. Release 7.4 added bulk upload of e-invoices, and its freeze, the moment after which code stops changing, fell on Friday 23 October, for shipping on Monday 26 October. Diwali was on 8 November, and Padmaraj Avhad, who ran customer success, reckoned that the fortnight after it carried about 1.6 times a normal fortnight's invoices.

The defect list that morning ran to 38 items. Pranjali Akhade, the engineering manager, had 14 engineer-days of fixing capacity left before the freeze. Sales wanted the date held. Padmaraj wanted nothing shipped that would phone his team during the festive peak. Neither was unreasonable, and without a rule Pavitra expected the argument to be won by whoever spoke last on Friday afternoon. Table 1 shows what was open.

TierMeaning at HindolaOpen
S1Shows a wrong tax or money figure, or loses data3
S2Degrades or blocks a task, but a workaround exists9
S3Cosmetic, or rare and trivial26
TotalAll open defects, 14 October38

Table 1. Open defects on release 7.4, by severity tier.

The cost of getting this wrong ran in both directions. Ship a wrong figure into a trader's return and the damage is to trust, which does not come back with a patch. Hold the release past the festive window and the commercial case for bulk upload weakens by the day.

2. The idea

A quality bar is the written minimum a release must meet before it ships, stated as limits on known defects by severity. A cut line is the point in the ranked work where capacity runs out and everything below is knowingly left undone. Negotiating the two means agreeing in advance, between product, engineering and whoever absorbs the consequences, what the bar is for each kind of release and who may waive it.

The problem it solves is old. The project triangle of time, cost and quality, usually credited to Martin Barnes in 1969, says one corner gives when another is held. In software, quality is the corner that gives silently, because nobody schedules it. Scrum's definition of done, the checklist that makes a piece of work finished and which Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland codified in the Scrum Guide, writes the bar down for one item of work. This topic applies the same discipline to a whole release, and adds the decision no checklist can make: what happens when the bar and the date collide.

Different releases deserve different bars, and Table 2 is the one Pavitra put on the wall.

Release typeS1 allowedS2 allowedS3 allowedSigners
Hotfix00 in changed areaanyEngineering manager
Standard0430Product and engineering
Major, tax-touching0220Both, plus customer success

Table 2. Hindola's bars, by release type.

The sentence she could repeat without sounding glib was this: we decide what we will ship broken before we are tired, and we write down who signed.

3. How it works

The mechanics have five steps, and practitioners usually leave three implicit. Figure 1 shows the flow, and the paragraphs after it walk Release 7.4 through it.

Figure 1. From release type to a recorded decision. Steps 4a to 4c are alternatives, often combined.

First comes classification. Release 7.4 changed upload and display but not the tax engine, so Pavitra and Pranjali filed it as Standard. That choice is itself negotiated, because the Major row is stricter, and the first implicit step is to agree who may classify and on what evidence.

Second is tiering. Every open defect receives a tier against the definitions in Table 1, and the second implicit step is that the person assigning the tier is not the person who would have to fix it. Third, the counts are compared with the bar. Release 7.4 had three S1 against a limit of zero, and nine S2 against four.

The fourth step is where the negotiation happens. A gap can be closed by fixing, by moving the date, or by a signed waiver. The third implicit step is pricing each, in engineer-days, in days of delay, and in how many customers meet the defect. Finally the decision is recorded, and after the release someone asks whether the bar was right.

4. A worked example, line by line

The three S1 defects cost 2, 3 and 1 engineer-days, which is 6 days and is not negotiable, since the bar for S1 is zero. That left 14 minus 6, or 8 days, for the nine S2 defects. The bar required fixing at least five. Table 3 lists them with the number of accounts that would meet each in its first 30 days after release, and a ranking by exposure per day of work.

Taking items in order of exposure per day, a heuristic that I checked against alternatives at each capacity used here, gives 1, 5, 2, 4, 3, which cost 1+2+1+2+2 = 8 days exactly. Four S2 defects remain open (items 6, 7, 8 and 9), meeting the bar, with 310+185+410+740 = 1,645 pairs still exposed. That is 20.2 per cent of 8,155.

Now change one input. On Wednesday 21 October Padmaraj reports a fourth S1: bulk-uploaded credit notes round tax to the wrong paisa. It costs 3 days. S1 work becomes 9 days, S2 capacity falls to 5, and the best use is items 1, 5 and 4, taking 5 days and covering 4,960 pairs. Six S2 defects stay open against a bar of four. The bar and the date now collide. Option C costs least, by ₹14,400 against B and ₹70,400 against A. The margin over B is thin. B overtakes C if the contact rate falls below about 16 per cent (at 15 per cent, B is ₹1,91,700 against C’s ₹1,95,900), and A overtakes B above about 29 per cent. At 30 per cent C is lowest, at ₹3,31,800 against A’s ₹3,77,400 and B’s ₹3,83,400. The model separates A from the others but not B from C, so what tipped Pavitra was that B breaches the bar by two items and C by one.

5. Seven nuances

A bar is not a target

A bar is the minimum for shipping. A target is what the team hopes to reach. Teams that treat four open S2 defects as the goal tend to arrive at four every time, since the bar then fixes what they stop at.

Severity is not priority

Severity is the harm a defect does when it occurs. Priority is the order in which it is fixed. A cosmetic flaw on the login screen may be low severity and high priority, because everyone sees it. The bar counts severity, and the cut line follows priority.

Counting hides distribution

Table 3 shows nine S2 defects whose exposure runs from 185 to 2,170 accounts. A bar of four treats item 7 and item 5 alike. Counts are cheap and legible, and exposure is closer to the truth, so use the count as the rule and exposure as the tiebreak.

Zero for S1 is a definition, not a law

The bar is only as firm as the tier definitions beneath it. If S1 is widened, the zero becomes unreachable and gets waived; if narrowed, the zero becomes easy and meaningless. Review the definitions whenever waivers cluster.

Release classification is the quiet lever

Whoever may call a release Hotfix or Standard may loosen its bar without anyone noticing. Fix the criteria in writing: touches tax logic, touches payments, changes data. Anything doubtful goes to the stricter row.

The signer must bear the consequence

A waiver signed only by those who benefit from the date is a permission slip. Padmaraj's team answers the phones, so customer success signs the Major row. Ask of any waiver who pays if it goes wrong, and whether that person signed.

The bar governs only defects you have found

Nothing here estimates the defects nobody has discovered. A clean bar on a thinly tested release is a statement about the testing. Ask how long the build has been in testers' hands, and what share of customer-reported defects in the last three releases had been unknown at ship.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

SettingThe bar leans onDistinct signer
Consumer appCrash-free sessions, staged rolloutGrowth or app-store owner
B2BContracts, named customers, workaroundsCustomer success
MarketplacePayments and trust on both sidesTrust and operations

Table 5. What changes the bar, by product type.

A consumer app cannot recall a binary already installed, so its bar rests on rollout, releasing to 1 per cent of users first with a crash threshold that halts expansion. Hindola, a B2B product, is different: the harm is concentrated, a few accounts feel a defect heavily, and contracts can make a named customer's S3 into someone's S1.

A marketplace has two customer sets, and a defect on the seller side surfaces as buyer distrust, so payment and listing flows get the strict row whatever their size. Scale changes the mechanism too. An early-stage company of ten engineers can have one conversation and one signer. A large one needs the bar as a published policy, because the people arguing may never meet.

7. Common mistakes

The first is renegotiating the bar every Friday. From outside you see the ship date never slipping while the count of open S2 defects creeps up release after release. The misunderstanding is treating the bar as an aspiration. The cheapest diagnostic is to plot open S2 at ship for the last six releases.

The second is letting the fixer or the seller assign severity. The symptom is an S1 count that is implausibly zero, or swings wildly between teams. The root is that tiering is treated as a judgement about people. Have a second person re-tier ten random defects and compare.

The third is the waiver with no owner and no expiry. The same defect appears in the release notes of three consecutive releases. A waiver was read as a permanent exemption. List every waiver older than one release and ask who still owns it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Release 7.4 reaches Friday with the argument already finished. Table 6 is the record Pavitra filed, short enough to read in a minute and specific enough that a stranger can audit it.
