SignedAmbulkar, Akhade, Avhad
ExpiresRelease 7.5

Table 6. The waiver record for Release 7.4.

Nobody is surprised by it, and the date moved only as far as the pricing said it should.

9. What Pavitra decided

She chose Option C. Shipping moved one working day, from Monday 26 October to Tuesday 27 October. Four S2 fixes went in alongside all four S1 fixes, and the waiver in Table 6 covered the breach, five open against four. She chose it because it was cheapest at the assumed rate and breached the bar by one item rather than two, because Padmaraj had signed although a Standard release did not require it, and because she could defend a one-day slip to sales with a number.

To learn next, read the definition of done, which fixes the bar for a single item, and then the economics of delay, which turns Hindola's ₹60,000 a day from an assumption into a measurement.

Two questions to sit with. Which of your own releases shipped a defect that was known and unspoken, and who would have signed had you asked? And if your S1 definition were read aloud to your most demanding customer, would they agree it covers what hurts them?
exp40v2-agile.quality.negotiation:
Delivery & Technology · Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

Negotiating Quality Bars and Cut Lines

What quality are we willing to ship this time, and who signs off?

Ledgerline, Kestrel Home and Fernway are composite companies, and their people are fictional. The figures in this case are illustrative but internally consistent. The named authors, books and practices in the intellectual history are real.

1 · OPENINGTwo rooms, two weeks apart

On Tuesday 7 November 2023, Priya Raman, vice president of product at Ledgerline, sat down to a release review she had expected to be routine. Ledgerline sells payroll software to about 1,800 mid-market employers. It has roughly 240 staff and a recent Series C. Release 24.1 carried the year-end changes customers need to run their final payroll and generate annual tax forms. It had to reach production by 15 December. That date belonged to the calendar and to the tax authorities, not to Ledgerline.

Daniel Mercer, the quality lead, put the open-defect list on the screen. Ledgerline's written bar for a major release was explicit: zero open severity-1 defects, no more than five severity-2, and every severity-2 accompanied by a documented workaround. The list showed one severity-1 and nine severity-2.

The severity-1 was a rounding error in retroactive pay. It appeared only for employees who had moved between states mid-period. Mercer estimated it would touch about 40 customers. Hana Ito, the engineering director, said a proper fix needed nine engineer-days. Clearing the severity-2 list down to five needed another fourteen. The team did not have twenty-three spare engineer-days.

Ito proposed cutting the release's headline feature, earned-wage access. That feature had been promised to three enterprise prospects whose combined contracts were worth about $1.1 million in annual recurring revenue. The chief revenue officer had already sent Raman a message: "We cannot be the company that slips EWA twice."

Two weeks earlier and four hundred miles away, Tomás Okafor had faced a different version of the same question. Okafor directs firmware product management at Kestrel Home, which makes smart thermostats. Kestrel has about 620,000 devices installed. Firmware 5.0 introduced a new scheduling algorithm and support for heat pumps. A retail partner had scheduled a heat-pump bundle promotion for 15 October, and the bundle depended on 5.0. The over-the-air rollout was planned for 2 October, before the heating season began.

The 14-day beta on 4,000 devices had produced two worrying numbers. First, 0.21 percent of devices rebooted unexpectedly at least once, against a baseline of 0.05 percent. Second, three devices, or 0.075 percent, had "soft-bricked": they needed a factory reset before they would work again.

Kestrel's written bar for an over-the-air release said zero bricks in beta and a reboot rate no worse than 1.5 times baseline. Both thresholds were breached. A thermostat that fails in January is not an inconvenience. In some homes it is a burst pipe or a cold infant.

Both protagonists had a written bar. Both were being asked, by competent colleagues with real money at stake, to treat that bar as a starting position rather than a commitment. This case is about what each should do. It is also about the general question underneath. When a team has written down what quality it is willing to ship, what is that document actually for, and when should it bend?

2 · THE IDEADefinition, history and the schools that disagree

A quality bar is a set of observable, pre-agreed conditions a release must meet before it ships. It typically covers open defects by severity, performance and reliability thresholds, security findings, accessibility, and data correctness. A cut line is the boundary drawn through a ranked list of scope. Everything above the line ships in this release. Everything below it waits.

The two concepts are partners. The cut line is the mechanism by which a team protects the bar when time runs short. The "negotiation" in the title is the conversation in which product, engineering, quality and commercial leaders decide which of the two moves. A bar is per release type because a hotfix, a quarterly feature release, a regulated filing release and a firmware update carry different costs of being wrong. And the bar lives, as the prerequisite topic notes, in the definition of done for the release as a whole, not just for individual stories.

The intellectual lineage runs through manufacturing. In the early 1960s the Martin Company's Pershing missile programme popularised "zero defects," and Philip Crosby, who worked there, carried the idea into Quality Is Free (1979). Crosby defined quality as conformance to requirements. On this view the cost of non-conformance always exceeds the cost of prevention.

Joseph Juran offered a rival definition, "fitness for use," which made quality relative to a customer's purpose rather than to a specification. Toyota's production system contributed the andon cord. Any worker could stop the line on detecting a defect, which turned quality from an inspection activity into a stopping rule that anyone could invoke.

Software inherited both definitions and argued about them. Barry Boehm's Software Engineering Economics (1981) popularised the claim that a defect costs far more to fix the later it is found. That claim underwrote decades of heavy pre-release gating.

In 1995 Edward Yourdon's IEEE Software essay "When Good Enough Software Is Best" argued the opposite emphasis. Delay is itself a cost, and the right quality is the one that maximises value, not the one that minimises defects. James Bach sharpened this into "good enough quality" (1997): a release is good enough when its benefits sufficiently outweigh its problems, and when further improvement would cost more than it is worth.

The same year, Michael Cusumano and Richard Selby's Microsoft Secrets documented the "synch-and-stabilize" method: daily builds, milestones that ended with stabilisation periods, and triage meetings that ranked bugs and decided which would be fixed. The vocabulary of "bug bars" and "ship rooms" spread through the industry from practices of this kind.

Two later contributions changed the terms of the debate. The Google book Site Reliability Engineering (2016) formalised the error budget. If a service promises 99.9 percent availability, the remaining 0.1 percent is a budget the team may spend on risky releases. When it is exhausted, releases stop. This converted a negotiation into a pre-committed number.

Separately, Jez Humble and David Farley's Continuous Delivery (2010) and the later research summarised in Accelerate (Forsgren, Humble and Kim, 2018) argued that release frequency and stability are positively, not negatively, correlated across organisations. On that reading, the right response to quality risk is often smaller and more reversible releases rather than higher gates.

The problem all of these were invented to solve is the same. Under schedule pressure, the person closest to the deadline systematically underweights risks borne by someone else, and quality is the corner of the triangle easiest to cut invisibly. A bar is a pre-commitment device. It records, in a calm moment, what the organisation believes so that it cannot quietly unbelieve it in a frantic one.

Where the schools part company is on what may legitimately move. The table below states, for each school, a proposition its adherents would sign and one they would refuse.

Exhibit 1

SchoolCore figuresWould signWould not sign
Conformance / zero-defectCrosby; andon tradition"The bar is fixed; when time is short, scope moves, never quality.""Some known severe defects are an acceptable commercial trade."
Economic / good-enoughJuran, Yourdon, Bach"The bar is a value judgement re-made for each release on the evidence.""A bar written months ago should bind a decision made with today's information."
Budgeted / SLOGoogle SRE"Express the bar as a number agreed in advance and enforce it mechanically.""Senior judgement at ship time should override the budget."
Reversibility / continuous deliveryHumble, Farley, Forsgren"Make it cheap to be wrong; then the pre-release bar can be lower.""Bigger pre-release gates reliably produce better outcomes."

The four schools can be placed on two dimensions. The first is whether the bar is fixed in advance or negotiated at ship time. The second is whether quality is secured mainly by gating before release or by limiting damage after it.

The map matters because most heated ship-room arguments are not about facts. They are about quadrants. Ledgerline's chief revenue officer is arguing a good-enough position, which re-weighs the evidence today. Mercer is defending a conformance position, which holds that the bar was set for exactly this moment.

Neither is confused. They hold different theories of what the bar is for. The thesis this case develops is that the height of a bar should be indexed to the irreversibility and blast radius of the release. Once that index is fixed, scope rather than the bar should absorb schedule pressure, except in specific, nameable conditions where the bar's own assumptions fail.

3 · MECHANICS IN DEPTHHow experts actually set, measure and defend a bar

Expert practice has six steps. Most organisations perform three of them and leave the rest implicit, which is where negotiations go wrong.

The bar is written per release type, before the release has a date. Ledgerline distinguishes hotfixes, monthly minor releases, and the annual year-end release. Kestrel distinguishes app releases, cloud changes and firmware. The bar for each is set by asking what a defect costs to reverse in that release type. A cloud configuration error at Kestrel can be rolled back in minutes. A firmware defect that bricks a device needs a person to touch it.

Severity is defined with worked examples, not adjectives. "Severity-1: incorrect money movement or tax filing for any customer; data loss; safety risk" is usable. "Severity-1: critical" is not. Without examples, severity labels drift with schedule pressure. This drift is the single most common way bars are breached without anyone admitting it.

The bar covers both known and estimated unknown defects. The open-defect count measures what has been found. The question that matters is what remains. During a stabilisation period, defect discovery usually decays. That decay can be modelled crudely but usefully, which is the quantitative core of the topic.

Ledgerline found 31 new defects in the first week of stabilisation, then 22, 16 and 11. Each week's count is roughly 0.7 of the previous week's. If the decay continues geometrically, the total still to be found by indefinite testing is about 11 × 0.7 / (1 − 0.7), or roughly 26 defects. Ledgerline's history shows that about 8 percent of late-found defects are severity-1 or severity-2. That implies about two serious latent defects at ship, in addition to the ten known. The class of models behind this calculation is called software reliability growth modelling; its best-known early example is Goel and Okumoto (1979).

The second-order point is that this model only works if testing effort is held roughly constant. If the team diverts testers to build earned-wage access, discovery falls. The curve will look as if the release is converging when it is merely being looked at less. Experts therefore report the decay together with the hours of testing behind it.

The cut line is drawn on a ranked list, not a list of features. A ranked list forces the conversation that matters: if we can only have one more thing, which is it? Scope items should be ranked by value per engineer-day, adjusted for whether a partial version is shippable.

Cutting a feature late leaves residue. Half-written code sits behind a feature flag. Migrations may have run. Documentation has been written. Sales has made promises. The true cost of a cut is the work forgone plus the cost of parking what was started. Teams that cut cleanly plan for this from the beginning, by building features dark and behind flags so that a cut is a configuration change rather than a revert.

One person signs, and the signer bears the downside. Mature organisations name a single accountable approver for each release type. Committees diffuse responsibility in exactly the way the bar exists to prevent. The approver should be someone who will personally own the consequence of a bad ship, which is usually the general manager or product leader for the affected customers. The quality lead's role is to certify the facts, not to make the commercial decision. The distinction is subtle and contested; it is taken up in section 10.

Exceptions are written, priced and given an expiry. When a bar is breached deliberately, the exception record states what was accepted, why, what mitigation is in place, who approved it, and by what date the defect will be fixed. Exceptions without expiry dates accumulate into a second, lower, unwritten bar.

The sociologist Diane Vaughan's study of the Challenger launch decision (1996) gave this process a name: the normalisation of deviance. Each accepted anomaly becomes the baseline against which the next is judged. The diagnostic is simple. Count how many exceptions in the last four releases expired without being fixed.

The budgeted school adds a final formal device. A 99.9 percent monthly availability target leaves 0.1 percent of a 30-day month, about 43.2 minutes, as an error budget. If Ledgerline's API team had burned 31 minutes by the twelfth of the month, the remaining 12 minutes would constrain how risky any further release could be. The decision becomes arithmetic rather than rhetoric. Its weakness is that it covers only what the service-level objective measures. A rounding error in retroactive pay consumes no availability at all.

4 · WHEN IT APPLIESFour testable conditions, applied to both protagonists

The standard advice is to hold the bar and move the cut line. That advice rests on four assumptions. Each can be stated as a testable claim. When one fails, the standard advice can mislead.

Exhibit 4

ConditionTestLedgerlineKestrel
C1. DetectabilityCan pre-release testing find defects of the kind that matter, at roughly the rate users would?Mostly. Payroll is deterministic; test fixtures for multi-state employees exist.Partly. Bricks appear at rates near the limit of what a 4,000-device beta can resolve.
C2. ReversibilityCan a shipped defect be undone quickly and cheaply?Code yes; filed tax forms and paid wages no.OTA can be halted, but a bricked device cannot be updated remotely.
C3. Observability of the barIs every clause measurable by someone other than its author?Yes: defect counts by written severity.Yes: reboot and brick telemetry.
C4. Separable scopeIs there scope that can be cut without damaging what remains?Yes: EWA is flagged and independent.Weakly: heat-pump support and the scheduler share a control loop.

Applied to Ledgerline, three conditions hold cleanly. The fourth, reversibility, fails in the direction that makes the bar more important. Once a wrong year-end tax form is filed, the error is not a bug report. It is an amended filing, which an employer has to explain to employees. The standard advice applies with full force: the bar holds and EWA is the natural cut.

Kestrel's case is subtler. Condition C1 is in doubt, because the beta is too small to measure the brick rate precisely. Condition C4 is weak, because the feature that justifies the release cannot easily be separated from the code suspected of causing the reboots. When both fail together, the correct move is often neither "hold the bar" nor "move the bar." It is to change the shape of the release, through a staged rollout and narrower eligibility, so that the bar's assumptions hold again.

There are three situations where the bar is actively misleading. The first is when the dominant risk is building the wrong thing, not building it badly. An early-stage product with zero defects and no users has met a bar that does not measure what matters.

The second is when the bar measures the wrong dimension. A team can meet every defect threshold and still ship something slow, ugly or confusing. Noriaki Kano's distinction between "must-be" and "attractive" quality (1984) is a reminder that a defect bar covers only the first.

The third is when meeting the bar is itself riskier than missing it. A security patch that fixes an actively exploited vulnerability should ship with known cosmetic defects. A bar that blocks it has inverted its own purpose. Mature organisations write this into the bar as an explicit exemption for hotfixes, rather than leaving it to heroics.

5 · HARD EDGE CASESSeams, sides, regulators, atoms and models

Multi-product. When several products share a component, such as an identity service or a design system, the component inherits the strictest bar of any product that consumes it. In practice, platform teams publish one bar and product teams discover in the ship room that it was set for the least demanding consumer. The organisations that handle this well require each consuming product to declare its requirements of the shared component. The platform's bar is then set by the strictest declaration, not by its own team's sense of adequacy. Those that handle it badly learn which product had the strictest need from an incident.

Two-sided products. A marketplace has two populations whose experience of a defect differs. A search-ranking regression that buyers barely notice can cut a long-tail seller's sales by a third. Bars written from the perspective of the side that is easier to measure, usually buyers through conversion, systematically under-protect the other side. The mature fix is a separate set of seller-side guardrail metrics with their own thresholds.

Regulated products. In medical-device software, governed by standards such as IEC 62304, and in automotive functional safety under ISO 26262, part of the bar is set outside the company and is not negotiable. The negotiation moves upstream into how the product is classified, because classification determines the bar. The cut line becomes the only lever available. Companies say they "never compromise on compliance." What they actually do is argue hard, early and with lawyers about which features fall inside the regulated boundary.

Hardware plus software. Kestrel has three bars that interact: the factory image shipped on new units, over-the-air firmware, and the cloud and app. The factory image has the highest bar because it ships on units sitting in warehouses for months. Over-the-air firmware sits in the middle, because rollout can be halted but bricked units cannot be reached. Cloud and app sit lowest.

The seam that matters is that a lower-bar layer can break a higher-bar one. A cloud change that sends malformed schedules can crash correct firmware. Mature companies test the layers together on fleets of reference devices, and they hold cloud changes that touch device protocols to the firmware bar.

AI-native products. When outputs are stochastic, "zero open severity-1 defects" has no clear meaning. The bar becomes a threshold on an evaluation set, for example 95 percent correct on 400 labelled cases. That moves the hard question to whether the evaluation set represents production.

The binomial arithmetic is sobering. A measured 95.5 percent on 400 items has a 95 percent confidence interval of roughly 93.5 to 97.5 percent. That interval assumes the evaluation set is a fair sample of the inputs customers will send, which it usually is not. The Fernway example in section 8 shows what happens when the assumption fails.

Across all five cases, the most dangerous place is the organisational seam. A defect that belongs to no team's bar belongs to no team's fix list. The diagnostic question for any release is: which defect classes in this release does no one's bar cover?

6 · NUANCESWhat separates the expert from the competent practitioner

1. The bar's value is mostly realised before the ship room. A competent practitioner treats the bar as a gate checked at the end. An expert treats it as a planning input. A team that knows on day one that the year-end release needs zero severity-1 defects schedules its stabilisation time accordingly, so the bar is rarely tested by a crisis. The tell-tale sign is the date on which the bar for a release was written. If it was written after the schedule, it is a description of what the team hoped to achieve, not a constraint on what it committed to. The obvious reading, that a bar exists to say no at the end, mistakes its least important function for its main one.

2. Severity labels inflate and deflate with the calendar. In the last two weeks before a date, severity-1s get reclassified as severity-2s and severity-2s become "known issues." Each reclassification is defensible on its own. The expert watches for it in aggregate: a sharp rise in downgrades during the final fortnight, or downgrades made by people who are not the original triager. The obvious reading is that the defect list is improving. Sometimes only the labels have improved.

3. A clean defect list can mean testing stopped. As section 3 showed, discovery rates are only meaningful against effort. When testers are pulled onto scope work, the list goes quiet and everyone relaxes. The tell is that the open count falls while the testing-hours line falls with it. An expert always asks how many hours of testing produced this week's number.

4. The cut line is a commercial conversation dressed as a technical one. Engineering estimates determine where the line could go. Customer commitments determine where it will go. Competent practitioners argue estimates. Experts get the account executives into the room early and ask which commitment can be renegotiated, and at what cost. The tell is a ship-room meeting with no one from sales present, followed by an escalation from sales two days later.

5. Partial features are not free cuts. Cutting half of a feature often costs more than cutting all of it, because the half that ships needs its own testing, documentation and support. Experts rank scope by "shippable increments," not by features. The tell is a plan that says "we'll ship the basic version" without anyone having defined what the basic version does on its own.

6. The bar should differ by customer segment within a release. A release can ship to segments whose risk differs. Kestrel can send firmware to homes in mild climates first. Ledgerline can enable a feature for single-state employers before multi-state ones. Experts use segmentation to keep the bar fixed while changing the population it applies to. The tell is a rollout plan that treats all customers as one population when the defect obviously does not affect them equally.

7. Who signs matters less than whether the signer pays. An approver who will not hear the support calls, see the churn or answer to the regulator is structurally inclined to ship. Experts check whether the signer's own scorecard includes the downside. The obvious reading, that seniority confers judgement, misses incentive alignment entirely.

8. Exceptions need expiry dates more than they need approvals. Most organisations require sign-off for exceptions. Few require that the deferred defect be fixed by a named date. Without that, exceptions accumulate. The tell is a "known issues" list that is longer each quarter and has an oldest item more than two releases old.

9. Reversibility is a property of consequences, not of code. Engineers rightly say that code can be rolled back in minutes. But a wrong payment, a filed form, a lost customer record or a bricked device cannot be rolled back by reverting the deploy. Experts assess reversibility by asking what the user will have done with the output before the rollback. The obvious reading, "we can always roll back," conflates the artefact with its effects.

10. A bar that is never breached is probably set too low. If a team meets its bar every release without visible effort, the bar is not constraining anything. The expert expects occasional hard conversations and treats their absence as a signal to revisit the threshold.

7 · ACROSS PRODUCT TYPES AND STAGESWhere the differences are real

The practice differs across product types, but less than practitioners assume. The underlying logic, indexing the bar to irreversibility and blast radius, is the same everywhere. What differs is where irreversibility lives and who bears it.

Exhibit 5

Product typeWhere irreversibility livesTypical bar emphasisWho usually signs
Consumer softwareTrust, reviews, data lossCrash rate, performance, data integrityProduct lead
B2B and enterpriseCustomer operations, contracts, audit trailsData correctness, backward compatibility, securityGM, often with customer success
Platform and marketplaceThird-party businesses built on youAPI stability, both-sided guardrailsPlatform lead, with partner input
Hardware and physical goodsUnits in the field, safety, returnsBrick rate, safety, factory imageHardware GM, often with legal
AI productsDecisions users act onEval thresholds, high-severity error classesProduct lead with applied-research lead

In consumer software the difference is real but often overstated. Releases are frequent and rollouts can be staged, so the bar can be lower than in enterprise. Data loss and privacy failures, however, are as irreversible in consumer products as anywhere.

In enterprise the difference is real and large. Customers have built processes on the product, and their tolerance for change, even beneficial change, is low. Backward compatibility becomes a bar clause of its own.

Platforms and marketplaces differ in that the people harmed are often not the people who are measured, as section 5 noted. Hardware is the most distinct case, because irreversibility is physical. AI is distinct because the bar is statistical, and because the gap between evaluation and production is a defect class in itself.

Company stage matters more than product type. At seed stage, the risk of building the wrong thing dominates, and a heavy bar slows learning. A two-line bar is usually right: no data loss, no security holes, everything else negotiable.

From product-market fit through growth, the cost of defects rises with the customer base and the bar must be written down. This is the stage at which most companies set their bar too late. Ledgerline wrote its current bar after a bad year-end release two years earlier.

At scale, the bar becomes per release type and per segment, and the risk shifts to bureaucracy. Mature organisations add more gates than they need, because each incident adds a gate and nothing removes them. The plain truth is that for a given release type and stage, the logic is the same across product types. Only the location of irreversibility changes.

8 · THREE WORKED EXAMPLESTwo that held and one that failed

Example A: Ledgerline's cut line, priced

Raman's team ranked the remaining scope and costs. The table sets out the arithmetic she would eventually take to the executive team.

Exhibit 6

ItemEngineer-daysConsequence if not doneExpected cost
Fix retro-pay severity-19~40 customers need corrections; churn risk~$116,000
Fix four of nine severity-2s14Breach of written bar; added support load~$35,000
Ship EWA23Three enterprise deals at risk~$330,000
Expected costs are estimates. The severity-1 figure is $60,000 of correction and support work plus a 5% churn increase on $1.12m of affected ARR. The EWA figure assumes a 30% chance of losing $1.1m of ARR.

On these numbers, EWA has the highest expected cost of being cut. But the comparison is incomplete in two ways. First, EWA's risk is a probability of losing deals, and that probability can be reduced by talking to the three prospects; the severity-1's cost cannot be reduced by talking to anyone. Second, the severity-1 sits in the year-end release, whose consequences are irreversible, while EWA could ship in January without harming anyone except the sales forecast.

Raman therefore asked the account executives to call the three prospects with a January date. Two accepted the new date. The third, worth $380,000, asked for a pilot in December. That pilot could be delivered behind a flag for that customer alone, with EWA's own testing scoped to one employer's data. That reduced EWA's expected cost to roughly $115,000, below the severity-1's, and the cut was clear.

Example B: Kestrel's beta, read correctly

Okafor's problem was statistical before it was commercial. Three bricks in 4,000 devices is a point estimate of 0.075 percent. Because the count is so small, the uncertainty is large. Using the Poisson distribution, the 95 percent confidence interval for three observed events runs from about 0.62 to 8.77 events. Scaled to the 4,000-device beta, the brick rate could plausibly lie anywhere from 0.016 to 0.22 percent. Across 620,000 devices, that means between roughly 100 and 1,360 bricked thermostats.

The calculation shows that a larger beta cannot resolve the question fast enough. To be 95 percent confident of seeing at least one brick if the true rate were 0.01 percent, Kestrel would need about 30,000 devices, from the formula 1 − (1 − p)n ≥ 0.95. A related rule of thumb, the "rule of three," says that if zero events are seen in n trials, the 95 percent upper bound on the rate is about 3/n.

The useful fact was not in the statistics but in the logs. All three bricks occurred during a schedule migration on devices with older flash memory chips, about 22 percent of the fleet. On the newer chips the brick count was zero, consistent with a rate below roughly 0.1 percent on 3,100 devices.

That reshaped the decision. Kestrel could hold its bar, zero bricks, for the segment where it had evidence, and exclude the older chips until the migration code was fixed. The same segmentation applied to reboots. The elevated reboot rate was concentrated among heat-pump installations, which used the new control loop.

Example C: Fernway, where the bar was met and the release still failed

Fernway sells an AI contract-review assistant to in-house legal teams. In spring 2023 it set a bar for its new clause-extraction feature: at least 95 percent accuracy on a 400-clause evaluation set, with no regressions on any clause type. The model scored 95.5 percent. The release shipped to 30 pilot customers.

Within three weeks, a customer's lawyer found that the assistant had missed an uncapped indemnity clause in a supplier agreement. Fernway sampled 600 clauses from production documents, with customers' consent, and measured accuracy at about 88 percent. On indemnity and limitation-of-liability clauses, the categories where errors were most costly, it was closer to 81 percent.

The diagnosis was that the evaluation set had been built from public contract templates. These were cleaner and more standard than the negotiated, marked-up agreements customers actually uploaded. The bar had been met. The bar's assumption, that the evaluation represented production, had not.

The failure was not that the threshold was too low. It was that the bar measured a population the product did not serve. A competent team checked whether the model met the bar. An expert team would have asked how the evaluation set was drawn and by whom.

Recovery took nine weeks. Fernway switched the feature to "suggest only" mode, requiring a human to confirm every extraction. It rebuilt the evaluation set from consented production samples and set separate thresholds by clause type: 98 percent for indemnity and liability clauses, 92 percent for low-stakes clauses. It added an ongoing production audit of 100 randomly sampled extractions each week.

Two of the 30 pilots churned. Fernway's chief executive later described the episode as the moment the company learned that for an AI product, the evaluation set is the specification. The bar is only as good as the sample it is measured on.

9 · FAILURE MODESEarly warnings, diagnostic questions, and the cost of lateness

The failure modes below recur across companies and product types. Each has an early warning sign visible weeks before the damage, and a diagnostic question that catches it.

Exhibit 9

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching late
Bar written after the dateBar document newer than the plan"Was this bar a constraint on the plan or a summary of it?"Bar collapses at first pressure
Severity driftSpike in downgrades in the final fortnight"Who reclassified these, and against which written example?"Severe defects reach customers labelled as minor
Testing starvationOpen count falls with testing hours"How many hours produced this week's discovery rate?"False convergence; latent defects ship
Exception accumulationKnown-issues list grows each quarter"How many exceptions expired unfixed last quarter?"Normalised deviance; a lower de facto bar
Unrepresentative evaluationEval set drawn from convenient sources"How does the eval distribution compare to production?"Bar met, product fails (Fernway)
Signer without downsideApprover not on the hook for incidents"Who answers the call if this goes wrong?"Systematic bias toward shipping
Seam orphansDefects bouncing between team queues"Which defect classes does no team's bar cover?"Cross-team incidents with no owner

The common thread is that every failure mode is a way for the bar to stop constraining behaviour while remaining nominally in force. A bar that is visibly abandoned is at least an honest failure. A bar that is quietly hollowed out is worse, because leadership continues to rely on a protection that has gone. The cost of catching any of these late is not just the incident. It is the loss of the bar's credibility for every later release.

10 · WHERE EXPERTS DISAGREEFour live disputes

Should a written bar ever move at ship time?

The conformance position holds that it should not. A bar that can be renegotiated under pressure provides no protection, because pressure is the only condition under which anyone wants to renegotiate it. The evidence is Vaughan's analysis of the Challenger decision and the experience of organisations whose bars eroded through a series of individually reasonable exceptions. For this position to be wrong, it would have to be shown that organisations which permit ship-time renegotiation do not, over several years, see their de facto bar fall.

The economic position holds that a bar written months ago encodes worse information than is available today. Refusing to update it is a commitment to a stale model. The evidence is that many defects which seemed severe at bar-writing time turn out to matter little in context. For this position to be wrong, it would have to be shown that decision-makers under deadline pressure are, on average, worse judges than the same people were months earlier. There is considerable evidence from behavioural research on time pressure suggesting they are, but no direct evidence from software ship rooms.

Does the cost of a defect really rise steeply with lateness?

The traditional view, descended from Boehm, holds that a defect found in production can cost one or two orders of magnitude more than one found in design. This underpins heavy pre-release gating. Laurent Bossavit's The Leprechauns of Software Engineering (2012) traced the citations behind the most-quoted versions of this curve. He found that much of the supporting data was thin, old or misquoted.

The continuous-delivery school adds that in modern environments with feature flags and fast rollback, the curve may be much flatter for many defect classes. For the steep-curve view to be wrong, it would need to be shown that production defects in modern systems typically cost not much more than pre-release ones. That is plausibly true for reversible defects and plainly false for irreversible ones, which is why this case argues that reversibility, not lateness, is the variable that matters. Not every expert accepts that reframing.

Who should hold the veto?

One position holds that the quality lead or engineering leader should hold an outright veto on shipping. They are closest to the evidence and least exposed to commercial pressure. Some organisations give a single reviewer the power to stop a release, in the spirit of the andon cord.

The other position holds that the decision is commercial and belongs to whoever owns the outcome, typically the general manager. The quality function certifies facts but does not decide. The evidence for the first position is that commercial owners demonstrably over-ship under pressure. The evidence for the second is that quality functions with vetoes become cautious and that releases slow without corresponding quality gains.

Neither side has persuasive comparative data. This case does not resolve the dispute, because it does not believe the field has resolved it.

Does reversibility substitute for gating?

The continuous-delivery school, supported by the Accelerate research, argues that organisations which deploy more frequently also have lower change failure rates and faster recovery. On that reading, investment in reversibility pays better than investment in gates. Critics note that the research measures correlation across organisations. High performers may both deploy frequently and have strong pre-release practices; frequency may not cause stability.

Critics also note that the research draws heavily on web services, where reversibility is cheap. It says less about firmware, payroll or regulated software. For the substitution view to be wrong in general, it would need to be shown that equally reversible organisations with lighter gates have worse outcomes. For it to be wrong in Kestrel's or Ledgerline's case, it is enough that the consequences themselves cannot be reversed.

11 · WHAT MASTERY LOOKS LIKEBehaviour, not vocabulary

Someone who has studied this topic can recite the four schools and the six steps. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in ways an observer can see.

They write the bar before the plan, and they write it per release type. They ask for testing hours alongside defect counts. They ask how the evaluation set was drawn before they ask what the score was. They know who will answer the phone if a release goes wrong, and they make sure that person signs.

In a ship-room dispute, they first identify which quadrant each person is arguing from, and then ask what evidence would change each person's mind. They treat a cut line as a commercial conversation and bring sales into it early. They track exceptions by expiry date and raise the alarm when the known-issues list grows.

Most distinctively, they reach for a third option before accepting the binary of "hold the bar" or "move the bar." That option is usually to segment the release, narrow its scope or change its rollout, so that the bar holds for the population it is meant to protect. They do this not to avoid the hard conversation but because they understand that the bar's purpose is to protect people from irreversible harm. Usually there is more than one way to do that.

And they accept, without resentment, that some disputes in this area are genuinely unresolved. They state the disagreement plainly, make the call, write down why, and revisit it when the evidence comes in.

12 · CLOSINGThe decisions

On 9 November, Priya Raman presented the priced cut line to the executive team. The bar would hold. The retro-pay severity-1 and four severity-2s would be fixed, bringing the open count to the bar's maximum of five severity-2s, each with a written workaround.

EWA general availability moved to January. The account executives had already secured new dates with two prospects. The third would receive a single-customer pilot behind a flag, staffed from an engineer freed in December. Raman signed the exception record herself, with an expiry of 31 January, and copied the chief revenue officer.

Her reasoning was that the year-end release was the one release in the year whose consequences could not be reversed. Its bar existed for precisely this situation. Commercial pressure, by contrast, could be negotiated with customers, and largely was.

Tomás Okafor's decision, on 28 September, was more complex. Kestrel did not ship firmware 5.0 to the full fleet on 2 October. It shipped to devices with newer flash chips and without heat-pump installations, about 61 percent of the fleet, in four waves over two weeks. Each wave was held until reboot and brick telemetry from the previous one met the bar.

The heat-pump bundle shipped with a factory image containing a fix for the control-loop reboots, which had been found in the meantime. Units sold under the promotion were therefore never exposed to the defect. Older-chip devices received 5.1 in November, after the migration fix had passed a 6,000-device beta with zero bricks.

Okafor's reasoning was that Kestrel's bar was set correctly, but the release had been the wrong shape for the evidence. Segmenting the fleet let the bar hold for the populations it could be measured on. The retail partner's promotion went ahead on 15 October, two days later than planned for the online listing, because Kestrel waited for the second wave's telemetry before confirming.

Both protagonists kept their bars. Neither did so by saying no. Each did it by changing what was below the cut line, and to whom the release applied, so that the bar could do its job.

Discussion questions

  1. Ledgerline's chief revenue officer argued that a single-customer pilot of EWA was itself a release, with its own risk and no written bar. Was he right, and what bar should have applied to it?
  2. Kestrel's original bar of "zero bricks in beta" could not distinguish a manageable brick rate from a serious one at a 4,000-device sample. Should the bar have been written differently, and if so, how, given that a larger beta would have delayed the season?
  3. If Fernway's evaluation set had been drawn from production from the start, would a 95 percent overall threshold have been appropriate? What does the answer imply about whether a single number can ever serve as the bar for an AI product?

13 · GOING DEEPERWhere this topic leads

Cost, quality, time trade-offs
The parent topic: why quality is one corner of the triangle, and why it is the corner most often cut invisibly. It unlocks a precise vocabulary for what the cut line trades against.
Definition of done
The bar is written in the definition of done for the release as a whole. Reading it next shows how story-level and release-level done fit together.
The software development lifecycle
Explains where stabilisation, testing and release gates sit in the overall process, and why their placement shapes how the bar is experienced.
Agile in practice
Shows how iterative delivery changes the bar's role from end-of-project gate to continuous constraint, and where agile mechanics can obscure rather than serve quality.
Kanban and flow
Brings work-in-progress limits and flow metrics to bear on quality, unlocking the idea that a bar can be enforced at each stage rather than only at release.
The execution rhythm
Covers the cadence of planning, review and release in which bars are set and tested, and how rhythm makes the bar predictable rather than a surprise.
Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing
The estimates that determine where the cut line can go. Understanding their uncertainty is essential to drawing the line credibly.
Backlog management and refinement
The ranked list on which the cut line is drawn. A well-refined backlog makes cuts quick and clean; a poor one makes them a crisis.
exp20v2-agile.scaled:
Scaled Delivery: Multiple Teams

Delivery & Technology: how several squads ship together without a programme office eating the product

1. Nine squads, one deadline

On Tuesday 3 March 2026, Tusharika Dhurat, chief product officer of Kothrud Pay Technologies, opened a spreadsheet with a number she disliked. Kothrud, a Pune company that builds QR and soundbox payment products for small merchants on India's UPI rails, ran nine squads, each a standing team of eight people owning one slice of the product. The coming quarter's backlog held 54 features. Thirty-one needed work from more than one squad. The largest, a merchant credit line offered through a partner bank, needed four, and the bank's launch window closed on 30 June. The next window, the partner had said, was in October.

Two colleagues wanted a decision by Friday. Tejendra Dhamankar, a programme director hired from a large bank, proposed a six-person programme office and a two-day planning event for all nine squads every quarter. Tamasi Dongerkar, who led platform engineering, wanted neither: she had watched coordination layers grow until the layer, not the product, set the pace. Each described a real risk. Dhurat's task was to establish what the company would actually pay for under each answer.

2. The idea

Scaled delivery is the practice of getting several teams, each working in short cycles, to release one coherent product. Nothing about a single squad changes. What grows is the number of places where one team's output becomes another team's input. A dependency is work that cannot finish until another team delivers something; a handoff is one such crossing.

The problem is old. In The Mythical Man-Month (1975) Fred Brooks noted that n people have n(n-1)/2 possible communication paths, so coordination outgrows capacity. Figure 1 applies the same arithmetic to squads: six have 15 pairings, nine have 36, twelve have 66. Brooks's figure is a ceiling, not a forecast. Kothrud's tickets showed 20 of its 36 pairs, 56 per cent, exchanging work, and that observed number is the one that matters.

The responses came from the 2000s onward. Craig Larman and Bas Vodde developed Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) through that decade; Dean Leffingwell released the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) around 2011; Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson described Spotify's squads, tribes and guilds in 2012. The sentence Dhurat could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "We are not choosing how many meetings to hold; we are choosing where to pay for each handoff, in waiting, in meetings or in redesign."

3. How it actually works

Whatever the framework, the mechanics reduce to five steps. First, make the dependencies visible: list each feature, the squads it needs and the order in which they must act. Second, fix a shared cadence and negotiate commitments together in one planning day, so that a request meets a squad's next planning point rather than a random one: who delivers what, by which sprint. The step usually left implicit is that each commitment needs a named owner, a date and an agreed fallback if it slips.

Third, run the sprints. Fourth, keep a cross-squad board reviewed weekly. Fifth, inspect the outcome. Measure how long multi-squad features take compared with single-squad ones, then change who owns what so fewer handoffs exist next quarter. SAFe puts its weight on step 2: a planning event, typically two days, at the start of each increment of roughly 8 to 12 weeks, for a "release train" commonly described as 50 to 125 people. LeSS puts its weight on structure: one product backlog and one product owner across all teams. Spotify's account stressed autonomy, with guilds and chapters carrying shared practice across squads.

4. A worked example

Table 1 shows how Dhurat tabulated the 54 features by the number of squads each touched. A feature touching k squads has k-1 handoffs, assuming they occur in sequence, which is the pessimistic case.

With two-week sprints (ten working days) and a request arriving at random, a handoff waits on average half a sprint: 5 days. Doing nothing therefore costs 46 x 5 = 230 handoff-days of waiting. She priced three options. Assuming a residual wait of 1 day (B) and 2 days (C), Option B is Dhamankar's: 72 squad members plus six others, 78 people for two days, 156 person-days, leaving a residual wait of 1 day per handoff. Option C brings only three people per squad, 27 in all, for one day, leaving a 2-day wait. The unknown is what a waiting day costs. A squad member whose work is blocked usually switches tasks and pays a restart cost; she assumed 0.5 person-day lost per handoff-day, then reran at 1.0, where the work is truly blocked.

The first pass is uncomfortable for the programme office. At 0.5, Option B costs 179 against 115 for doing nothing (meetings of 156 plus 23 of waiting), a net loss of 64 person-days. At 1.0 it flips: 202 against 230, a gain of 28. One unmeasured input reversed the verdict, and B breaks even with doing nothing at about 0.85 person-day per handoff-day (156 divided by the 184 handoff-days it saves). Option C wins in both passes, gaining 42 at 0.5 and 111 at 1.0 against doing nothing. The model counts only waiting and meetings. It ignores the value of the 30 June date, which dwarfs both.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

The unit is the dependency, not the team.

Headcount tells you the ceiling; the ticket history tells you the load, and the observed load can sit well below the ceiling, as 20 pairs against 36 did (56 per cent). Re-cutting ownership can remove handoffs for good, while a planning event only schedules them. The two are not substitutes: Kothrud's 46 handoffs would still need a cadence even after the three costliest were removed.

A framework bundles three separate answers.

Coordination (a planning cadence), structure (how teams are cut) and governance (how money and priorities are decided) are different levers. People who adopt "SAFe" or "the Spotify model" often import one lever and believe they have all three, then wonder why autonomy has not appeared, or why the planning event changed nothing.

Each approach has a strongest case and assumptions.

SAFe's best argument: in regulated, hardware-linked or legacy-heavy firms, dependencies cannot, in its argument, be removed within a year, so a shared cadence beats improvisation. It assumes stable, long-lived trains and tolerance for planning overhead. LeSS argues that fewer roles and one backlog remove handoffs rather than manage them; it assumes teams can learn the whole product. Spotify's squads assume loosely coupled software and high trust. Kniberg described a snapshot, not a framework to copy.

Architecture sets the floor.

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that systems mirror the communication structure of the organisations building them. If the code is entangled, re-cutting squads without re-cutting services only relocates the handoffs. Dongerkar's real argument at Kothrud was architectural: a few shared services sat behind much of the cross-squad work, and no meeting schedule would shorten that.

Comparative claims need measurement that does not exist.

"Framework X outperforms Y" would require organisations of similar size, domain and architecture, allocated to each framework independently of their prior problems, with identical outcome definitions (lead time, defects, revenue) tracked for years. Firms choose frameworks because of their circumstances, and published evidence is mostly vendor case studies and self-reported surveys. The defensible claim is narrower: organisations using X report Z, under conditions we cannot separate from the choice.

Coordination is not scope control.

A programme office is one way to coordinate. It is often also asked to police scope and report status to executives, which are different jobs with different incentives. Confusing them is how an office that was hired to speed up handoffs ends up defending a plan. Ask which of the three jobs a proposed office is actually being hired for.

It cannot tell you what to build.

Nine well-coordinated squads can ship the wrong thing quickly. Dependency management lists the work that crosses squads; scaled delivery decides how it will cross. Before relying on any approach, ask what a waiting day costs here, what you would measure to know it worked, and whether the answer would change your choice.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

In consumer products, features are often loosely coupled and experiments dominate, so shared metrics collide more than code does; the constraint is usually a common funnel, such as one onboarding flow that six squads all want to change in the same fortnight. In B2B, customer commitments carry dates, so the dependency board effectively becomes a promise register, and a slipped handoff is a conversation with a customer, not just a delay. In a marketplace, supply and demand squads share a matching or pricing service, so one platform team becomes the hub of most handoffs, as Dongerkar's platform group does at Kothrud.

Size changes the answer more than category. With three squads, Figure 1 gives only 3 possible pairs, and a lunch table does the work; a framework is usually more apparatus than three squads need. At hundreds of people, shared cadence and explicit structure are very hard to avoid unless dependencies are few, and the live question becomes how heavy the apparatus must be.

7. Common mistakes

Importing ceremonies without their premise. Symptom: planning events where teams list dependencies that are never resolved. Misunderstanding: that the event creates alignment, rather than recording agreements someone will enforce. Cheapest diagnostic: the share of last quarter's planned handoffs delivered on the agreed date; as a rule of thumb, well under half suggests the event is theatre.

Counting teams instead of dependencies. Symptom: reorganisation proposals argued from headcount. Misunderstanding: treating Brooks's ceiling as the load. Diagnostic: build the dependency table from the backlog, and the observed-pairs count from last quarter's tickets, in an afternoon, as Table 1 and Figure 1 do.

An office that measures its own activity. Symptom: status slides stay green until the week before a deadline. Misunderstanding: that reporting is coordination. Diagnostic: compare median lead time for multi-squad and single-squad features; if the office cannot produce it within a day, it is not measuring coordination.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Dhurat's quarter begins with the dependency table in hand, not a framework name. The four squads behind the credit line sit in one planning day, each commitment carries an owner, a date and a fallback, and a weekly board shows which handoffs are late. Programme staff are few and measured on lead time, not slide production. At quarter's end the company compares multi-squad lead time with its baseline, then moves ownership to remove the two most expensive handoffs. Nobody on the team could name a framework she had adopted, but each could say who they were waiting for and until when.

9. What she decided

On Friday Dhurat chose Option C with a condition. She rejected the six-person office, because on her own numbers it beat doing nothing only if a waiting day cost more than about 0.85 person-day (156 divided by the 184 handoff-days it saves), and beat C only above about 2.8 person-days (129 divided by 46), and nobody had measured either. She rejected doing nothing because both passes showed it losing. She asked Dhamankar to run the representative day and the dependency board, and asked Dongerkar to nominate the two handoffs her platform team would most like to remove by re-cutting. Both objections were answered, neither wholly. The quarter review would count lead times, and the October window sat behind it as the price of being wrong.

To learn next, study dependency management, since a coordination mechanism is only as good as the dependency list that feeds it, and revisit agile in practice to see what a single squad assumes before it is multiplied.

Two questions to sit with. First, what would you have to observe at your own organisation to estimate the cost of one waiting day, and who would resist counting it? Second, which of the dependencies in your current plan exist because of how teams are cut rather than what the product needs?
exp40v2-agile.scaled:
Scaled Delivery: Multiple Teams

Delivery & Technology · the structure, the queue and the clock behind coordinating many squads

1. Two decisions, taken in the same week

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, Vedashree Endait, senior vice-president for product at Lakshvedh Health Systems in Hyderabad, had eighty working days before a four-hundred-bed hospital chain went live on her company's clinical software, on Monday 1 February 2027. Lakshvedh sells a hospital information system to private chains and runs fourteen squads of nine. Two lieutenants had sent incompatible memos. Virochan Eklahare, who ran the delivery office until it was disbanded in December 2025, wanted the quarterly all-squad planning event restored; the squads, he wrote, had stopped talking. Vaidurya Ekshinge, director of platform engineering, wanted no event. Her evidence was one line of the ticket export: in the thirteen weeks to 30 September every one of the other thirteen squads had waited on the clinical data core squad.

Two days later, on Thursday 15 October, Vilas Edke faced a differently shaped version of the question at Lohagad Mobility in Chennai, which builds electric two-wheelers and runs seven squads: firmware, battery, vehicle control, cloud, app, dealer systems and diagnostics. The next variant had a start of production on Monday 1 March 2027, and the Automotive Research Association of India required a frozen firmware build ten weeks earlier, on Monday 21 December 2026 — forty-eight working days away. Of the thirty-four features his teams shipped in the six months to 30 September, nine touched firmware; those nine had a median lead time of forty-one working days against fourteen for the other twenty-five. Vinamra Endole, his firmware lead, proposed halving the integration cadence to three weeks.

Both get filed under scaled delivery. They are different problems with different arithmetic, and three measurements — a structure, a queue and a clock — separate them in an afternoon.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

Scaled delivery is the set of choices by which several teams, each able to release on its own, produce one coherent product: how teams are cut, how work crossing them is sequenced, and how the waiting between them is priced. It is not dependency management, which tracks crossings one by one; scaling asks what generates them.

The history runs through four moves. Melvin Conway argued in 1968 that a system's interfaces mirror the communication structure of the organisation building it, and Fred Brooks in 1975 supplied the combinatorial ceiling on communication paths. Donald Steward's design structure matrix, published in 1981, was the first apparatus to treat dependency structure rather than count, and it is still the standard apparatus. James Herbsleb and Audris Mockus reported in 2003 that work spanning sites took substantially longer than comparable same-site work. Alan MacCormack, John Rusnak and Carliss Baldwin compared matrices of similar open-source and proprietary codebases in 2012 and found the proprietary ones markedly more tightly coupled — Conway's claim with a measurement attached.

Donald Reinertsen's 2009 treatment supplied the economics the frameworks lacked: queues, batch size, a cost of delay. They disagree more sharply than their adopters notice.

Table 1. Five schools, with the proposition each defends and the one it rejects.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
SAFe (Leffingwell, 2011)In regulated or legacy-heavy estates dependencies cannot be removed inside a planning horizonThat dependency count should be driven to zero this year
LeSS (Larman and Vodde, from 2008)Most coordination demand is manufactured by how backlogs and teams are cutThat a planning apparatus is the thing that scales
Flow economics (Reinertsen, 2009)Queue length and batch size explain most delay, which has a computable priceThat the unit of decision is a framework rather than a queue
Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019)Choose an interaction mode per pair; collaboration is expensive and temporaryThat coordination is fundamentally a scheduling problem
Spotify account (Kniberg and Ivarsson, 2012)Autonomy needs an explicit alignment mechanism or it decaysThat it described a transferable model; its author has said so

Nexus and Scrum@Scale sit near SAFe with lighter apparatus. The dispute is whether the shape of the problem can be changed this year or must be scheduled around.

3. Mechanics: a structure, a queue and a clock

The structure.

Build a matrix whose rows and columns are the squads, and mark row r, column c when squad r consumed something from squad c last quarter. Then reorder so that as many marks as possible fall below the diagonal, the schedulable part.

The matrix carried 61 marks among 182 ordered pairs, 33.5 per cent. Partitioning left two irreducible blocks, of six squads and two, holding 25 of the 61 marks, 41.0 per cent; the other 36 cross between blocks and sequence cleanly. The 25 are not unschedulable — this ordering already places 16 of them below the diagonal — but the blocks cannot be sequenced as blocks, so work inside them returns every increment. Only the reciprocal pairs force a mark against any ordering, and there are nine: 9 of 61, 14.8 per cent, is the irreducible residue.

The queue.

Structure says where work crosses, not how long. Treat the serving squad as a server. In the sixty-six working days of the quarter to 30 September 2026, eighteen cross-squad requests reached Lakshvedh's clinical core, each consuming on average 3.3 working days of the capacity reserved for such work, so utilisation is 18 × 3.3 ÷ 66 = 0.90. The single-server result puts expected items in the system at ρ/(1−ρ) = 9, which is what Ekshinge's board showed open on an average day, and time in system at 9 ÷ (18/66) = 33.0 working days, of which 29.7 is queueing.

The model assumes one server, memoryless arrivals and service, no priorities and no abandonment; a squad is none of those. Kingman's approximation prices the variability you do have: multiply the queueing term by (ca2 + cs2)/2, where both are squared coefficients of variation, so ca2 = 1.0 with cs2 = 2.0 gives a factor of 1.5 and a wait of 44.6 days. The curve, not the point, is the finding: 13.2 days at 0.80, 7.7 at 0.70.

Table 2. Four interventions at the clinical core, priced on the same model.

InterventionRequestsService, daysρWait, days
Observed, quarter to 30 Sep183.30.90029.7
Two more engineers in the core squad182.80.7649.0
Five request types moved to self-serve133.30.6506.1
Both of the above132.80.5523.4
Restore the all-squad planning event183.30.90029.7

Wait is ρ/(1−ρ) × service time computed from unrounded ρ, where ρ = requests × service ÷ 66 working days. The last row moves neither term.

The clock.

A handoff ready today still waits for the receiving squad's next planning point, so a chain of h hops can cost up to h full planning periods, and about half that if work arrives at random within a period. Collapse each cyclic block to a single node and the longest path through Lakshvedh's condensed graph, on the 2025 structure, runs five nodes deep — four hops. At a ten-working-day sprint that is up to forty working days, half of Endait's eighty. Lohagad's chain is shorter and its periods are not: the firmware candidate comes every thirty working days and the app ships weekly, so a feature crossing both can spend thirty-five of the forty-eight days remaining, 72.9 per cent of the window, waiting.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three claims, each testable from a ticket export, state the conditions.

Claim one: multi-squad work takes materially longer than single-squad work. At Lakshvedh in 2025 the medians were 38 working days against 12, a ratio of 3.2; in the quarter to September 2026, after the re-cut below, 21 against 11, a ratio of 1.9. At Lohagad the split is not multi-squad against single-squad but firmware-touching against the rest: 41 days against 14, a ratio of 2.9.

Claim two: the delay is concentrated at one server. At Lakshvedh it is, decisively: all thirteen other squads consume from the clinical core, whose utilisation on cross-squad work was 0.90. Lohagad's firmware squad is slow for another reason: its nine firmware-touching features over 131 working days, at an assumed six working days of firmware capacity each, give a utilisation of 9 × 6 ÷ 131 = 0.41 and about 4.2 working days of queueing — a small share of a forty-one-day median, and nowhere near the thirty-five-day cadence term.

Claim three: the structure contains cycles. Lakshvedh's matrix still holds four reciprocal pairs and a three-squad block. Lohagad's seven squads produced sixteen directed dependencies among 42 ordered pairs, 38.1 per cent, denser than Lakshvedh's 33.5, but with one reciprocal pair and no larger block: its only cycle is that two-squad pair, so re-cutting has little to find.

The idea actively misleads when the binding constraint is external. Lohagad's freeze is set by a homologation submission, not by any squad. Halving the integration candidate to fifteen working days takes that term from thirty-five to twenty and buys fifteen days inside the window, which is real. It does not move the date, and a programme measured on coordination metrics will report a triumph in a quarter ending with features deferred.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product estates. When one platform serves several profit centres, each draws its own matrix and nobody owns the union. The queue is rationed by escalation, and the symptom is that arrival rate is uncorrelated with roadmap rank. The fix is allocating the server's capacity by product in advance.

Two-sided products. Supply and demand squads have not a sequencing dependency but a synchronisation one: a pricing change landing on one side alone is not a partial release, it is a defect. Partitioning tells you little, because the pair is reciprocal by construction; the move is a shared train for that pair alone.

Regulated software. A change to clinical decision support re-opens verification, and verification is a server whose utilisation nobody manages because it is not a squad. Conformance work for national digital health interfaces arrives in bursts tied to published deadlines, not the product's cadence. Teams that model only engineering queues find the longest one sits in quality or regulatory affairs.

Hardware plus software. Lohagad's freeze converts a soft dependency into a date, and the second-order effect is the interesting one: scope that misses the freeze migrates into over-the-air releases, re-creating the dependency against a fleet in customers' hands.

AI-native products. The shared asset is a model and an evaluation harness, and a downstream squad cannot regression-test against something that moves; done becomes a distribution, not a state. Mature teams pin a model version and publish an evaluation contract beside it — the service mode with a version number. What they say is that they retrain continuously.

Organisational seams. Where two budgets meet, dependency resolution becomes a negotiation about money, and no framework adjudicates money. Mature companies name one executive who can override, and publish an internal service level. In public they call this adopting a framework.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Direction and reciprocity, not presence.

The tell is a board on which the same two squads appear every fortnight. The obvious reading is that those two plan badly. The expert reading is that they form a cycle, which re-negotiates itself for ever: the eight reciprocal pairs inside Lakshvedh's six-squad block were re-planned every increment of 2025 and never resolved.

The queue is at the server, not in the plan.

The tell is a platform squad with a long intake list and a reputation for slowness. The obvious reading is to add people to the squads waiting on it. Utilisation says otherwise: at 0.90 the clinical core produced 29.7 days of waiting on eighteen requests; the same eighteen at 0.76 produce nine days.

Cadence multiplies through chain depth.

The tell is a lead time that is a clean multiple of the sprint length. The obvious reading is poor estimates. The expert reading is that the item spent its life at planning boundaries: Lohagad's firmware features ran a median of forty-one working days against a full-period cadence of thirty-five, which if the cadence ran full would leave six for building.

A planning event is a batch.

The tell is that commitment quality falls away after the first half-day. The obvious reading is weak facilitation. Batches have a cost curve: holding every cross-squad decision for one two-day event a quarter maximises the delay of the earliest decision in it, the one most likely to sit on the critical path.

A platform converts many dependencies into one bottleneck.

The tell is a platform backlog growing at a stable ratio to capacity. The obvious reading is under-investment. The structural reading is that the service mode works only when the service is self-serve; a ticket queue with a human at the end is a dependency with branding. Lakshvedh's edges fell from 61 to 47 while every squad still depended on one node.

The commitment hit rate is the cheapest instrument, and it is rarely kept.

The tell is that nobody can produce last increment's planned-versus-delivered within a day. The obvious reading is poor data hygiene. The expert reading is incentive: the number is owned by the function whose existence it judges. Lakshvedh's first-increment rate of 41 of 96 was computed only after the office was disbanded.

Re-organisation is the highest-variance intervention, and it is priced as free.

The tell is a proposal that counts dependencies removed and says nothing about the months of rebuilt context. The obvious reading is that structure is cheap to change because it is only a chart. An honest proposal states the steady-state gain and the quarter it costs to reach it.

Alignment meetings substitute for a published contract.

The tell is a recurring cross-squad meeting whose output is shared understanding rather than a versioned interface. The obvious reading is that communication is working. The expert reading is that a meeting is what you hold when there is no contract.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the code is loosely coupled and collisions are over shared surfaces, not shared services: six squads wanting the same onboarding flow in one fortnight is a priority conflict, and treating it as a dependency builds an apparatus that solves nothing. In enterprise B2B dates are contractual, so the dependency board becomes a promise register and a missed handoff is a customer conversation, as at Lakshvedh. In platform and marketplace businesses the hub is structural and the queueing treatment is most of the analysis.

Hardware changes the problem qualitatively, because a freeze is not negotiable at any cadence. AI products sit between: the model is a platform dependency that changes behaviour without changing its interface, so version pinning does the work an API contract does elsewhere. Stage matters simply. Below about five squads the matrix is small enough to hold in view and a framework is overhead. What governs the choice is not density but blocks — Lohagad's seven squads are 38.1 per cent dense with no block larger than a pair. Above roughly fifteen the structure exceeds what anyone holds in their head, and the only question is how heavy the apparatus must be.

8. Three worked examples

The failure. Through 2025 Lakshvedh ran the full apparatus: a two-day planning event for all 126 people at each of four increments, and a five-person delivery office. The direct cost was 126 × 2 × 4 = 1,008 person-days of planning plus 5 × 220 = 1,100 of office time, 2,108 in all. In the first increment, Q1 2025, 41 of 96 cross-squad commitments landed on the agreed date, 42.7 per cent, and the median lead time for multi-squad items rose from 31 working days in 2024 to 38. The year's structure explains it: the event sequenced the 36 crossings between blocks and re-negotiated the 25 inside them four times without changing any.

The recovery. What worked was structural: Lakshvedh published a versioned contract for the clinical core, moved two squads' routine requests behind it, and re-cut billing rules so billing and identity stopped feeding each other.

Table 3. Lakshvedh before and after the re-cut. Lead times are medians in working days.

Directed dependencies (Q4 2025; Q3 2026)6147
