Periods differ by row, as labelled. 2026 cost is two people for 220 working days; 2025 is 1,008 person-days of events plus 1,100 of office time.

The near-miss. Endole's proposal halves the firmware integration candidate to fifteen working days, dropping the cadence term from thirty-five to twenty and the median for firmware features from forty-one towards the mid-twenties. Against forty-eight working days to the freeze it buys room for perhaps one more feature, not five. Improvement and deadline run on different clocks, and only one reaches the board.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The planning event as theatre. Warning: nobody measures the commitment hit rate. Diagnostic: what share of last increment's cross-squad commitments landed on the agreed date? Catching it late cost Lakshvedh 2,108 person-days and a year of worse lead time.

The platform as a ticket queue. Warning: the intake list grows while the squad reports being fully busy. Diagnostic: what is the serving squad's utilisation and arrival rate? The cost compounds non-linearly — moving from 0.85 to 0.90 added eleven working days of expected wait, from 18.7 to 29.7.

Re-organisation as the first move. Warning: the proposal has a dependency count and no lead-time baseline. Diagnostic: what was last quarter's median multi-squad lead time, and what will the change be judged against? The cost is a quarter of lost output with nothing to show.

Coordination metrics owned by the coordinators. Warning: reporting stays green until a fortnight before the date. Diagnostic: who computes the hit rate, and whose budget does it justify? The cost is that the first honest number arrives too late.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether structure is changeable inside the horizon. The descaling position holds that most dependencies are self-inflicted and that re-cutting teams and backlogs removes them; its evidence is cases like Lakshvedh's, where nine reciprocal pairs became four in three quarters. The synchronising position holds that in regulated, hardware-linked or legacy estates the entanglement sits in the asset, not the chart, and a year of re-cutting buys less than a quarter of disciplined cadence; its evidence is the mirroring literature. It would be wrong if firms that re-cut showed no durable fall in cyclic blocks.

Whether coordination is a role or a rhythm. One camp argues a dedicated function is the only reason anyone computes the hit rate. The other argues it inevitably measures itself, and that rotating representatives keep knowledge where the work is. Neither has a controlled comparison.

Whether framework choice matters. The strongest sceptical position is that no credible evidence distinguishes the frameworks, and it is right. Showing one outperforms another would need organisations of comparable size, domain and architecture, assigned independently of the problems that drove their choice, with identical outcomes tracked for years. That study does not exist and probably cannot be run. The defensible claim is narrow: firms adopting X report Z, under conditions inseparable from the adoption. The open question is not which framework wins but whether cadence or structure is the larger term — answerable firm by firm.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this arrives with a framework and a rollout plan. Someone who has internalised it arrives with three questions and answers them from existing data first: what does the partitioned matrix look like, what is the utilisation of the busiest serving squad, and how many planning periods deep is the longest chain. They know that 41.0 per cent of Lakshvedh's crossings sat inside cyclic blocks before they know which framework anyone prefers. They treat collaboration between two squads as temporary, something that should end in a contract. And they will say that a change improves coordination and will not move the date, the sentence that separates an adviser from an advocate.

12. What each of them decided

Endait declined the all-squad event, funding two engineers into the clinical core and committing to a self-serve contract for five recurring request types, which on her model takes utilisation from 0.90 to 0.55 and expected waiting from 29.7 working days to 3.4. She placed the remaining three-squad cycle under one director with a single backlog for two quarters, and wrote the test down in advance: if the median multi-squad lead time is not below fifteen working days by the end of March 2027, the re-cut did not work. Eklahare kept the dependency board and the hit-rate calculation.

Edke accepted the three-week integration candidate and told his board in the same meeting that 21 December would not move. He ring-fenced four of the nine firmware features for the freeze and assigned the other five to an over-the-air release after start of production, each with an owner and a date.

Three questions for discussion. First, Endait's two advisers read the same ticket export and reached opposite conclusions; which of the three claims in section four could your own organisation test this month, and which would need instrumentation you do not have? Second, the queueing treatment rewards running a serving squad well below full utilisation — when is that the wrong call, and who in the organisation pays for it? Third, Edke's numbers say the cadence change buys fifteen working days and does not move the freeze; what would have to be true of the five deferred features for that trade to be the wrong one?

13. Going deeper

Each instrument has a neighbouring topic that sharpens it. Dependency management is the layer beneath the matrix, supplying the ticket data no partition can be drawn without. Agile in practice defines the single-squad process this topic multiplies, and its assumptions break first under scale. Kanban and flow develops the queueing argument, with work-in-progress limits as the lever on utilisation. The execution rhythm governs the clock: cadence length, synchronisation and the planning boundaries. The software development lifecycle explains why verification and release become servers of their own. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing matters because the service-time term above is an estimate. Backlog management and refinement decides whether a crossing is found at planning or at integration. Definition of done is the contract at each handoff; a vague one turns a sequenced dependency back into a cycle.
exp40v2-agile.eng.velocity.myths:
Velocity, throughput and what not to measure

Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

1. Two flat lines, two different problems

On Thursday 1 October 2026, Gayathri Mylswamy, head of product at Varnam Pay, a Bengaluru payments and credit app with 4.1 million monthly active users, studied a chart that had not moved since June: velocity, story points completed per two-week sprint, had sat between 60 and 64 for eight sprints, 1 June to 18 September. The chief executive drew the obvious conclusion and asked for twenty-five per cent more by December, when a partner bank's co-lending window opened. At sprint eight's close 54 stories still stood between Varnam and a credit line on UPI under the Reserve Bank's framework. An answer was due Monday 5 October.

She had a second set of figures nobody had asked for. Her engineering director, Geethika Mandapaka, had spent two quarters making the work smaller: the mean story shrank by a third between the first four sprints and the last four, and mean time from accepted specification to production fell from 19.1 to 12.0 operating days. None of it appeared on the board's chart, and the instruction just given would, honoured literally, undo it.

Gowtham Madhavaram faced the mirror image. Vilakku Diagnostics, in Chennai, sells point-of-care haematology analysers — instrument, firmware, cloud reporting — to 310 hospital chains and NABL-accredited laboratories, 1,840 units installed at 30 September 2026. On Tuesday 13 October its board asked him for an engineering productivity dashboard by Friday 6 November, with velocity on it. Vilakku has never used story points: firmware ships four times a year because every release carries a verification pass on physical instruments and a notification to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. His problem was not a number that had stopped meaning something but one that never meant anything there.

2. What the measures are, and who disagrees about them

Velocity is the sum of the story-point estimates of the items a team completed in one sprint. Three things in it do the damage: the estimates are relative sizes unrelated to hours, "completed" means whatever the definition of done says, and the unit is one the team mints. Throughput counts items finished in a period, unsized. Cycle time runs from starting an item to finishing it, lead time from the customer's request. Work in progress is the number started and not finished. Varnam's sprint one booked 61 points on 16 stories, 3.81 each; sprint eight, 62 on 31, or 2.00.

Velocity was invented for forecasting, not judgement. Kent Beck's Extreme Programming, set out in 1999, sized the next iteration from the team's recent record — "yesterday's weather" — so that teams would stop promising on hope; Scrum, described by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland at OOPSLA in 1995, kept it inside the team. The flow measures are older: John Little proved his queueing identity in 1961, J. F. C. Kingman published his heavy-traffic approximation the same year, and the Toyota lineage reached software through Mary and Tom Poppendieck in 2003 and David Anderson's Kanban in 2010. Ridgway had explained in 1956 what happens to a measure once someone is held to it.

Four schools disagree, each signing a different proposition. The estimate school signs "a team forecasts from its own record, in its own units" and refuses "velocity compares teams". The flow school, through Anderson and Daniel Vacanti, signs "a cycle-time distribution forecasts as well as estimates" and refuses "velocity can be corrected for inflation". The capability school, resting on the DORA programme reported by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim in 2018, signs "deployment frequency, change lead time, change failure rate and time to restore predict firm performance" and refuses "the four keys are team targets". The economics school, Donald Reinertsen in 2009, signs "quantify cost of delay first" and refuses "flow metrics justify themselves".

3. Mechanics: three identities and one inequality

Expert practice refuses to look at velocity until the stream has been measured. Geethika's instrumentation records when each story enters and leaves every stage, splitting the time into touch time — somebody actively working — and wait time. Table 1 and Figure 1 give the mean per story in operating hours.

Table 1. Varnam Pay: mean elapsed operating hours per story, by stage

A ten-hour day, fifty-hour week: 119.8 operating hours is 12.0 working days. The train wait is 21.0, not 25.0, because merges cluster before the Thursday cut.

Flow efficiency comes first, touch time over total: 21.0 of 119.8 operating hours in sprints five to eight, 17.5 per cent, against 29.5 of 191.0, or 15.4 per cent, in sprints one to four. That answers the board's question. If a story is worked on for 17.5 per cent of its life, making everyone work twice as fast removes half of 21.0 hours — 10.5 of 119.8, an 8.8 per cent gain. Twenty-five per cent cannot come out of effort, because effort is not where the time sits.

The second identity is Little's law: over a window in which the system is stable and all arriving work departs, mean work in progress equals mean throughput times mean cycle time. Being an identity rather than a model, it checks instrumentation. Varnam finished 17.75 stories a sprint in sprints one to four and 27.0 in five to eight, or 1.775 and 2.70 a day; the daily board count averaged 34 items in flight, then 32. The law implies mean cycle times of 19.15 and 11.85 operating days against the 19.10 and 11.98 the stage table measured, agreeing to 0.3 and 1.1 per cent. And since work in progress fell only 5.9 per cent, throughput bought nearly the whole lead-time fall.

The third is the identity the board never saw. Velocity is throughput multiplied by the mean size of what was finished, so any movement in it decomposes exactly into those two. Varnam's throughput rose 52.11 per cent between the halves while pooled points per story fell from 3.4930 to 2.3056, or 33.99 per cent; 1.52113 times 0.66006 is 1.0040, so velocity rose 0.40 per cent, from 62.00 to 62.25. Figure 2 indexes all three to sprint one: the flat line is the product of two large movements in opposite directions, not a team that stopped improving. Is the movement even real? From the per-sprint figures the standard errors of the two differences are 1.109 and 2.016: the 0.25-point velocity gap is a quarter of its own, which is noise, while the 9.25-story throughput gap is 4.6 times its own.

The inequality is Kingman's. Varnam has one staging environment, attended ten hours a day. A run holds it for a mean of 3.0 hours with a standard deviation of 3.0, a coefficient of variation of 1.0; arrivals bunch before the Thursday merge cut, at 1.5. At 2.70 arrivals a day the slot runs at 0.810 utilisation, and the mean wait is roughly the utilisation ratio times the mean of the squared coefficients times the service time: 4.2632 times 1.625 times 3.0, the 20.8 operating hours Table 1 records. Figure 3 is the argument: at 0.891 the wait is 39.9 hours and at 0.972 it is 169.2. At 1.0125 utilisation — what twenty-five per cent more merged work produces — there is no steady state. The dashed curve halves the service time to 1.5 hours: the same arrivals then sit at 0.405 utilisation and wait 1.7 hours.

4. Five conditions, stated so that they can fail

Velocity carries information only when five conditions hold, each testable. First, the people who do the work make the estimates on a scale that holds still, and what they size stays comparable. Varnam's scale held, but mean item size fell 33.99 per cent, so its early and late velocities are not the same measurement; Vilakku cannot fail the condition, having no scale. Second, items are small relative to the period and arrive without a forced batch: Varnam now passes, Vilakku cannot, its batch set by a regulator's notification and a hospital's maintenance window. Third, the system is stationary across the averaging window, Little's law's precondition rather than a nicety: Varnam's work in progress moved 5.9 per cent over eight sprints, so its averages hold.

Fourth, nobody is accountable for the number — the condition Varnam's board destroyed on 1 October. Fifth, a customer-visible outcome exists at a shorter lag than the metric's own noise: Varnam has daily approval rates, Vilakku a ninety-day field-defect window, so it manages on its verification cycle instead. Where the measure turns actively misleading is worth naming. Across teams, always. Within a team that changed size. On cycle time wherever the clock's start is under the team's control. And on deployment frequency when flags decouple releases from deployments.

5. The seams, where the measures stop agreeing

The hardest cases are organisational seams. A change crossing three teams, each with a median cycle time of 4.0 operating days and handoff waits of 9.0 and 11.0 days between them, reaches the customer in 32.0 days, of which 20.0 days, or 62.5 per cent, is handoff. Every dashboard is green, nobody owns the 20.0 days, and no team measure sees them.

Platform organisations invert it: a platform team's throughput is consumed by the queues it serves, so its numbers improve as its customers' lead times lengthen. In a two-sided marketplace one backlog's throughput averages two economies with different costs of delay, and belongs to neither. Hardware plus software is Vilakku's world, where a firmware change needing a revised reagent cartridge inherits a fourteen-week tooling queue and a metric in days reads as noise against a clock in quarters.

AI-native products break the unit of work. A prompt change is not a commit, the verification is an eval set, and agent-assisted coding inflates commit counts without inflating anything a customer sees, so by 2026 the only defensible unit is a reviewed change in production. What mature companies do, as against what their dashboards imply, is work a weekly list of the oldest items in flight, escalating by name. The dashboard is decoration; the ageing list is the mechanism.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

A slow team is usually a queue. The sign is flow efficiency under a quarter; Varnam's 17.5 per cent is ordinary, not bad. The obvious reading, that people are not working hard enough, fails arithmetically, not morally: with touch time under a fifth of elapsed time, the largest available effort gain moves single digits.

High utilisation is a promise that the queue will grow. The sign is a shared resource booked solid: one staging slot, one reviewer who approves everything, one compliance officer. Managers read full calendars as efficiency, which in a factory of identical parts they nearly are. But Kingman's curve is convex: the last ten points of utilisation cost more wait than the first eighty.

Aged work in progress beats every average. Cycle time lags by construction: an item's is known only once it finishes, after the moment you could have helped. The sign is a board whose oldest card outlives the eighty-fifth percentile.

A date from a mean is close to a coin toss. Varnam's lead time fits a lognormal with median 9.8 and mean 11.98 operating days, sigma 0.634: the mean is beaten only 62 per cent of the time, the eighty-fifth percentile is 18.9 days, the ninety-fifth 27.8. The sign is a date quoted with no percentile attached.

Throughput is gameable too; the gaming is merely visible. Varnam's throughput rise against its size fall is indistinguishable, on those two numbers alone, from slicing work to flatter a count. What separates them is that lead time fell 37.3 per cent while work in progress did not rise. Real gaming shows counts up with lead time flat.

Counter-metrics are paired, never averaged. The sign is a single delivery health score. An index lets one leg pay for another, the thing a pair exists to prevent: throughput beside change failure rate forces the trade open; a weighted mean hides it.

Flow efficiency is nearly scale-free. Varnam cut lead time 37.3 per cent while flow efficiency moved only from 15.4 to 17.5 per cent, because halving a story halves its waiting along with its working. The sign is a team claiming one as a win while the other holds still.

"Measure outcomes, not output" is true and nearly useless at the delivery layer. An outcome's feedback lag is months; a queue needs a signal this week. The sign is an outcome objective with no delivery instrumentation under it, yielding neither. Experts keep both, in different rooms.

7. How it changes with product type and company stage

Consumer software is where flow measures work best: deployment is cheap, feedback arrives in a day, cycle time binds. In enterprise software the relevant clock is the customer's. Vattam Systems shipped to its own production in a median 7.1 days while its logistics customers took a further 23.0 days to adopt a release, so the real lead time to value was 30.1 days and Vattam's number covered a quarter of it. Platforms and marketplaces meet the seam problem of section 5. Hardware inverts the economics, as Vilakku's tooling queue shows: batch size is then the only lever worth arguing about. AI products are unsettled, the unit of work contested.

Stage matters more than any of this. Below about ten engineers, measurement overhead exceeds its value. Growth stage is where velocity targets get installed, the first point at which an executive cannot see the work, and where nearly all the damage is done. At scale, capability measures turn necessary because nobody can see any team; in a listed company a delivery number reaching an investor deck cannot be protected from Goodhart. The arithmetic does not change: Little's law and Kingman's inequality are indifferent to what you sell.

8. Three worked examples

Varnam's forecast, and its queue priced twice. The 54 remaining stories at the pooled 2.3056 points each are 124.50 points; over the 62.25-point velocity of sprints five to eight, 2.00 sprints. Throughput gives 54 over 27.0, also 2.00 — the methods agree exactly because the currencies match. Sized at the old 3.4930 points, 188.62 in all, the same velocity would have said 3.03 sprints, 51.5 per cent longer: a currency error, not a forecasting disagreement. The mean is the wrong statistic anyway. The last four sprints delivered 23, 25, 29 and 31 stories, mean 27.0 and standard deviation 3.65, so two sprints have a mean of 54.0 and a standard deviation of 5.16; on a normal approximation the eighty-five per cent floor, 1.04 deviations down, is 48.6 stories against the 54 outstanding. Three sprints are needed, not two: counted from sprint nine, which began Monday 21 September, they end Friday 30 October.

Geethika's remedy has three parts: a pull policy cutting the specification queue from 26.0 hours to 9.0, a parallelised suite halving service time to 1.5 hours, and a daily rather than weekly release train, taking that wait from 21.0 to 5.0. Priced naively these give 66.2 operating hours, a 44.8 per cent cut implying 81.1 per cent more throughput at constant work in progress. They do not. The plan's own success refills the queue it drained: with 71 per cent more arrivals the slot settles at 0.693 utilisation and waits 5.5 hours, not 1.7. The fixed point is 70.0 operating hours — a 41.6 per cent cut and 71.1 per cent more throughput. The naive figure overstates the gain by ten points, in the direction a sponsor hopes for.

Vilakku's batch economics. Table 2's eight releases carry 280 changes over two years, 140 a year at a mean batch of 35.0. Gowtham prices a release at ₹18.4 lakh of transaction cost and a deferred change at ₹2.4 lakh a year of delay cost. The batch optimum, the square root of twice transaction cost times annual demand over delay cost, is 46.33 changes or 3.02 releases a year, fewer than Vilakku already does. The actual batch of 35.0 means four releases, so ₹73.60 lakh of transactions plus ₹42.00 lakh of delay on an average half-batch of 17.5: ₹115.60 lakh against ₹111.20 lakh at the optimum. The cadence argument is worth ₹4.40 lakh, and the money is not there. A rig at ₹1.10 crore, or ₹110 lakh, cuts transaction cost to ₹4.6 lakh, moving the optimum to 23.17 changes and 6.04 releases a year and the annual cost to ₹55.60 lakh — a ₹60.00 lakh saving, paying back in 1.83 years. Table 2's escape rates rise with batch size, pointing the other way.

Where it failed: Vattam Systems. Vattam, a Pune firm selling warehouse software to third-party logistics operators, put the four DORA measures on dashboards in 2025 Q1 and targets on three of them. Gokila Mallidi, its chief technology officer, hit every target and lost two quarters doing it (Table 3). The mechanism was not fraud: failures were reclassified as planned remediation, incidents closed on a workaround and reopened as fresh tickets, and flag flips — the acts reaching customers — were not deployments. Recovery took three quarters: the measures stayed, the targets went, a reviewer outside the delivery line declared failures, and the goal became customer-visible. 9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Velocity as a target. Sign: points per story rising. Diagnostic: has mean story size moved? Caught late, a quarter of forecasts sit in a currency nobody can convert.

Starting more to look busier. Sign: items started but not finished climbing while throughput is flat. Diagnostic: how old is the oldest item in flight? By Little's law cycle time rises with work in progress, so this slows everything while resembling effort; caught late, the rise is banked.

Gaming the capability measures. Sign: a declared change failure rate falling while customer-reported incidents rise. Diagnostic: who declares a failure, and are they measured on it? Vattam lost two quarters and two engineering managers before anyone asked.

Measuring a stage instead of the stream. Sign: every team green, the customer late. Diagnostic: how long from the customer's request to the customer's hands? Caught late, three teams spend a year optimising 12.0 days of a 32.0-day journey.

Moving the start of the clock. Sign: cycle time falling while lead time from request rises. Diagnostic: who can move the clock's start? Caught late, every historical cycle time is worthless.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first argument is whether estimates earn their keep. The flow school's strongest form is empirical: on the same backlogs, forecasts resampled from throughput alone match or beat estimate-based ones, while estimating costs hours a sprint. The estimate school's is that sizing is a conversation whose by-product is shared understanding of scope, and that throughput-only forecasting assumes a stable size distribution — the assumption Varnam's 33.99 per cent size fall violated. Either side is wrong if sizes behave unlike its claim.

The second is whether delivery measures should leave the team. The capability case is that hiding them is how bad delivery survives for years, and that the four keys measure capability, not output. The team-only case is that the evidence is cross-sectional and self-reported, that correlation with firm performance is no licence to target, and that Ridgway settled it in 1956. For the capability school to be wrong, published measures would have to degrade under observation as fast as targeted ones; nobody has measured it.

The third is live. One camp holds that AI-assisted development has merely moved the unit of work to the reviewed change. The other holds that when generation is nearly free the constraint moves wholly into review, so a count of completed items measures nothing a customer receives. There is not yet enough instrumented data to settle it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes Goodhart and installs a dashboard; someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They ask what the denominator is and when it was measured before discussing a rate. They work the ageing list before the averages. They quote dates with a percentile attached — 30 October at eighty-five per cent, not "late October". And asked for more velocity they decompose the request — more items, bigger items, or the same work measured differently — answering the question meant, not the one asked.

12. What each of them decided

Gayathri refused the velocity target on Monday 5 October, offering three numbers instead: Friday 30 October at eighty-five per cent confidence, a lead time of 12.0 operating days falling to 7.0 if the queue work is funded, and a weekly count of stories reaching production. She kept velocity and took it off the board pack: a forecasting input belongs to the forecaster. Her closing line was arithmetic, not principle: on the only reading that leaves the measure intact, twenty-five per cent more merged work asks the staging slot to run at 1.0125 utilisation.

Gowtham declined the dashboard, offering two numbers for 6 November — escapes per 100 changes and the verification cycle in instrument-days — with the rig's case attached. He was explicit that Vilakku's cadence is not its problem, and that eight releases cannot prove a defect saving.

Three questions. First, Gayathri ruled out story-slicing with lead time and work in progress; what must a manager holding only a velocity chart and a story count do to tell the two apart? Second, Vilakku's cost model prefers 3.02 releases a year while its defect data prefers smaller batches than four a year gives; which goes before the board, and what does showing both cost? Third, Vattam kept the four measures and deleted the targets; what did that cost, and how would it now spot a team that really was slow?

13. Going deeper

Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing — velocity's numerator, and why inflation hides without a size series. Counter-metrics and Goodhart's law — the general law of which this is one case. The software development lifecycle — the stages Table 1 decomposes. Agile in practice — the ceremonies producing these numbers. Kanban and flow — work-in-progress limits and the policies that make Little's law hold. The execution rhythm — how often to review which measure, and in whose room. Backlog management and refinement — the specification queue, 26.0 of Varnam's 119.8 hours. Definition of done — what "completed" means, and so what velocity counts.
exp20v2-agile.eng.velocity.myths:
Velocity, throughput and what not to measure

1. A target on a flat line

On Friday 31 July 2026, the last day of sprint 6, Eshan Lakshmikanthan, head of product at Tarangam Freight Technologies, a Hyderabad marketplace matching truck operators with shippers, left a board review with an instruction he disliked. The chief executive, Eswarya Lingaraju, had seen a chart of the engineering team's velocity, the number of story points it completed in each two-week sprint, and noticed it was flat. The team of seven had averaged 35.3 points across its first six sprints, 11 May to 31 July. She wanted 20 per cent more, 42.4 points, from the sprint beginning Monday 3 August. The reason was concrete: a proof-of-delivery release, promised to the anchor shipper for 20 November, had 41 stories waiting.

Ezhilan Lokanathan, the engineering manager, said little in the room and a great deal afterwards. A target on a number, he argued, is a request to change the number, and numbers can be changed in more ways than by working faster. By Friday 11 September, sprint 9 had ended, the chart looked superb, and the release felt further away. On Monday 14 September Eshan had to tell the chief executive whether the team was slow or Tarangam was measuring the wrong thing. A wrong guess would either press a good team into worse work or let the customer discover a late release on 20 November, in a year when two earlier Tarangam dates had already slipped.

2. The idea

Velocity is the story points a team completes in one sprint. A sprint is a fixed work period; a story is a small piece of user-visible work; a story point is the team's own relative size estimate for a story, with no fixed link to hours. Kent Beck's Extreme Programming practice, developed in the late 1990s, introduced velocity for a narrow purpose: forecasting. If recent sprints finished about 35 points, assume the next will too, which Extreme Programming called "yesterday's weather". The idea was never to judge people; it was to stop the team promising work on the strength of hope.

Throughput is the count of items finished in a period, with no sizing at all. Cycle time is how long one item takes from start to finish. The distinction matters because velocity needs estimates and the other two do not. Throughput and cycle time both come from lean manufacturing and the Kanban method, which David Anderson brought to software in the mid-2000s. Eshan's sentence for the meeting: "Velocity is a forecasting tool a team uses on itself, so the moment we make it a target it stops measuring anything."

3. How it works, including the implicit steps

The team sizes each story, often by T-shirt sizes (small, medium, large) mapped to points. At the sprint's end it counts only stories that are completely done, with no credit for 90 per cent. It averages the last few sprints, then divides the remaining backlog by that average. The implicit steps matter most: the people who build the work must do the sizing, the scale must stay constant, "done" must mean the same thing every sprint, and three to six stable sprints are needed before the average means anything.

Flow measures add one identity, Little's law, a result from queueing theory by John Little in 1961. Work in progress (WIP) is the number of items started but not finished. Average cycle time equals average WIP divided by throughput. Figure 1 shows it for Tarangam: with 6 cards in progress and 11.83 stories finished per ten working days, a card takes about five days. Nothing in the identity can be argued with; only WIP or throughput can change, which is why limiting WIP is the most direct lever on cycle time.

4. A worked example, line by line

Figure 2 and Table 1 give what Eshan pulled from the tracker. Sprints 1 to 6 total 212 points and 71 stories, a mean of 35.33 points and 11.83 stories, or 2.99 points per story (212 divided by 71). Sprints 7 to 9 total 139 points and 32 stories: a mean of 46.33 points, up 31.1 per cent, but 10.67 stories, down 9.9 per cent. Points per story rose from 2.99 to 4.34, a 45 per cent increase. The chart improved because the unit shrank, not because more got done.

So 41, less the 32 finished, plus 51 leaves 60 stories on 14 September. Those 60 stories, at the old 2.99 points each, are about 179 points. 5. Seven nuances

Points are not hours

A point expresses relative effort and uncertainty to one team, so one story's 3 points and another's 5 mean only that the second looks bigger or riskier. Converting points to days, or crediting a person with "three points a day", invents a precision the estimate never had, and it quietly turns a planning aid into a timesheet.

Velocity is local to one team

Another team's 60 points may be Tarangam's 25, because each team calibrates against its own reference stories. Comparing velocities across teams is meaningless, and a league table invites each team to inflate its scale until it tops the list.

Throughput assumes similar-sized items

Counting stories works only if stories are roughly comparable. In sprints 1 to 6 points per story ranged from 2.75 to 3.27, so a count was a fair proxy; one huge story would break it. The check is cheap: split the finished stories by size band and see whether the mix changed.

Cycle time is not lead time

Cycle time starts when work begins. Lead time starts when the customer asks. A story can have a five-day cycle time and a ninety-day lead time if it queued for a quarter.

None of them measures value

A team can finish every story on time and build the wrong release. Flow metrics diagnose delivery, not whether the proof-of-delivery feature changes what the shipper does, and they cannot tell a team with a good plan from one steadily delivering a bad one.

Goodhart's law applies at once

Named for the economist Charles Goodhart, and put in its modern form by the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Real complexity growth cannot be ruled out from the tracker alone, and fewer finished stories would fit it. Ezhilan therefore looked for like-for-like evidence: one story template, adding a document field to the booking form, was sized at 2 points in June and 5 in August with the same code paths touched. That is the cheapest sign that the scale moved, not the work.

Ask four questions first

Who sizes the work? Has the scale stayed fixed? Has the team stayed stable, with no new joiners or long holidays? What does "done" mean? Without answers, any number from this page's methods is decoration.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

A consumer product ships many small experiments, so throughput of experiments and cycle time matter more than any point count. A B2B product like Tarangam's carries dated customer commitments, so the forecast range is the real deliverable and a slipped date is a contract conversation, not a statistic. A marketplace has two sides, and supply-side and demand-side work compete for one team; flow metrics should be read per lane, or a busy supply lane hides a starving demand lane.

Whatever the product, the lesson is the same: choose the unit the work naturally comes in. An early-stage company with four engineers has too few sprints for a stable average, and individual cycle times tell more than any mean. A large company has the opposite temptation, the one the nuance above warned against: dozens of teams, a dashboard, and a pull towards ranking teams by velocity. Counting finished items needs no shared scale, so it aggregates safely where points do not.

7. Common mistakes

Treating velocity as a target

Symptom: points rise while stories shipped stay flat or fall. Misunderstanding: points are a currency that can be printed. Cheapest diagnostic: chart points per story each sprint, as in Table 1, where 2.99 became 4.34 within three sprints.

Counting partly done work

Symptom: reviews full of "nearly done" items. Misunderstanding: effort spent is value delivered. Diagnostic: compare stories started with stories finished each sprint, and watch WIP; if starts keep outrunning finishes, cycle time is already lengthening.

Forecasting from one number

Symptom: the promised date moves every sprint. Misunderstanding: a mean is a promise. Diagnostic: list the minimum and maximum of recent sprints and forecast with both; over sprints 1 to 6, 60 divided by 13 and by 11 gives 4.6 to 5.5 sprints.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Eshan does not argue about the chief executive's instinct. He arrives on 14 September with three things. A chart of stories finished and cycle time per sprint, in the team's own words, sits beside a forecast stated as a range rather than a date. The velocity figure stays inside the team, used for planning and never reported upward. And a second measure, points per story, watches the first for damage. Such a second measure is called a counter-metric. The chief executive hears a risk and an option, not a defence of the team. Eshan also asks her what she would do with a date she could trust, since that answer decides which stories can move out.

9. The decision

Eshan withdrew the points target and proposed three changes. Report stories finished and cycle time, not velocity. Cap WIP at 6, the level that gave a five-day cycle time. And move 10 of the 60 stories out of the 20 November release. Fifty stories fit five sprints even at the weakest observed sprint of 10 stories, and at the 11.83 mean they need 4.2 sprints. Eswarya accepted, on condition that the chart return to her monthly, and Ezhilan agreed to publish it unedited. He reasoned that her real question was never speed but whether the date was safe, and a count of finished stories, set against a stated range, answers that honestly where a points chart could only flatter.

Next, study cumulative flow diagrams and probabilistic forecasting, which turn a throughput history into a calibrated range of dates. Both build on the estimation and counter-metric ideas this page leans on. Before then, sit with two questions. If your own team's velocity rose 30 per cent next quarter, which two other numbers would you check before celebrating? And which measure you report upward today would change its meaning the day someone set a target on it?
exp40v2-agile.hw.sw.integration:
The Socket and the Train

Integrating hardware and software release trains

1. Two decisions, five days apart

On 6 March 2026, in Bengaluru, Lathika Torgal had fourteen days left to change a number. Dilasa Medical Systems, where she ran product, made the P2, a handheld ultrasound probe paired with an Android tablet and a cloud service. A state maternal-health programme had ordered 4,200 for delivery on 1 September. Design freeze fell on 20 March; production would run from 1 June to 1 August in Hosur.

The number was the compute module inside the probe. Lomash Tamhankar, who led embedded software, wanted 2 GB rather than 1 GB, at ₹1,850 more a unit, or ₹77.7 lakh across the order. Nothing shipping in September would use it. The case rested on a model that did not yet exist: v3 of Dilasa's gestational-age estimator, 2.4 times the size of the v2 on the probe, and the only version able to run offline at the accuracy the 2028 renewal was drafting into its specification. Lokita Tendse, the regulatory lead, observed that memory bought nothing by itself: under the Medical Device Rules 2017, a change to a performance claim goes back to CDSCO whatever silicon it runs on.

Five days later, in Pune, Laveena Talaulikar had no freeze to worry about and no headroom to buy. Dishari Retail Systems leased payment soundboxes to small merchants; 7.40 lakh were in the field across three hardware revisions. Her host application shipped every seven days, her firmware four times a year. A partner bank's settlement rails would open on 1 July, and the feature using them, collections split across two merchant accounts, needed firmware 4.2, which left on the train of 1 June. Four weeks after that train, on 29 June and two days before the rails opened, Lajita Toraskar's rollout model put 4.43 lakh devices on 4.2, 59.9 per cent of the fleet, with 2.10 lakh Rev A units that could never run it. Sales wanted a line in the price list. Laveena had to decide what that line could truthfully say.

Figure 1 shows why these are one problem. What matters is not how fast either clock runs but how long a commitment on the slow clock stays binding, and what revising it costs. Lathika's could be revised on 20 March for ₹77.7 lakh and, once the line started on 1 June, not at all. Laveena's lasted thirteen weeks and could be revised only by moving a date a bank also held.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A release train is a fixed-cadence departure: software ships on the day the train leaves with whatever is ready, and what is not ready waits for the next. Integrating hardware and software release trains means arranging a product so that a unit frozen once can safely host behaviour released many times, and both sides always agree about what that unit can do. Three artefacts carry the agreement: a capability declaration the unit makes about itself, a flag service deciding per unit what to enable, and an update channel that can replace software after sale.

Three traditions collided to produce it. Hardware inherited a single integration milestone from Clark and Fujimoto's heavyweight-project literature and from stage-gate practice, where the design freeze is where variety stops. Software, through Cusumano and Selby's account of Microsoft's synchronise-and-stabilise discipline and later Leffingwell's agile release train, learned that fixing the departure date and varying the content is cheaper than the reverse; Reinertsen supplied the reason, that cadence limits accumulated variability and makes queues visible at the price of latency. The third tradition is operational: once Tesla began delivering car firmware over the air from 2012, and Android's Project Treble split the vendor implementation from the framework in 2017, a shipped unit stopped being a finished artefact and became a managed one.

Practitioners who share that vocabulary still disagree sharply, and not about mechanism but about what a launch is for.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Late bindingA unit should ship with more memory, compute and sensing than its launch features need: the freeze binds the socket, not the feature.That an incomplete carton is fine because an update is coming.
Whole boxAnything on the carton or in the price list must work from the carton, with no network.That a staged rollout substitutes for a complete launch build.
Fleet operationsThe unit of management is the installed base's version distribution: a percentile of firmware age, not a launch-day count.That launch day is when integration is judged.
Configuration controlThe faster a shipped device can be changed, the more change-control evidence the firm must hold, not less.That a flag is reversible and therefore not a change.

3. Mechanics, and the arithmetic underneath

The five observable steps are familiar: declare capabilities at the freeze, extend the device-to-cloud interface without changing what existing messages mean, report version and capabilities on each connection, decide behaviour per unit in a flag service, and offer firmware when a newer image exists. What separates expert practice is the matrix those steps create, because that matrix is the cost.

Dishari's naive matrix had three hardware revisions, three live firmware versions and four supported host-app versions: 36 combinations at 38 minutes a regression pass, or 1,368 minutes of rig time against a 600-minute overnight window. Most do not exist. Rev A, built in 2023 and 2024, holds 128 MB of flash and runs only the 3.9 line; Rev B and Rev C run 4.1 and 4.2. That leaves five real configurations and 20 pairs, 760 minutes, still over the window.

The reduction that works is an equivalence argument, not a cut. Rev B and Rev C differ only in modem vendor, and no capability depends on the modem. If two revisions declare an identical capability set, every gate in the cloud and the app treats them alike, so they are one test class. Three classes against four host versions gives 12 pairs, 456 minutes.

The step usually left implicit is that the merge is a claim about the registry, and claims decay. Lajita made it falsifiable: a six-minute conformance probe runs nightly on one unit of each revision and fails the build if two revisions in a class answer differently. Three probes cost 18 minutes, so the night's work is 474 minutes and leaves 126 of the 600-minute window spare. The probe is not coverage; it audits the assumption that bought the reduction. Its second-order effect matters more: a supply-chain substitution that changes what a unit can do becomes a red build rather than a customer complaint, and sourcing acquires a mechanical reason to tell engineering what it changed.

4. When the approach applies, stated as tests

Four conditions decide whether late binding is a strategy or an excuse. Each is testable before the freeze and resolves differently for the two firms.

ConditionDilasa, P2 probeDishari, soundbox fleet
Value accrues per unit, not only when the whole fleet has it.Holds. One probe with offline inference serves one clinic.Holds. Split settlement helps a merchant alone.
The gating property is something the unit can report about itself.Holds. Memory size is readable at boot.Failed in 2025. An amplifier substitution was invisible to the firmware.

The idea is most misleading where it is most quoted. If the hardware is the safety envelope rather than a host for features, late binding turns an engineering margin into a liability, and the answer is to overbuild and freeze hard. If the fleet is small and serviced, as Dilasa's 4,200 probes are, flags, staged rollouts and rig farms can cost more than visiting. And where value is realised only at full coverage, Dishari's 59.9 per cent at 29 June is not 59.9 per cent of the benefit; it is close to none.

5. Hard edges

Two-sided products inherit a third cadence. Dishari's bank partner certifies a device-and-firmware pair, not a device, and certification takes six weeks. Against a thirteen-week firmware quarter that leaves seven weeks, 54 per cent, in which code can change. Teams counting only their own train are habitually six weeks optimistic.

Regulated products invert the usual relation between speed and paperwork. Lokita's estimate for a fresh CDSCO submission on a changed performance claim was eleven weeks of review, which no cadence absorbs. The expert move, borrowed from what American regulators call a predetermined change control plan, is to define at the freeze the envelope within which future model versions may move, so a change inside it needs no new submission. The envelope is cheap to widen in March 2026 and expensive in 2028, the real reason the compute-module question had a deadline.

AI-native products push hardest on the capability abstraction. A model is the fastest-moving layer in the stack and the least describable as a feature flag. Dilasa's registry therefore does not say supports-v3; it says the probe can host a model of up to 420 MB at twelve frames a second. Capability becomes a resource envelope and the gate a comparison of two numbers. At the organisational seam, mature firms describe one integrated plan and in fact run a platform group owning the registry, the rig farm and the rollout service; they escalate through whoever owns the factory slot, the only irreversible resource in the system.

6. Eight distinctions an expert makes and a competent practitioner does not

There is no single freeze.

Mechanical freeze, BOM freeze and the build loaded at production validation falls on different dates with different reversal costs. The tell is a plan with one bar labelled freeze. The obvious reading, that the date is when change stops, is wrong: change stops in stages, and the expert asks which freeze a date means and what reversing it costs.

A part substitution is a hardware revision.

Sourcing approves second-source parts without opening the revision list; engineering keeps a revision list that never cites part approvals. The tell is two documents that do not reference each other. The obvious reading, that a drop-in replacement changes nothing, holds electrically and fails behaviourally, as Dishari learned for ₹12.71 lakh.

Headroom is bought, not wished for.

The tell is a BOM review where the memory line is defended with the phrase future-proofing and no number. An expert converts it into a break-even probability: ₹77.7 lakh against ₹3.60 crore of renewal margin is 21.6 per cent, which is an argument; future-proofing is not.

Reach has a ceiling, and the ceiling is a hardware fact.

The tell is a rollout dashboard denominated in reachable devices. At week 4 such a chart reads 90.8 per cent, 4.43 of 4.88 lakh, on a base excluding every unit that can never qualify. Dishari's honest number is 59.9 per cent of 7.40 lakh, under a 65.9 per cent ceiling that no update engineering moves.

Cadence buys predictability by spending latency.

The tell is a hardware team asking software for a date and being given a train number. On a quarterly firmware train, a change that misses its departure waits 45.6 days on average, half of 91.25. That is the price of predictability, and it should be priced.

A flag set off is not an absent feature.

The dormant code path, its strings and its permission prompts all ship. The tell is a security review that finds functionality the product team believes is absent. In a regulated device, dormant code is code in the file; a flag changes behaviour, not scope.

The rollback path ages.

The second firmware slot holds a version the cloud has stopped speaking to fluently. The tell is a downgrade that nobody has performed since the last interface change. A kill-switch that has not been exercised against today's cloud is a plan, not a control.

Channel inventory is a time machine.

Dishari found boxed stock fourteen months old at distributors. A unit sold then boots with month-zero firmware, defaults and certificate chain, and meets a cloud fourteen releases ahead. The tell is that nobody can name the oldest stock age in the channel.

7. How this changes by product type and stage

The mechanics do not change across settings: declare, report, decide, offer, revert serves probe and soundbox alike. What moves is the binding constraint.

SettingThe binding constraint
Consumer hardwareLaunch-day matching, with channel inventory age a common hidden variable in first-week failures.
B2B and enterpriseThe customer owns the update window and may freeze firmware for a contract term, so the matrix widens by customer, not version.
Platform and two-sidedA third party certifies the pair, so your train carries a dependency on somebody else's cadence.
MarketplaceThe platform cannot flash anything and must trust self-reported capability, the exact trust a part substitution breaks.
AI productsThe model moves fastest and resists feature language; capability must be expressed as a resource envelope.

Stage changes the failure, not the method. At seed and Series A, with one revision and a few hundred units, the apparatus is overkill and the danger is we can always update them used to end a conversation. At growth the first revision split arrives and the registry must become real; this is where the Dishari defect class lives. At scale the registry, rig farm and rollout service belong to a platform group, and the arguments move to the contract between that group and each product line.

8. Three worked examples

The first is Lathika's. A single build at 2 GB costs ₹1,850 × 4,200, or ₹77.7 lakh. A split build, 1,400 probes at 2 GB and 2,800 at 1 GB, costs ₹25.9 lakh, saving ₹51.8 lakh and adding a second revision to the field. Against ₹3.60 crore of contribution on the 2,600-probe renewal, the single build pays if the chance that v3 arrives within the P2's production life exceeds 77.7 ÷ 360, or 21.6 per cent. If only half that renewal turns on offline inference, ₹1.80 crore, the break-even is 43.2 per cent. The split build cannot be scored the same way: its option covers a third of the units and the 2028 scope is unwritten.

The second is Lajita's. Of 7.40 lakh devices, 5.30 lakh are eligible for 4.2; 42,000 of those, 7.9 per cent, are dormant and will never take it, leaving 4.88 lakh reachable. On the 4.1 rollout, 45 per cent of reachable devices took an update each week.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first argument is whether over-the-air capability makes a freeze date less consequential or more. The late-binding position rests on real evidence: an update's marginal cost is near zero, a factory re-flash is not, and the phone and vehicle industries absorbed the model without collapse. It is wrong wherever reach has a hard ceiling set by hardware and dormancy, and Dishari's 65.9 per cent is exactly that. The opposing position holds that over-the-air delivery does not remove cost but moves it off the profit and loss account onto customers and field staff, where nobody measures it. That would be wrong in a firm that prices field cost; Dishari's ₹310 visit line means it can, where many firms have no such line.

The second argument is who owns the capability registry. The hardware view is that the device is the only honest source of truth: it reports what it is. The platform view is that a device cannot report what it does not know it is, as the amplifier substitution showed, so the registry belongs in the cloud, keyed to serial ranges. What would settle it is narrow: whether every property the business gates on is readable from an identifier on the board.

The third is whether capability-class equivalence is a legitimate reduction or a way of not testing. Its defenders cite 456 minutes against 760, and the untested pairs are untested only if the equivalence claim is false. Its critics note that 61,000 units were once a fourth class nobody had drawn. Both are right; what separates them is whether a nightly probe audits the claim.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in small ways. They ask which freeze a date refers to. They carry a reach ceiling rather than a rollout percentage, and state its denominator unprompted. They will not take an equivalence claim without the probe that audits it, and they write the trip-wire before they know the result. Above all they decline to let we can update it later work as an argument until somebody has said how many units, by when, and at what cost to whom.

12. The two decisions, and three questions

Lathika took the single build at 2 GB for all 4,200 probes, paying ₹51.8 lakh more than the split build to keep a second revision out of a field where the registry was young. She commissioned the change-control envelope at the freeze rather than at submission, reasoning that memory is useless without the regulatory right to use it and that the envelope is cheaper to widen in March. Laveena announced split settlement on 1 July but refused the fleet-wide price-list line, publishing a per-device eligibility check in the merchant app instead. Her trip-wire, written down before the rollout, was 55 per cent of the fleet on 4.2 by 29 June: the week-3 level, one week of slack under the 59.9 per cent forecast. Replacing the 2.10 lakh Rev A units at ₹1,150 each would have cost ₹24.15 crore, which ended that conversation.

Three questions are worth an hour. First: Lathika's break-even of 21.6 per cent treats the renewal margin as the whole prize. What else does the 2 GB module buy that her calculation omits, and would it change the split-build comparison or only the headline? Second: Laveena's trip-wire sits on a quantity she already models well. Which quantity is she not modelling, and what would a trip-wire on that look like? Third: Dishari answered the amplifier failure by adding a registry field. Under what conditions does adding registry fields stop being a fix and start being the problem?

13. Going deeper

Hardware development cycles explains what EVT, DVT and PVT each close, and unlocks reading a hardware plan for reversal costs rather than dates. Companion apps and cloud services holds the other half of this contract, where the flag service lives. The software development lifecycle supplies the branches and support windows the pairing matrix is built from. Agile in practice is the source of the train metaphor and most of its misuse. Kanban and flow gives the queueing reasoning behind cadence and the 45.6-day expected wait. The execution rhythm governs two cadences in one calendar. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing matters because a train works only if content can be sized against a fixed departure. Backlog management and refinement decides what is ready to board, the one lever a product manager holds over a train they cannot slow.

Two Clocks, One Thermostat

Integrating hardware and software release trains

1. The review of 8 September

On 8 September 2025, Kshemal Satoskar, vice president of product at Camber Climate in Pune, opened a review she expected to be routine. Camber made a Wi-Fi thermostat, and its second generation, the Hub 2, was due in shops on 20 October. Its firmware, the software stored permanently on the device's chip, had been frozen on 1 September: no further change could enter the version that the contract manufacturer in Chennai would load onto every unit. That version was 1.0. Production would start on 22 September and build 36,000 units in eighteen days.

Kunaal Sarpotdar, who led the mobile app and cloud services, brought a timing problem. His team released an app every seven days, so seven releases stood between the freeze and launch. The Hub 2's headline feature, a geofenced setback that lowers the temperature when everyone leaves home, needed a capability that firmware 1.1 would add. Kartikay Sarnaik, the firmware lead, expected radio-conformance testing of 1.1 to finish on 13 October, three days after the last unit left the line and seven days before launch.

Kshemal had two options. Chennai could re-flash all 36,000 units at ₹95 each, ₹34.2 lakh, and launch on 3 November. Retail partners' festival display slots ended on 31 October, so that launch would miss them. Or she could launch on 20 October with 1.0 inside the boxes, ten thousand first-week orders at ₹6,490 each, ₹6.49 crore, riding on an update arriving later. Chennai needed the plan by 12 September.

Figure 1 shows why the choice was hard. The brown bar, the factory run, ends three days before the red diamond, so no unit can leave Chennai carrying 1.1. Seven green releases, however, fall inside the same window, and the app Kunaal ships on launch day will be seven versions newer than anything the firmware team could have imagined at the freeze.

2. The idea

A release train is a fixed schedule of departures: software ships on the train that leaves on its day, with whatever is ready, and anything unready waits for the next. Integrating hardware and software release trains means making a device that changes once with software that changes weekly, so that they never disagree about what the device can do. It rests on three devices: capability declarations in the hardware, flags that switch behaviour on per unit, and over-the-air (OTA) updates that replace firmware after sale.

Release trains were formalised in the Scaled Agile Framework from about 2011, notably in Dean Leffingwell's work. Phone makers and, from about 2012, some carmakers made OTA updates routine. The problem all of them faced was that a shipped unit cannot be recalled to a developer's desk. The sentence Kshemal could repeat in a meeting was this: “Hardware ships a capability once; software releases the behaviour weekly; and each unit tells us which of the two it can run.”

Figure 2 states the problem in its simplest form. Between two hardware launches the software clock ticks 52 times, and each tick can touch a device that was designed once. Left unmanaged, one clock drags the other: either hardware waits for software, or software slows to the pace of hardware. Integration is the discipline that lets both run at their natural speed.

3. How it actually works

Five steps carry the mechanism, and two things practitioners rarely say aloud sit around them. First, at the freeze the device declares its capabilities: a list of what the hardware and frozen firmware can do, such as geofence-report or two-stage-heating. Second, the interface between device and cloud is versioned and only extended: new message types may be added, but no existing message changes meaning, so old firmware talking to a new cloud meets no surprise.

Third, at every connection the device reports its firmware version and capability list to the cloud (arrow 1 in Figure 3). Fourth, the cloud's flag service, a table of switches that turn behaviours on for particular devices, combines that report with a rollout rule and returns a decision (arrow 2); the app draws only what the decision permits. Fifth, the update service offers a newer firmware image when one exists (arrow 3), and the device installs it when idle. Commands from the user go to the cloud, which relays them to the device (arrow 4).

Launch-day matching is the name for lining these layers up: on the day the boxes open, the app in the store, the flags in the cloud and the firmware on offer must form pairings that someone has actually tested. The unspoken parts matter as much. App stores review each release for one to two days, so launch-day app code must be final days before the boxes open. And every layer needs a way back: each flag has a kill-switch, and the device keeps two firmware slots so that a failed install reverts to the slot that worked.

4. A worked example

Kunaal's first calculation concerned the test rig, a bench of real thermostats wired to automated software. One full regression run against one pairing of app version and firmware version takes 45 minutes. Camber supported each app release for eight weeks, because some users never update. With weekly releases, versions aged 0 to 7 weeks are all in the field: 8 versions. After 13 October two firmware versions exist, so 8 × 2 = 16 pairs, or 16 × 45 = 720 minutes. The overnight window is ten hours, 600 minutes, which holds 13 pairs at most (600 ÷ 45 = 13.3).

The second pass changes one input, the support window, from eight weeks to four. Versions in the field fall from 8 to 4, pairs from 16 to 8, and the run from 720 to 360 minutes. Weekly cadence survives; what shrinks is the tail Camber agrees to carry. A third firmware version at the original window would instead give 8 × 3 = 24 pairs, 1,080 minutes, or 18 hours.

Kshemal's second calculation was what customers would see. Of 10,000 units sold in week one, Kartikay's pilot, run on pre-release 1.1, suggested that 85% of units would connect within 24 hours of first power-on, and that 92% of those connected units would complete the update at the first attempt.
