The sites cover 06:30–19:30 IST between them, so the window holds 54.6 covered hours and 46.2 uncovered, 2.6 of them gated and the rest idle.

That caption carries the arithmetic disciplining the rest: a clock day costs thirteen covered hours. Hands-on, queued and zone-blocked elapse only on shift, so lead time in days is covered hours over thirteen: 11.0 + 32.4 + 6.0 plus 5.2 daytime gated hours is 54.6, and 54.6 ÷ 13 = 4.2 days.

The queue row is modelled. Nine reviewers each reserve 4.0 of a 9.0-hour shift, so 36.0 reviewer-hours a day meet 24 requests at 1.2 hours, or 28.8: utilisation 0.80. Because reviewing gets four hours in nine, a 1.2-hour review occupies 1.2 × 9.0 ÷ 4.0 = 2.70 shift hours, and nine independent queues, one per reviewer, give ρ/(1−ρ) × 2.70 = 10.8 shift hours a round, 32.4 over three. Pool the nine at the same load and the wait collapses by an order of magnitude — cheaper than any geography, which is why the discipline must be named.

The zone-blocked row is a weighted average over every ordered pair, not the worst. Shares of the components an item touches, from a year of commit ownership rather than headcount, are 0.55 Bengaluru, 0.25 Manila, 0.20 Dubai, so the squares sum to 0.405 and 0.595 of transitions cross. Figure 2 shows how sharply direction matters: weighted by p·p the expectation is 1.20 hours a transition, 6.0 over five, where pricing every crossing at the Bengaluru–Manila 4.50 would give 13.4. Those waits also contain night hours Table 2 books separately, so 6.0 is generous.

So 6.0 of the 100.8 hours, or 6.0 per cent, is geography. Consolidation removes six covered hours, leaving 48.6 and 3.74 days, or 89.7 hours; against an excess over target of 64.8 hours it closes 17.1 per cent. The largest component, 43.6 of 100.8 hours or 43.3 per cent, is time nobody works at all, which no address change touches. Feature slicing is what breaks the independence this model assumes, which is why it works where rebalancing headcount does not.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

A platform team in a multi-product company is the classic seam, becoming a crossing for every stream at once. Mature companies do not solve this with service levels on a ticket queue, whatever the handbook says; they make the platform self-service with a documented escape hatch, so only the exception costs a crossing. Two-sided businesses break differently: operations run on the customer's clock, so Jaltarang's Dubai trust-and-safety desk is synchronous by obligation while its engineers are asynchronous by design. The seam lies between an org that cannot batch and one that must.

Regulated work removes the most powerful asynchronous instrument: a default-proceed rule cannot lawfully apply to a signature that must be attributable and non-repudiable, which is why Jalvayu's step 6 is a human and not a timer. Hardware plus software adds a constraint no process change relieves: Jalvayu's chambers are all in Nashik, which is why row B keeps two Nashik crossings and why buying the chamber out of the path makes things worse. AI-native products cut both ways — non-determinism makes approve-with-comments unsafe, since the reviewer cannot predict what the amended version does, yet a trustworthy evaluation suite is the strongest asynchronous gate yet invented.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Overlap is a price, not a capability

The tell-tale sign is an overlap window holding one recurring meeting and nothing else. The obvious reading is that the team protected its shared hours; the expert reading is that it spent the whole budget on a ritual, leaving nothing for the decision that arrives on a Tuesday.

The binding term is usually the uncovered hours

The sign is lead time barely moving when two sites shift hours to overlap more. Everyone expects it to help, because the gap is the visible feature. It does not: the dominant term is the eleven hours a day nobody works, and shifting hours redistributes coverage rather than extending it.

Decision rights travel; documents do not

The sign is hand-off notes getting longer while clarifying questions stay flat. The obvious diagnosis is that the writing needs work. The real one is that the note carries authority it does not have: the receiver asks not what was meant but who may decide, and no prose answers that.

A default-proceed rule turns on reversibility, not trust

The sign is one twenty-four-hour default applied to a feature flag and a schema migration alike. Teams argue as though the question were trust. It is whether the action can be undone for the price of noticing — Amazon's one-way and two-way doors — so the test is the cost of reversal.

Utilisation is the hidden multiplier

The sign is that adding a reviewer moves lead time more than adding an hour of overlap, which nobody believes until the queue is measured. Because ρ/(1−ρ) is convex, a team at 0.80 utilisation waits four service times and one at 0.60 waits 1.5. Distribution gets blamed for a queue that would exist on one floor.

Context decay makes the author pay twice

The sign is rework hours rising with review latency even when the comments do not change. The obvious reading is pickier reviewers. The expert reading is that an author returning a day later must rebuild the state they held when writing, at a cost scaling with the wait.

Someone pays for the overlap, and attrition finds them

The sign is the same two names on every early call for a year. It reads as commitment and is usually a rota nobody wrote down. The cost surfaces late and in the wrong ledger, as regretted attrition at one site, taking the knowledge that made those two worth asking.

Calendars diverge more violently than clocks

The sign is an unmodelled lead-time spike in Diwali week and across the Christmas fortnight. Offsets are stable and get the attention; holiday calendars are not, and a four-day gap at one site costs more coverage than a two-hour offset does in a year. Expert teams publish a combined calendar and plan around its holes.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products most changes are reversible behind flags, so default-proceed can be the norm and the constraint moves to incident response, which honestly means a paid rota. In B2B and enterprise, the customer's day joins the delivery clock: Jalvayu's distributor raises defects at 10:00 in Guadalajara, 21:30 in Nashik, so support must be sliced by customer geography even when engineering is not. In platforms the difference is large: a documented, versioned interface is the only mechanism that reliably takes a crossing to zero. In marketplaces the asymmetry is operational, not geographic. For hardware, test capacity pins work to a place and the only lever is more rigs, as row C shows. For AI products, evaluation suites substitute for synchronous judgement as nowhere else.

Stage changes the calculus more than type does. Below roughly fifteen engineers no slice is big enough to own end to end, so the answer is one core zone and everything else an exception; Jalvayu at 96 engineers can afford two owned slices, Jaltarang at 140 four. Above a few hundred it becomes a question of platform boundaries, because crossings are then set by the architecture, not the org chart.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Jaltarang's reviewer arithmetic. Three more reviewers take capacity to 48.0 reviewer-hours against the same 28.8 of demand, so utilisation falls to 0.60 and the wait to 1.5 × 2.70 = 4.05 shift hours a round, 12.2 over three rounds instead of 32.4. Continuous deployment clears the gated hours, and covered hours fall to 29.2, or 2.25 days — against the 3.74 that moving all 140 engineers to Bengaluru buys.

Jalvayu's follow-the-sun experiment, which failed. Over the seventy-five days from 14 April to 27 June 2025, Nashik handed the firmware build to Guadalajara at end of shift and Guadalajara continued it. Throughput rose sharply: 61 changes reached the field against 34 in the preceding seventy-five days, up 79.4 per cent. Field defects within thirty days rose too, from 3 of the 34 changes, or 8.8 per cent, to 14 of the 61, or 23.0 per cent.

The honest reading is more interesting than Jalvayu's. The difference of 14.1 points carries a standard error of 7.3, so it stands at 1.95 standard errors — just short of conventional significance — and the window was confounded by the Mark 4 launch, which put unusually risky changes into that period. What justified stopping was the cause analysis, not the rate: the three largest escapes all traced to a hand-off note omitting the rig's calibration state, a defect of the hand-off rather than of either side. The excess is not the raw 14 − 3: at the old 8.8 per cent rate, 61 changes would have produced 5.4 escapes, so 8.6 are extra, and at roughly ₹1.9 lakh per field visit that is about ₹16 lakh.

Jaltarang's default-proceed rule. In the quarter to December 2025, pricing changes proceeded if nobody objected within twenty-four hours. Median time-to-live fell from 31 hours to 7, and rollbacks rose from 3 of 388 changes to 16 of 412 — 0.8 per cent to 3.9, a difference of 2.96 standard errors and, unlike Jalvayu's, a real one. Refunds rose from ₹0.6 lakh to ₹6.2 lakh. The recovery scoped the rule rather than abandoning it: from January it covered only changes behind a flag with automatic rollback, and January's 151 gave 3 rollbacks.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signThe diagnostic question, and the cost of catching it late
Overlap meeting as information channelAttendance decays; the same questions recurHow many decisions here could not have been written? Late: the team decides asynchrony failed and buys meetings.
Ownership by layer rather than sliceMost tickets carry two sites' namesWhat share of items touches two sites? Above a third, redraw. Late: headcount goes to the busiest layer, raising crossings.
Done defined as mergedFriday's finished work cannot ship on MondayCan another site release this from the record alone? Late: it surfaces as a missed customer date.
Coverage bought without context designThroughput and escaped defects rise togetherWhich defects trace to the hand-off, not the change? Late: the cost lands in field service, read as warranty.
 Table 3. Row four is Jalvayu's follow-the-sun experiment; row two was Jaltarang before February 2026.

What makes all four expensive is the delay between cause and signal: a crossing rate that is too high surfaces as a lead-time number weeks later and as attrition months later, by which time the organisation has explained it with a story about culture.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether co-location shrinks the item or only the wait. Table 2 assumes touch count is a property of the work. The overlap school denies it: when clarification is free, items need fewer touches, so moving everyone to Bengaluru would not merely delete 6.0 covered hours but shorten the chain generating the other rows. Its evidence is Allen's curve and the 2003 finding that cross-site items carried more people. For it to be wrong, touch count must be invariant to proximity — testable on items falling wholly inside Bengaluru.

Whether follow-the-sun is a real gain. A believer sees 79.4 per cent more throughput abandoned on a result at 1.95 standard errors, in a window confounded by a hardware launch: a working programme killed by a null. The sceptic answers with the cause analysis. For the believer to be wrong, the escapes must be attributable to the hand-off; for the sceptic to be wrong, the three traced defects must be coincidence.

Whether writing substitutes for presence or merely reveals modularity. The written-first school points to Apache and the kernel: profound design done on mailing lists for decades. The architecture-first school answers that those projects were modular first and wrote second, so writing is the symptom. Both read the 2021 finding as support. No experiment separates them, and until one does this should be left unresolved.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this reaches for the overlap calendar and the handbook. Someone who has internalised it measures before redesigning, and asks how many touches an item needs before asking how many hours two sites share. They treat overlap as a budget with a ledger and a rotation, and can say without looking which of the five states dominates their lead time. They tell a reversible default from an irreversible one by the cost of undoing. And when the lever left is item size, they go to the backlog, not the org chart.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Chandavarkar declined Chodankar's consolidation. She gave Guadalajara the regulated audit-trail slice against a frozen device-event contract, kept the rig test in Nashik because the chambers cannot move, and bought one hour of overlap at 17:30–18:30 IST by shifting Guadalajara to a 06:00 start, reserved for contract changes. She did not restart follow-the-sun, and row C killed the chamber. Chimulkar declined Chanekar's consolidation too, added three reviewers, moved to continuous deployment, and took the rest of the distance to item size. Halving touches from six to three gives hands-on 5.5, 1.5 queue rounds at 4.05 for 6.1, and two transitions at 1.20 for 2.4: 14.0 covered hours, or 1.08 days. The target is reachable, then — but only through item size, the slowest lever in the building, and the halving is assumed rather than shown. She committed to 2.25 days by June and left 1.5 to the backlog.

1. Table 2 attributes 6.0 per cent of lead time to geography. What measurement would persuade you that the true figure is much higher because the touch count is itself a consequence of distance?

2. Jalvayu stopped a programme on a difference of 1.95 standard errors. Was the cause analysis sufficient grounds, and what would you have required instead?

3. Chandavarkar bought one hour of overlap and spent it on contract changes only. Who at Jalvayu pays for that hour, and what would make the price fair?

13. Going deeper

The execution rhythm is the parent: a cadence built for one room assumes a daily synchronisation a distributed team must buy or replace, and this page is what replacing it costs. The software development lifecycle locates where crossings sit, since a change crosses different boundaries at specification, build and release stages. Agile in practice is a warning: written-first teams need fewer rituals, not relabelled ones. Kanban and flow supplies the apparatus — work in progress, cycle time, Little's Law — that makes the decomposition routine. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing becomes a latency instrument once item size drives touch count. Backlog management and refinement holds the last lever, and definition of done is the contract that makes a hand-off safe across a twelve-hour gap.
exp20v2-agile.hw.dev:
Hardware Development Cycles

Why agile bends when the product is made of atoms

1. A week to the freeze

On Monday 27 April 2026, Iresh Panse, head of product at Arkavi Wearables, a Pune company that designs fitness bands and has them assembled by a contract manufacturer in Chakan, had a decision due within the week. The second-generation Arkavi Band was scheduled to reach retailers on Monday 5 October, in time for the festive buying season. Its mechanical design had to be frozen on Monday 4 May, because that day the tool shop would begin cutting the steel moulds that shape the plastic housing, an eight-week job that nobody could start twice.

On Friday 24 April the bench results for the first fifty engineering units had arrived. Eleven of the fifty let stray light reach the optical heart-rate sensor under a bright-light test. Indrayudh Pawaskar, the mechanical lead, believed a revised gasket seat would cure it, but had tested the idea only on paper. Ivin Parkar, the firmware lead, offered to filter the noise in software. Sales forecast 12,000 units in the first month at a contribution margin of ₹1,100 each. Freeze on time and risk a defect locked into steel, or hold and risk the season? Figure 1 shows the plan Panse inherited: five stages in sequence and, beneath them, the fourteen two-week sprints a software team would run in the same twenty-eight weeks.

2. The idea

A hardware development cycle is the sequence of build-and-test stages by which a physical product moves from first working prototype to volume production. Each stage ends in a freeze: a date after which a defined part of the design may change only through a formal, costed exception. Freezes exist because atoms cannot be refactored. A software team recompiles in minutes; a hardware team waits for a mould, a circuit board or a certification slot, so a mistaken design costs weeks and lakhs rather than hours.

The practice descends from stage-gate reviews, which Robert Cooper formalised in the 1980s, and from electronics contract manufacturing, which settled on the stage names used here in the following decades. Agile was articulated for software in 2001. Barry Boehm's 1981 observation that the cost of fixing an error rises steeply with the stage at which it is found is the root of the freeze. Panse's sentence for the meeting was this: "Software lets us be wrong cheaply every two weeks; hardware lets us be wrong cheaply only before a freeze, so we spend our agility early and our discipline after." The sentence is not a rejection of agile; it relocates it.

Software teamHardware team
Unit of changeA code commitA tool, board or part
Typical loopTwo weeksSix to eight weeks
Cost of a late errorA patchSteel, stock, certification

3. How it actually works

Four named stages carry a product to market. Engineering validation test (EVT) builds a few dozen units on soft tooling, meaning cheap, short-life moulds, and asks whether the design works at all. Design validation test (DVT) builds a few hundred units on production-intent steel tools and asks whether the product meets specification, including regulatory certification. Production validation test (PVT) builds on the real line at near-volume and asks whether the factory can repeat the result. Mass production (MP) is the ramp. Table 1 divides Arkavi's twenty-eight weeks accordingly.

StageUnitsWeeksStarts (Mon)Ends (Mon)
EVT50623 Mar4 May
Steel toolingnone84 May29 Jun
DVT300629 Jun10 Aug
PVT1,500510 Aug14 Sep
MP rampvolume314 Sep5 Oct
Total 28——

Table 1. Arkavi Band stage plan.

Several steps stay implicit. The calendar is computed backward from the ship date, so twenty-eight weeks before 5 October puts the start on 23 March; Arkavi had no slack at the front. Lead time is not effort: steel does not cut faster with more engineers. Every stage inherits the freezes of the one before. And each build needs a test plan stating in advance which result would count as failure; otherwise it merely produces units.

Figure 2 prices one change, the gasket seat, across four moments. The jump from ₹0.4 lakh to ₹9 lakh is not the part cost; it is steel to be cut or welded, parts already built, and tests to be repeated. The ₹9 lakh quote reappears in the next section. The curve is the reason for the whole structure. Early on, a mistake can be repaired with a printed part and an afternoon; later, repair means stopping a line. Teams therefore try to move discovery leftward, running the questions most likely to kill the design in EVT, while reserving expensive commitments for questions already answered.

4. A worked example

Panse first priced a week. A month of 12,000 units is 3,000 a week; at ₹1,100 each that is ₹33 lakh of weekly margin. Adding ₹6 lakh of weekly programme cost makes ₹39 lakh per week of delay, treating festival sales as lost, not deferred. Next, the chance that DVT on steel confirms the leak. No such probability had been measured. Panse took the 22 per cent failure rate of the soft-tool units (eleven of fifty) as a stand-in, an assumption, with a standard error of about 5.9 points and a 95 per cent band from 10.5 to 33.5 per cent. Option A freezes on 4 May; if DVT confirms the leak, the tool shop quotes four weeks to modify steel plus three to retest, seven weeks, and ₹9 lakh. Option B holds the freeze one week to test a revised gasket, assuming that test resolves the question.

Line (₹ lakh unless stated)A: freeze, 7-week reworkA: freeze, 3-week reworkB: hold one week
Certain slip (weeks)001
Slip if leak confirmed (weeks)730
Tool modification if leak confirmed990
Cost if leak confirmed28212639
Expected cost at p = 0.2262.0427.7239.00
Break-even p against B13.8%31.0% 

Table 2. Cost if leak confirmed = weeks of slip × 39 + tool modification (7 × 39 + 9 = 282; 3 × 39 + 9 = 126; 1 × 39 = 39). Break-even p = 39 ÷ cost if confirmed.

With a seven-week rework, B is cheaper by ₹23.04 lakh. Changing one input, rework of three weeks, reverses the answer: A then costs ₹27.72 lakh against ₹39 lakh, provided the steel-safe premium is under ₹11.28 lakh (39 − 27.72) and the modification stays at ₹9 lakh. The seven-week answer, conversely, flips if p is below 13.8 per cent, which the band includes. The decision turns on a quote, not on the sprint rhythm.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A freeze is a gradient, not a switch.

Different layers freeze on different dates. Table 3 shows what is locked and what stays open after each stage. Asking "is the design frozen?" is a poor question; "which layer, since when?" is the useful one, and the answer tells a newcomer which conversations are still cheap. A product manager who proposes a change should first locate it in this table.

Stage completedFrozenStill open
EVTHousing drawingBoard layout, firmware
DVTBoard layout, steel toolsFirmware, packaging
PVTProcess, test limitsFirmware updates after shipping

Table 3. Illustrative freeze layers for the Arkavi Band.

Prototype fidelity differs by stage.

A soft-tool EVT unit answers whether the idea works; it says little about steel-tool tolerances. Eleven failures on soft tooling may overstate, or understate, what hard tools will do. The honest label on an EVT result is therefore "directional": strong enough to schedule a question, too weak to close one.

Agile practices survive inside the stages.

Firmware, test automation and the companion app can still run sprints, and should. What bends is mechanical and electrical change after a freeze, not the habit of short feedback. Panse could, and did, keep Parkar's team on two-week sprints throughout, because a firmware change costs a build, not a mould.

Lead time is not cycle time.

Eight weeks of tool cutting is waiting, not work. Adding people shortens neither the cut nor a certification queue, so the useful question is what could be started in parallel. Certification paperwork, packaging artwork and test fixtures can all begin before the steel is finished, and teams that discover this late waste weeks.

Small samples and correlated units.

The 5.9-point error assumes fifty independent units. If the eleven failures shared one gasket batch, the true uncertainty is wider and the 22 per cent is softer than it looks. Treating the band as a guess about a range, not a point, is what separates a calculation from a ritual.

Optionality can be bought.

Cutting a tool "steel-safe", leaving metal where change is likely so it can be machined away rather than welded back, shortens later rework. It costs something now, which is why it is not priced in Table 2. The rework quote is therefore a negotiable number, not a fact of nature, and negotiating it early is a legitimate use of a product manager's week.

Software cannot launder hardware debt.

Filtering sensor noise in firmware helps, but it spends battery and cannot recover light that never reached the sensor. The two schedules still have to meet: a firmware release that assumes a sensor revision not yet built is a hidden dependency, which later pages on release-train integration address.

What the cycle cannot tell you.

It sequences risk; it does not say whether customers want the band. Before relying on it, ask which assumptions each build actually tests, and which remain untested until a customer wears the band for a month.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace, early and late

SettingWhat changes
ConsumerFixed retail windows turn every week of slip into lost season
B2BCertification and customer sign-off lengthen DVT; changes follow contract terms
MarketplaceHardware is rare; where a platform issues devices to merchants, the device is a fixed cost beneath fast-moving software
Early stageDev kits and contract design shorten EVT; one product bears all tooling risk
Large companyPlatform reuse and parallel programmes cut risk but add coordination

The pattern holds across these cases: the more committed the money, the earlier the freeze. A start-up can afford fewer builds because it has fewer commitments; a large firm tends to freeze shared components early because many products depend on them. In every setting the useful question is the same: what has already been paid for, and what would it cost to unpay it?

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Sprinting past the freezeDesign changes keep arriving in DVTFreeze is a preferenceCount change requests per stage
Scheduling forwardShip date slips in whole tool-lead-time blocksStages can compress with effortRecompute backward from ship date
Counting builds as learning300 units built, no failure dataUnits equal evidenceAsk what result would change the decision

Each symptom is visible without opening the design files: a change log, a slipping date, a pile of untested units. Each diagnostic is a ten-minute exercise with an existing spreadsheet, which is why it belongs in a weekly programme review, not a post-mortem.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Panse's decision leaves a short written record before 4 May, shown below. The threshold is explicit, the uncertainty is declared rather than hidden, and a named owner holds the one-week experiment while most other layers freeze on time. Pawaskar prints and tests the revised seat within the week, Parkar keeps the firmware filter as a fallback rather than as the fix, and the tool shop receives a dated release so its queue is not left to guess. Nothing is sprinted past the freeze; one question is answered before it.

QuestionDoes gasket seat B stop the leak?
Owner, datePawaskar, 8 May
TriggerWritten 3-week quote, premium under ₹11.28 lakh, reverses the call

9. Closing

Panse held the freeze to Monday 11 May and moved shipment to Monday 12 October. The three-week rework was a hope, not a quote; the tool shop had put in writing a four-week modification quote, plus three weeks to retest. At that figure the hold cost ₹39 lakh against an expected ₹62.04 lakh, though the choice does not survive every value of p in the band: it flips below 13.8 per cent. He also asked Ikshvaku Palkar, the tool shop manager, for a written steel-safe quote on the gasket seat; a three-week commitment with a premium under ₹11.28 lakh would have reversed his decision. The reasoning rested on the quote and the stated assumption about p, both of which he could name; it did not rest on optimism about either.

Next, study EVT, DVT, PVT and mass production stage by stage, then how hardware and software release trains integrate. Two questions to sit with. Which layer of your own product is already frozen, and who decided? And what would you pay today to turn a seven-week rework into a three-week one?
exp40v2-agile.hw.dev:
Hardware Development Cycles

Pricing irreversibility: why agile bends for atoms, and the cases in which it does not bend at all

1. Two freezes on the same Monday

On Thursday 5 March 2026, Jaivik Raiturkar, head of product at Belwadi Instruments in Pune, had three days to decide what to write into a technical file. Belwadi builds the PC‑40, a point‑of‑care haematology analyser sold to hospital chains and district laboratories, and the design freeze that locks the file for the notified body under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 was set for Monday 9 March. On Tuesday 3 March the bench report arrived: 3 of 40 design‑validation units had leaked at the reagent seal, 7.5 per cent. Jisha Ramdasi, Belwadi's regulatory and quality lead, pointed out that the acceptance limit already written into the file was 6.0 per cent. Validation testing was planned to run to Monday 10 August, and a state health tender for 240 analysers — ₹7.50 lakh of revenue and ₹2.25 lakh of contribution each, ₹540 lakh in all — closed on Tuesday 15 September, leaving just over five weeks of slack.

In Bengaluru the same week, Jamini Renavikar, vice‑president of product at Bakula Devices, faced a freeze on the same Monday. The Bakula Nook is a home camera that runs its detection model on an on‑device neural processing unit. Jinendra Ratnagirkar, programme manager at the contract manufacturer in Hosur, needed the housing tool released on 9 March to hold twelve weeks of cutting and trials. Jalpesh Rendalkar, Bakula's hardware lead, wanted a fortnight more on the thermal design. Channel fill was Monday 21 September, ahead of Diwali on Sunday 8 November; the eight‑week season was planned at 48,000 units and ₹1,500 of contribution each, ₹720 lakh. A week lost inside that window costs 6,000 units, ₹90 lakh.

The conventional reading is that both are hostages to the same physics. They are not. The hardness of atoms is not the variable that matters; two others are, and they differ sharply between these companies: where in the programme the irreversible money is spent, and what shape the cost‑of‑delay curve has.

 Belwadi PC‑40Bakula Nook
Product typeRegulated B2B instrumentConsumer connected device
First‑window volume240 analysers48,000 units
Contribution per unit₹2.25 lakh₹1,500
Binding commitmentA validated design in a technical fileA long‑lead chip and a steel tool
Cost of a week's slipNil, until a tender date₹90 lakh, every week

Table 1. The two programmes as they stood on Thursday 5 March 2026.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A hardware development cycle is the ordered sequence of build‑and‑test stages that carries a physical product from first working prototype to volume production, punctuated by freezes. A freeze is best defined not as a date on which change stops but as the moment at which the marginal cost of change steps up discontinuously, because money has been spent that cannot be recovered. That definition is more useful than the calendar one, because it tells you what to look for: the step, not the date.

The intellectual lineage has three strands. Robert Cooper's stage‑gate reviews, formalised through the 1980s, gave the structure its gates. Barry Boehm's 1981 finding that the cost of correcting a defect rises steeply with the stage at which it is caught gave the structure its justification. Kim Clark and Takahiro Fujimoto's study of automotive development in the late 1980s added the counterweight: overlapping problem‑solving between stages, rather than strict sequence, was what gave the shorter programmes their lead‑time advantage. Agile, articulated for software in 2001, inherited the argument rather than starting it.

Three live schools disagree about what follows. They are not degrees of the same opinion; each would refuse a proposition the others accept.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Front‑loading and hard gates (Cooper; Boehm; Thomke on cheap early experiments)Move discovery left; a gate passed on incomplete evidence is a debt that compoundsThat a freeze date is negotiable once the programme is under way
Flow and small batches (Reinertsen; the agile–stage‑gate hybrids)Queues, not work content, dominate hardware lead time; shrink batches and expose the waitThat batching changes is free of delay cost
Set‑based concurrent engineering (Ward, Sobek and the Toyota literature)Carry several designs past the point a point‑based team would have chosen oneThat the first feasible concept should be developed to completion

Table 2. The three schools, stated so that each refuses something the others accept.

The second and third schools contradict each other outright on batch size, and this page's own numbers come down on opposite sides of it.

3. Mechanics: the ladder, the queue and the price of a change

Expert practitioners do not plan a freeze. They plan a ladder of freezes, each rung set by a supplier's lead time and counted backward from a single build date. Figure 1 shows Bakula's ladder for the design‑validation build that starts on Monday 1 June 2026.

Two consequences follow, and the second is the one teams miss. First, the earliest freeze is not a drawing but a purchase order: the chip was committed on 29 December 2025, ten weeks before the tool. Second, the ladder's top rung is set by a supplier, not by the programme, so the question "when do we freeze?" is mostly answered outside the building. A product manager who can recite the mechanical freeze date but not the long‑lead buy date is reading the second page of the schedule.

The second mechanic is queueing, and it is where hardware calendars actually go. Belwadi books electromagnetic compatibility runs at an external accredited laboratory: four working days of service per run. Treat the chamber as a single server with random arrivals and the expected wait before service is ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) × 4 days. Figure 2 plots it.

Belwadi cannot make a laboratory run cooler, but it can choose a less loaded one or reserve slots. The model assumes random arrivals and one server, and it is optimistic: real arrivals bunch at stage boundaries, so the true wait is worse. Belwadi's programme was not slow because its engineers were slow.

The third mechanic is the price of a change, and here the usual advice inverts. At Bakula a single engineering change order raised after the steel is released costs ₹2.90 lakh, of which ₹2.20 lakh is retest and requalification and ₹0.70 lakh is the change itself; the same change before release costs ₹0.60 lakh, a ratio of 4.8 to one. But because retest is a fixed cost paid once, three changes gathered into one dated window cost ₹2.20 lakh plus 3 × ₹0.70 lakh, or ₹4.30 lakh — ₹1.43 lakh each against ₹8.70 lakh for the same three raised singly. Batching halves the price of a change. Expert hardware teams therefore publish change windows, not change bans. The wait that buys the saving is short: ₹4.40 lakh across three changes is 0.049 of a week at Bakula's ₹90 lakh, about a third of a day. Where the step is that shallow the flow school is right; where requalification is heavy it is not.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as claims that can be tested against a real programme, and the two companies separate immediately.

Testable claimBelwadi PC‑40Bakula Nook
A late change costs at least four times an early oneHolds: ₹11.60 lakh against ₹1.40 lakh, 8.3×Holds: ₹2.90 lakh against ₹0.60 lakh, 4.8×
The cost of delay is continuous and materialFails: nil for five weeks, then a stepHolds: ₹90 lakh a week
The irreversible commitment cannot be deferred affordablyHolds: no instrument bridges a licenceFails: a bridge tool insures it for ₹18.95 lakh

Table 3. Three conditions, applied. Neither company satisfies all three; they fail different ones.

The idea misleads when a team imports the whole apparatus simply because the product is physical. If the long‑lead part is a commodity held in distributor stock, there is no top rung. If first‑year volume is 300 instruments, soft tooling carries the year and the steel freeze is imaginary. If the design is a rebadged original‑design‑manufacturer platform, the governing freeze is the supplier's. Figure 3 shows why the second claim drives behaviour.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Across a platform the ladder's top rung belongs to nobody. When one chip serves three products, the platform group commits it and each product team inherits a constraint it did not price. Mature companies charge for this rather than debate it: the platform group publishes the date and a product wanting a later one pays for the buffer stock. Companies that claim to handle it by alignment usually have an unowned slack buffer instead, spent without a paper trail.

Where a platform issues devices to its own merchants or riders, the binding hardware is not the next build but the installed base. If 38 per cent of terminals in the field carry the older board, the oldest hardware sets the ceiling for every software release, and the freeze that matters was taken three years ago by somebody who has left.

Regulation changes the kind of constraint, not only its size. A change after design validation triggers requalification under the quality system, so Belwadi's freeze is legal rather than economic and cannot be bought out at any price. The hardware‑plus‑software seam produces two freezes on one bill of materials: the firmware image submitted for certification is frozen while the shipping firmware updates monthly, and the two diverge until somebody reconciles them.

The AI‑native case is the sharpest version of the whole problem. The Nook's NPU has a 256 MB inference allocation, of which 48 MB goes to frame buffers and 28 MB to the runtime, leaving 180 MB for weights. The model team's 2027 candidate quantises to 310 MB. That ceiling was frozen on 29 December 2025 by a purchase order, two years before the model that will hit it exists. The part of the product that cannot be frozen is constrained by the part that had to be.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The first freeze is a purchase order.

The tell‑tale sign is a team that can state the mechanical freeze date to the day and has to look up the long‑lead buy date. The obvious reading — that design precedes procurement — is backwards whenever lead times exceed design time, which for custom silicon and optics is routine.

A freeze is a commitment device aimed inward.

Its primary function is not to protect the tool shop but to stop the organisation reopening settled questions. The sign is that freezes are enforced hardest against the people least able to have caused the problem. Read as a physical necessity it looks arbitrary; read as a commitment device it is doing exactly its job.

Batch changes; do not ban them.

An organisation reporting zero change orders during validation is not disciplined, it is mislabelling. The sign is a rising count of "drawing clarifications" with no engineering change order behind them. Because requalification is a fixed cost, the small batch that agile prizes is the expensive one here.

Shared test capacity is the schedule.

The sign is a plan built from service times with no wait in it, and slips that are always attributed to "the lab" afterwards and never forecast from its booking calendar beforehand. Utilisation above 0.90 is not efficiency; Figure 2 prices what it costs.

The shape of the delay curve beats its height.

The sign is a single rupees‑per‑week figure quoted in March and again in October. Belwadi's curve is worth more per week than Bakula's at week six and nothing at week two. A team with one number buys acceleration in flat regions and none at the step.

Correlated concepts make parallel sets more valuable, not less.

Three concepts at 0.60 each fail together with probability 0.40³ = 0.064 if independent, and 0.298 if a common cause kills all three one time in four. The obvious reading is that correlation destroys the case for sets. It inverts it: a sequential search meets the same shared failure once per attempt in calendar, and calendar is what a set buys. The sign is a team justifying sets by the chance one works rather than by the week saved.

Updatability relocates irreversibility; it does not remove it.

"We will fix it in firmware" is accurate about a threshold and false about a thermal budget. The sign is a mechanical or electrical limit being discussed as though it were a software default. What over‑the‑air updates buy is a later freeze on behaviour, paid for with a permanent freeze on capacity.

Your supplier prices your indecision.

A rework quote obtained in week four is not the quote available in week twenty, because by then the tool shop has your programme's history. The sign is a quote with no stated date of validity. Experts obtain written, dated rework prices early, while they are still a hypothetical.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The real differences are in the cost‑of‑delay curve and in who owns the top rung. Consumer hardware has a steep, capped, seasonal curve and owns its own ladder. Enterprise and regulated hardware has a flat curve with tender‑ or certification‑shaped steps, and the gating commitment is a document rather than a tool. Where platforms build hardware at all, the binding constraint is the installed base.

The difference that is not real is the one most often asserted: that AI products are somehow exempt. They are the most constrained of all, because model size, memory bandwidth and thermal envelope are frozen by silicon procurement years before the model is trained. By stage, an early company has one programme and no platform rung, which makes it faster and leaves all tooling risk on one product; a large company freezes shared components earliest and spends its advantage on buffer stock and second sources rather than on speed.

8. Three programmes, with numbers

The first is Bakula's bridge tool. Renavikar released the steel on Monday 9 March as drawn and separately bought an option against being wrong about the thermal design: an aluminium bridge tool at ₹14.00 lakh, four weeks of lead against steel's twelve, good for the first 9,000 units at a piece price of ₹96 against steel's ₹41. The premium there is ₹55 × 9,000 = ₹4.95 lakh, so the option cost ₹18.95 lakh. The thermal change was confirmed, and modifying the steel moved usable tooling from Monday 1 June to Monday 29 June; unbridged, channel fill moves from Monday 21 September to Monday 19 October. Four weeks of festive exposure at ₹90 lakh is ₹360 lakh — nineteen times the option's cost. The lesson is not that bridge tooling is good. It is that the freeze date Bakula treated as given had a price, and nobody had asked for it.

The second is Belwadi's reagent seal, and it runs the other way. Each sealing concept costs ₹3.50 lakh and two weeks on the bench, and succeeds independently with probability 0.60. Belwadi has five weeks of band before the tender step at ₹540 lakh.

Expected cost, ₹ lakhPoint‑based, one at a timeSet‑based, three in parallel
Concept spend5.4610.72

Table 4. Point‑based spend = ₹3.50 lakh × (1 + 0.40 + 0.16) = ₹5.46 lakh; it breaches the band when the first two attempts both fail, p = 0.40² = 0.1600, giving 0.1600 × ₹540 lakh = ₹86.40 lakh. Set‑based spend = ₹10.50 lakh + 0.064 × ₹3.50 lakh = ₹10.72 lakh; it breaches only if all three fail and a fourth attempt also fails, p = 0.40³ × 0.40 = 0.0256, giving ₹13.82 lakh. Set‑based components are rounded; the exact total is ₹24.548 lakh.

Carrying the set is worth ₹67.31 lakh here, and the obvious objection — that the three concepts share a failure mode — strengthens the case once the correction is applied to both columns, not just one. Let a common cause kill every concept with probability 0.25. A single attempt then fails with probability 0.25 + 0.75 × 0.40 = 0.55 and two in a row with 0.25 + 0.75 × 0.16 = 0.37, so the point‑based path costs ₹6.72 lakh of concepts plus 0.37 × ₹540 lakh = ₹199.80 lakh of delay, ₹206.52 lakh in all. The set's first round now fails with 0.25 + 0.75 × 0.064 = 0.298, leaving a breach probability of 0.1192 after a fourth attempt and ₹75.91 lakh in all. The advantage grows to ₹130.61 lakh. What would kill it is a shallow step: ₹5.26 lakh of extra spend buys a 0.1344 fall in breach probability, so the set stops paying below a step of ₹39.14 lakh.

The third programme failed. The Bakula Perch, the Nook's predecessor, was run as "hardware agile": a mechanical change permitted at every sprint boundary and no ladder. Eleven change orders arrived between steel release and production validation, the tool was recut twice, and because the chip was ordered before the thermal budget closed, 4,100 of 6,000 units bought at ₹1,040 each were orphaned — ₹42.64 lakh written off. The ship slipped nine weeks and missed the season entirely. The recovery is the instructive part. Bakula did not impose a freeze; it moved the irreversible spend, paying a ₹118 premium per unit on a distributor‑stocked chip for the first 14,000 units, ₹16.52 lakh, to buy a six‑week lead time while the design settled. Then it published a change‑order price list.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Table 5. Each warning is visible from outside engineering, in a requisition, a change log, a booking calendar or a finance model.

All four share this: the evidence exists before the slip, held by somebody who is not in the programme review. The diagnostics are corridor questions; the costs appear a quarter later, attached to a different name.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The front‑loading school is strongest where requalification dominates. Its evidence is the convex cost curve and the fact that Belwadi's late change costs 8.3 times its early one; it would be wrong if that ratio were flat, which modular architecture, bridge tooling and updatable function are steadily making it in consumer electronics. The test it would accept: measure the realised ratio over your last three programmes, and if it is under four, your gates are overpriced.

The flow school is strongest where waiting dominates, and Figure 2 is powerful evidence: little engineering improvement available at Belwadi matches twenty days a booking. It is wrong wherever retest is a large fixed cost per batch, as section 3 shows. The two schools are not in a general argument; each is correct in a regime, and the regime is set by the ratio of fixed retest cost to variable change cost.

The set‑based school rests on Toyota's results and on arithmetic like Table 4's. It would be wrong wherever variants fail together, which section 6 prices, and wherever an organisation cannot actually kill a set, at which point carrying options becomes carrying scope.

The open question is empirical. Boehm's curve comes from a 1981 software dataset, and no comparable public dataset exists for hardware, least of all for Indian contract manufacturing. The 10‑to‑1‑per‑stage rule repeated in programme reviews is folklore borrowed from another discipline. Belwadi's 8.3 and Bakula's 4.8 are both real and differ by about 1.7 times.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this runs the stages correctly. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They ask the price of a freeze date before accepting it, in writing and dated, while it is still hypothetical and cheap. They can draw their own cost‑of‑delay curve and its steps from memory. And when a schedule slips they look first at a shared resource's booking calendar and only then at the engineers.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Raiturkar did not freeze on 9 March at 7.5 per cent. He computed what evidence would move the number. On a uniform baseline the posterior mean on 3 failures in 40 is 4 of 42, 9.5 per cent, and 25 further failure‑free units bring it to 4 of 67, 5.97 per cent — just under the limit, but with only about 56 per cent probability that the true rate is under it, bought for ₹4.60 lakh of units at ₹18,400 each in a flat stretch of his curve. A mean below a limit is not clearance. He also made Ramdasi's prior explicit on that same baseline: the previous programme's 2 failures in 50 gives 6 of 92, 6.5 per cent, which still fails. The pooled figure quoted instead, 5 failures in 90 across both programmes, is 5.6 per cent and is not computed on the same baseline. He wrote all three into the file. Renavikar released the tool on time and bought the bridge.

Three questions. First: in your own programme, what is the date of the earliest irreversible commitment, and who signed it? Second: draw your cost‑of‑delay curve for the next twelve months and mark its steps — how many weeks of the year are actually flat? Third: section 5 argues that a platform group should charge for a later freeze rather than negotiate one — what would your company have to be able to measure before that charge could be made credible?

13. Going deeper

  • The software development lifecycle — the baseline this topic deforms; it unlocks why freezes are the exception.
  • EVT, DVT, PVT and mass production — the stage names assumed here; it unlocks reading a manufacturer's plan.
  • Integrating hardware and software release trains — the seam in section 5; it unlocks two freezes on one bill of materials.
  • Agile in practice — what survives inside stages; it unlocks separating agile's habits from its cadence.
  • Kanban and flow — the formal grounding for Figure 2; it unlocks seeing queues as the schedule.
  • The execution rhythm — how ladders and sprint calendars coexist; it unlocks catching slips early.
  • Engineering estimates and T‑shirt sizing — why lead time resists estimation; it unlocks honest commitments.
  • Backlog management and refinement — where change orders come from; it unlocks the change window in section 3.
  • Definition of done — what "frozen" means per layer; it unlocks each stage's exit criteria.
exp20v2-agile.design.eng:
Design–engineering handoff: keeping intent intact

1. Sixty-six small differences

At 4:40 pm on Friday 11 September 2026, Charulatha Jambunathan, group product manager at Rathna Commerce, a Chennai-based marketplace for handloom textiles and home goods, sat through the review of sprint 14. A sprint is a fixed work period, here two weeks (31 August to 11 September), after which a team shows what it built. This one had rebuilt the checkout: twelve screens designed over three weeks by Charan Jeganathan and built on Android by the team of Chinmay Jeyaraj.

Everything worked and nothing looked right. The pay button stood 44 pixels tall where the design said 52. The coupon field showed its error in grey, not the brand red. Spacing on the address cards drifted by a few pixels from one card to the next. That afternoon Charan had compared the build against his files property by property: of 300 design properties (a colour, a size, a spacing, a type setting), 66 differed, or 22 per cent.

The festive sale opens on Monday 19 October, and checkout will carry every order. Two full sprints (14 to 25 September, 28 September to 9 October) and a freeze week remained, the final days before launch when no new code may be added. Any customer who met a grey error on a coupon field would meet it in the busiest fortnight of Rathna's year, and support would hear about it first. Charan proposed more detailed annotated drawings. Chinmay answered that his engineers were not ignoring the drawings; they were guessing between them. Neither man was wrong about the symptoms, and each blamed a different link in the chain. Charulatha had to decide whether to fix 66 items one by one, or change how design reached engineering.

2. The idea

Put plainly, the problem is that a design file and a running app are different objects, and anything not written down in the first must be reinvented in the second.

A handoff is the transfer of a design to the people who will build it. It was invented because the two groups hold different halves of the product. Designers hold the intent, the reason a thing looks and behaves as it does; engineers hold the constraints of the platform. Early software shops moved the design on paper as a spec, a written description of what to build. Through the 2000s that became the redline, an annotated image marking distances, sizes and colours, named for the red lines draftsmen drew on drawings.

Redlines record the result but not the rule behind it. From about 2013, teams building shared design systems (a library of agreed components and rules) began storing decisions as design tokens: named values such as space-16 or colour-danger that both designers and code refer to. Jina Anne, then at Salesforce, is generally credited with coining the term around 2014, and design-system teams elsewhere adopted it within a few years. The sentence Charulatha could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: a handoff succeeds when engineering can rebuild the design from the system without asking, and can ask without penalty about what the system cannot say.

3. How it actually works

Four steps carry a design across, and the third is the one practitioners leave implicit. First, the designer states the intent in a sentence per screen: "the pay button is the only filled element, so the eye lands there." Second, the designer publishes the spec: layout, components, and every state (default, pressed, loading, error, empty), expressed in tokens rather than raw numbers. Third, engineer and designer hold a short walkthrough before building, where the engineer names what the platform will not do. Fourth, design QA: the designer checks the running build against the design inside the same sprint and files any mismatch as a ticket.

Take the pay button. At step one Charan wrote that it is the only filled element on the screen, so the eye lands there. At step two he bound its height to a size token rather than typing 52, and drew its pressed, loading and disabled states. At the walkthrough, Chinmay pointed out that the small-phone layout left room for a 48-pixel button at most, and the two agreed a rule, not a number: the button stays at its 52-pixel size token where it fits and shrinks to the 48-pixel touch-target token on small phones, never below that. At step four Charan found the build matched. None of those four steps is expensive; each is skipped under deadline pressure because its absence is invisible until later.

The figure shows why the loop matters. Without step four, a mismatch survives until a customer meets it. Without step three, the engineer meets a state the spec never drew, such as a coupon rejected by the server, and invents one. Note also that "inside the sprint" is the only agile idea this topic needs: the check happens before the work is called done, not in a later release.

4. A worked example

Charan's audit divided the 300 properties by how each was set. In 150 (50 per cent) the build used a token; in the other 150 an engineer typed a raw value. He then counted mismatches in each group. Token-bound properties mismatched at 4 per cent, since the value comes from one place; hand-typed ones at 40 per cent. Each mismatch cost about 25 minutes across the loop: spot it, write the ticket, fix it, re-check it.

Pass one: 150 × 4% = 6 mismatches, plus 150 × 40% = 60, gives 66, or 22.0 per cent of 300. At 25 minutes each, 66 × 25 = 1,650 minutes, or 27.5 hours of loop time in one sprint.

Pass two changes one input: suppose the token share rises from 50 to 75 per cent, with both mismatch rates unchanged. Now 225 properties are token-bound and 75 are hand-typed: 225 × 4% = 9, plus 75 × 40% = 30, gives 39, or 13.0 per cent. The loop shrinks to 39 × 25 = 975 minutes, or 16.25 hours. The tokens are not free. Suppose migrating those 75 properties costs engineering 10 minutes each, 750 minutes or 12.5 hours. The saving is 27.5 − 16.25 = 11.25 hours per sprint, if a comparable volume of work passes through each sprint, so the migration repays itself in the second sprint (12.5 hours against 11.25 after one sprint, 22.5 after two). Now check the movement: 75 properties changed from a 40 per cent to a 4 per cent regime, which avoids 75 × 36% = 27 mismatches, and 66 − 27 = 39.

GroupPass one (50% tokens)Pass two (75% tokens)

Total / average30022.0%6630013.0%39
