Total-row rates are pooled: total mismatches over total properties, not a mean of the two group rates.

The figure makes the point the table hides: nearly all the saving comes from the hand-typed segment, which shrinks from 60 to 30 while the token-bound segment grows by three. The arithmetic assumes tokens do not worsen the 4 per cent rate and that the properties moved are as error-prone as those left; both are assumptions, not findings.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Spec is not intent. A spec says what; intent says why. When the 52-pixel button met a narrow phone, only the stated reason (the thumb must reach it) told Chinmay's team what to do.

A redline is a picture of one answer. It records distances for one screen size. A token or a component records the rule, so it survives a different screen, which is why mature teams treat redlines as the exception, used for a genuinely new pattern and then folded back into the system.

Raw values and semantic tokens differ. red-600 names a colour; colour-danger names a job. Code that uses the first breaks when the brand changes; code that uses the second follows it. Teams that tokenise raw values only have renamed their hard-coding.

The unrendered states are most of the work. Designers draw the default view; engineers must build loading, error, empty and offline. If the spec does not draw them, they are decided by whoever types first.

Tools do not hand off for you. Inspection modes that print measurements from a design file remove transcription error. They do not remove the missing state or the missing reason. They also invite a belief that the file is the spec, so nobody writes the reason down because the measurements are already there.

The review loop must sit inside the sprint. A mismatch found after release costs a ticket in a later sprint, competing with new features; found inside, it is part of finishing. Put design QA in the team's definition of done, the checklist a task must pass before it counts as complete.

Handoff cannot tell you whether the design is right. A perfect transfer of a poor checkout produces a faithful poor checkout. Ask first whether tokens exist for this screen, who owns them, and what happens when engineering needs a value that has none. A thoughtful newcomer also asks how stale the file is: a design edited after the walkthrough is a different design.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

In consumer products, polish drives trust, so token fidelity and motion matter most, and Rathna's case is typical. In B2B products, density dominates: tables, filters and permissions generate hundreds of states, and the state inventory matters more than pixels. In marketplaces, there are two audiences, buyer and seller, often built by different teams; the shared token layer is what keeps a seller's dashboard recognisably the same product as the buyer's checkout.

Size changes the method. A ten-person start-up can hand off by sitting together, and a formal token layer may cost more than it saves. Once several squads build against the same screens, conversation stops scaling, and the system has to carry the intent, with a named owner and a published change process. The mistake at that size is the opposite one: a token committee so slow that engineers hand-type values to meet the sprint, which restores the 40 per cent regime.

7. Common mistakes

Redline inflation. The symptom: specs grow to forty annotated pages and are still wrong. The misunderstanding: more description equals more fidelity. Cheapest diagnostic: count the number of raw values in the spec; each is a place a rule should be.

Handoff as an event. The symptom: designers vanish after Friday and return at launch to a surprise. The misunderstanding: design finishes when the file is shared. Diagnostic: ask when the designer last saw the running build; more than a week is too long.

Tokens without ownership. The symptom: three near-identical greys appear in the library. The misunderstanding: a token is a file, not a decision. Diagnostic: ask who can say no to a new token; if no one, no one owns the set.

8. What good looks like

The same Friday handled well: Charan's checkout files already reference tokens, each screen carries a one-line intent, and the five states are drawn. Chinmay's team has a 20-minute walkthrough on Monday and raises the offline case before building. Design QA happens on Wednesday of week two, in the sprint, on a real phone. The review finds 39 differences at the 75 per cent token share, not 66, and each is closed before Friday. The designer and engineer disagree twice, once about a transition that costs battery on low-end phones, and settle it in a ten-minute call using the stated intent, not rank. The review loop is a working conversation, and nobody feels audited by it.

9. Closing

Charulatha chose the second path. She rejected the one-by-one patch because it would repeat on every screen added before 19 October; she rejected more redlines because the audit showed 60 of the 66 mismatches sat in hand-typed values. Sprint 15 would migrate the twelve checkout screens to tokens and put design QA in the definition of done, with a target of at least 75 per cent token-bound properties. She also said what the audit could not tell her: that the new checkout was better for customers, which only an experiment would show.

To learn next: the design-system topic, since tokens and components are what gets handed off, and agile in practice, for how the sprint holds the loop. Two questions to sit with. If your team's next handoff were audited like Charan's, what share of properties would be hand-typed, and who would you ask to find out? And which state of your most important screen has never been drawn by anyone?
exp40v2-agile.design.eng:
Design-engineering handoff

How a design reaches engineering without losing its intent, what the losing actually consists of, and why the best-argued answers to the problem contradict each other.

1. Two decisions, eight days apart

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Divya Kesavan had an audit spreadsheet open and a calendar invitation she did not want. Kesavan is VP Product at Sthirata Systems, a Bengaluru firm of 310 whose wealth-operations software is white-labelled to fourteen banks and distributors. Ninety-six engineers and eleven designers ship on a fortnightly train, the next leaving on Tuesday 20 October. A fortnight earlier a tenant's compliance head had found a nominee-consent screen in production with the mandated disclosure below the action button rather than above it. Sthirata's CTO wanted "design sign-off" added to the definition of done as a release blocker. Deven Kumaravel, who runs the design system, wanted those hours spent elsewhere; Durga Kanniappan, the platform engineering manager, calculated that a blocking gate would cost the train a day a sprint. Kesavan's only evidence was the spreadsheet: an audit of the epic, decision point by decision point.

On Wednesday 14 October, in Pune, Dhaval Kottapalli had a bench unit on his desk and the same question in a harder form. Kottapalli is head of product at Sahastra Devices, which has 18,400 of its C3 billing-and-weighing counter terminals in kirana and sweet-shop use across seven states. The C3's 7-inch screen is 800 x 480, a diagonal of 933 pixels, so it resolves at 133 pixels per inch. Forty-six engineers and four designers serve both the terminal and the shopkeeper's Android companion app from one component library. On Friday 18 September, Dileep Kakarla, the firmware lead, noticed that the gap between the weight label and its value was rendering two pixels - 0.38 mm - tighter than drawn, because a shared spacing token had changed for the phone. Firmware had been tagged on 29 July. The fix would wait 105 days. Thursday 15 October was the design freeze for the build after that, and Kottapalli had to decide whether to split his token set in two.

Both face the same question - how a design reaches engineering without losing its intent - and neither can answer it without first saying what gets lost.

2. The idea, and the five camps that disagree about it

Handoff is the transfer of design intent - the decisions a design embodies - to the people who will encode them in software, together with whatever artefacts, conversations and tests make it checkable. The unit worth counting is not the screen but the decision point: a question whose answer changes what gets built: a breakpoint, a loading state, a validation string, a focus order, an overflowing locale. Specification coverage is the share of a surface's decision points answered before implementation begins.

Two more terms earn their keep. A redline is an annotated overlay stating measurements the component library does not already fix. A design token is a named, platform-neutral value - colour.surface.raised, space.md - resolved at build time into each platform's units, so handing off a value becomes handing off a name. And the distinction that organises everything below: a fidelity defect is built-not-as-drawn; an intent defect is wrong in the drawing itself, or missing from it. Review loops catch the first, and are blind to the second exactly where the code faithfully matches a wrong drawing - which is the form that reaches users.

The practice is inherited, not invented. Mechanical drafting had solved it by 1966, when ASME Y14.5 formalised geometric dimensioning and tolerancing: a drawing states a dimension and the permitted deviation. Software redlines almost never state a tolerance, the part of the inheritance that did not survive the copy. Massimo Vignelli's 1970 standards manual for the New York City Transit Authority specified a system rather than an artefact, and is the design system's ancestor. Parnas, in 1972, made the interface the thing one specifies; Brooks, in 1975, called the goal conceptual integrity. Boehm's 1981 cost-of-change curve supplied the economics everyone quotes, and Bossavit's later archaeology showed how thin its samples were. The Agile Manifesto of 2001 was read as abolishing the spec, and the Poppendiecks' lean reading of 2003 put handoffs among the wastes outright. The component lineage ran in parallel: pattern libraries, atomic design, Salesforce's Lightning system, where "design token" was coined around 2014, and the W3C Design Tokens Community Group's attempt, from 2019, to make the token a portable interface rather than a house style.

3. Mechanics: counting the decision points, then pricing them

Kumaravel's audit did what almost nobody does: enumerate the questions before scoring the answers. The epic covered seven screens, and three breakpoints across those seven gave 21 layout questions. Five screens carried the full six-state set - default, loading, empty, partial, error, success - and two confirmation screens two states each, so 34. The four input screens held 23 validation rules; focus order and screen-reader announcement were two questions a screen, so 14; three shipped locales across seven screens gave 21 overflow questions; six new components raised one each about brand versus semantic colour; and five asynchronous calls one each about what the user sees while they run. The total is 124.

Sixty-one of the 124 were answered in the design file: 49.2 per cent. Another 18 were settled in the spec or in critique before anyone wrote code, taking coverage to 79 of 124, or 63.7 per cent, and leaving 45 for implementation. Kumaravel then priced each point by the stage at which it was settled, counting designer and engineer hours from first question to landed code.

Two second-order effects fall out of that table. The first is the fourth row: seventeen points were guessed and never argued about, at zero cost - cheaper than the 0.3 hours a file answer costs - so any policy driving coverage to 100 per cent pays to answer them. The second is an incentive. Of the 45, 28 eventually cost something and 17 did not. Kumaravel split the 45 by whether a designer could have answered them alone: 29 could, while 16 needed an engineering fact first, such as how a token resolves under a tenant's brand colour. Of the 29, 12 were contested at a mean 4.23 hours and 17 absorbed free, so guessing on a design-answerable point carries a 12-in-29 chance - 41.4 per cent - of a 4.23-hour argument: an expected 1.75 hours, against the 1.90 an asked point costs. Both are firm hours, designer plus engineer, from first question to landed code, so neither is a latency and neither falls on the engineer alone; and the nine-minute gap lies between unlike populations, 1.90 being the mean of all 14 asked points, engineering-fact ones included, against 4.23 over only the 12 design-answerable contested ones. The weaker claim survives and is still decisive: at Sthirata's price of an answer, asking buys no measurable saving over guessing, so the lever is the price.

That also bounds the prize. Move all 28 contested points into the file at 0.3 hours each and their 116.9 hours become 8.4, a saving of 108.5 hours or 74.3 per cent of 146.0 - but only if a designer could have answered all 28, and 16 could not. Restrict the move to the 12 design-answerable ones and the saving is 47.2 hours, 32.3 per cent: a range whose upper end is a bound, not a forecast.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three testable claims, each applied to both firms. First: a handoff artefact earns its cost only when the answer it records stays valid through implementation. Both clear it - Sthirata's fortnight, Sahastra's 64 days of frozen firmware between the 29 July tag and the 1 October window - so the claim does not explain why Kottapalli's specs are long and Kanniappan's short. What does is the margin: a wrong answer costs Sthirata a fortnight and Sahastra 64 days. Second: continuous collaboration substitutes for specification only where asking costs less than guessing. At Sthirata it does not - 1.90 firm hours an asked point against an expected 1.75 - so embedding a designer does not fix this; cutting the cost of an answer does. Third: token-level handoff dominates screen-level handoff only where the library already answers the surface. True of Sthirata's six new components against a mature library; false at Sahastra, where the dimensional tokens do not transfer between form factors.

The idea misleads twice over. When the design is a hypothesis rather than a decision - a discovery spike meant to be thrown away - grading it for fidelity turns an experiment into a deliverable. And when the surface is generated rather than drawn there is no geometry to redline, so the habit produces a document precise about everything that does not matter.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulators and firmware

Kottapalli's problem shows the hard case at its plainest, because the regulator, not the org chart, draws the handoff boundary. Sahastra's counsel reads the Legal Metrology Act regime as putting the C3's display of weight inside the model-approved pattern, so a change to that surface needs re-submission while a change 40 pixels away does not. The result is one screen with two handoff regimes on it, and a design file that looks uniform.

Multi-product and platform organisations hit the seam differently. Sthirata's fourteen tenants mean every colour decision is really about who owns the colour, and a token named for a hue rather than a role transfers that ownership to whoever wrote the name. Two-sided businesses meet a sharper version: Sandhan Exchange ships a shipper app and a trucker app from one library, and the trucker side's one-handed, gloved, sunlit use invalidates the dimensional tokens the shipper side depends on - Kottapalli's split with a market rather than a regulator on each side. AI-native surfaces move the problem again: the geometry is generated, so the handoff specifies outcome classes and latency bands. Mature companies mostly relocate these seams rather than resolve them, into a named owner for the contested token set, then describe the arrangement as a single system.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners do not

Coverage is the wrong number; contestedness is the right one. The seventeen points Sthirata guessed free were the cheapest decisions in the epic. The tell-tale is a team that lifts coverage toward 100 per cent and watches cycle time rise with no fall in escapes. The obvious reading fails because the marginal answer is bought where contestedness is lowest.

A design review sees less than its log suggests. All 11 points Sthirata settled at design review sat inside the 45 the drawing never answered, so review was not checking fidelity: it was deciding, at 4.8 hours a point, in the last slot before QA. The tell-tale is a review log whose entries are decisions rather than discrepancies. What review cannot see is code that faithfully matches a wrong drawing - the disclosure under the button, placed there by the file, passed review perfectly.

A redline without a tolerance is not a specification. Drafting has stated permitted deviation since 1966; design files state 16 px and stop. The tell-tale is an engineer who asks "how close is close enough" once, gets no answer, and never asks again. The tolerance then exists as whatever that engineer privately decided.

A token hands off a name, and the name's meaning is a resolution rule. The tell-tale is a colour in the token name. With fourteen brandable tenants, blue-600 is not a badly labelled value but a missing rule about who may override it, which surfaces as a tenant onboarding no screen review predicted.

No single multiplier can scale a design across viewing distances. A 16 dp label at 160 ppi is 2.54 mm and subtends 0.485 degrees at a 300 mm reading distance. Hold that angle at the C3's 700 mm counter distance and it needs 5.93 mm, which at 133 ppi is 31 pixels: a factor of 1.94. But a 48 dp touch target is 7.62 mm of finger, and 7.62 mm at 133 ppi is 40 pixels - a factor of 0.83. Type scales with visual angle, touch with physical size. The tell-tale is a density setting that makes buttons harder to hit.

Asking costs more than guessing. At Sthirata, 1.90 firm hours against an expected 1.75. The tell-tale is a strong engineer who has quietly stopped asking, which reads as seniority. The response is not to moralise but to cut the price of an answer until a question costs minutes.

The artefact's real reader is next year's maintainer. Handoff documents get judged by whether this sprint's engineer needed them, which is the wrong test: that engineer sat next to the designer. The tell-tale is that nobody can say why a spacing value is 12 rather than 16. The rationale, not the value, is what the token cannot carry.

Coverage has a ceiling, and it is not where teams put it. Sixteen of Sthirata's 45 open points needed an engineering fact before a designer could answer them, which caps designer-reachable coverage at 108 of 124, or 87.1 per cent. Sthirata sits at 79, twenty-nine points below its own ceiling, so the hard 16 cannot be what holds coverage in the sixties - more design time genuinely would move it. The tell-tale is a team citing the 16 to excuse a gap the 16 cannot account for.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The differences are smaller than the literature implies, with three exceptions. Consumer and B2B differ mainly in who complains: consumer teams find intent defects in funnel metrics, enterprise teams in a tenant's acceptance test weeks later, which is why Sthirata's three acceptance points cost 12.5 hours each against 4.8 at review. Platform and marketplace work really differs, because the handoff goes to an unknown implementer and the artefact must be a versioned contract. Hardware differs in kind: Kottapalli's 105-day wait is not a long version of Kanniappan's day but a different decision, which is why the no-handoff school has almost no hardware adherents. AI products differ in what is specified. Sthirata's document-extraction feature has five outcome classes and three latency bands, so 15 states against the six a deterministic form needs - two and a half times - and its one drawn spinner answered none. By stage: a twelve-person startup does not need redlines, the designer being the engineer's neighbour; the practice turns load-bearing when a second team consumes components it did not draw, which at both firms happened around 40 engineers.

8. Three worked cases

Sthirata's nominee-consent epic. 124 points, 49.2 per cent file coverage, 146.0 hours of settlement, 61.8 per cent of them in the last two stages, a ₹2,70,100 bill. If the quarter's eleven epics held the same mix and size the settlement bill would come to ₹29,71,100 - about ₹29.7 lakh - though this epic was unusually regulated and almost certainly above the mean.

Sahastra's token arithmetic. The shared set holds 212 tokens: 148 semantic and 64 dimensional. Of the 64, Kakarla's analysis put 41 on the visual-angle rule (x1.94), 9 on the physical-size rule (x0.83), and 14 on neither, because they encode a relationship - an icon-to-label gap, an optical baseline shift - that no single factor preserves. One multiplier would therefore have been wrong on at least 23 of the 64 - the 9 and the 14 if the factor chosen were x1.94, the 41 and the 14 if it were x0.83 - and the two-pixel weight gap was one of the 14.

The attempt that failed. In FY26 Sthirata tried design-in-code, its designers authoring components directly. Four of the eleven learned the toolchain. Over five months they authored 23 components, of which 9 - 39.1 per cent - were reverted by engineering for accessibility or performance regressions, and the median designer pull request waited 9 days for review against 1.4 days for an engineer's. It failed not because designers cannot write code but because the review capacity the model assumes did not exist. The recovery kept a narrow version: designers own the 212-token file by pull request, engineers the component code. Token requests now merge in a median 0.6 days, and onboarding a new tenant theme fell from 11 days to 3.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

10. Where the experts genuinely disagree

Is low coverage a cause or a symptom? The specification camp points at Sthirata's 108.5-hour upper bound and argues the artefact is the cheapest place to put an answer. The no-handoff camp points at the same table's fourth row - 17 answers nobody needed - and at the 16 no designer could have answered, and argues the seam, not the document, is the defect. The first position is wrong if raising coverage from 49.2 to 80 per cent leaves late-stage hours flat; the second is wrong if a full-time embedded designer still leaves more than 16 contested points, the 16 no designer can answer being the floor. Neither firm has run the test.

File or code as source of truth? Code's advocates have Sthirata's failure only partly on their side: 9 reverts of 23 is evidence about review capacity, not files. The file camp has the 0.6-day token median, showing a narrow code interface working. What would settle it is whether the 14 tokens that follow no rule can be expressed declaratively at all; if not, something has to be code.

Is pixel fidelity a quality attribute? Sthirata spent 52.8 hours on 11 points at design review and has no measurement that the resulting changes altered what a user did. The steelman is not aesthetics but compounding: in a 212-token system an uncorrected drift becomes a precedent, and the twentieth exception is what makes a theme unmaintainable. The falsifier is cheap and nobody runs it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this arrives with a template. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a question: which decisions here cannot be made by the person drawing, and when does the answer stop being changeable? They enumerate before they document, price the stages before they add a gate, read a coverage plateau as information about the question mix, and can name the tolerance on their own redlines. Most distinctively, they are relaxed about guesses nobody contested and intolerant of the ones that were, the opposite of how handoff quality is usually audited.

12. What each of them decided

Kesavan declined the blocking gate. Her table put 11.3 per cent of the points against 61.8 per cent of the hours, and 16 of the 28 contested points were not design questions, so she bought a 45-minute walkthrough of the open points at each epic's start, funded Krishnaswamy's suite at a tolerance that still sees 48 pixels, and kept the end-of-sprint review timeboxed and non-blocking. Kottapalli went the other way, forking the 64 dimensional tokens into terminal and phone sets, keeping the 148 semantic tokens shared, and giving the metrology-adjacent surfaces their own earlier freeze.

Three questions for discussion:

  1. Kesavan's data prices the avoidable waste between 32.3 and 74.3 per cent of 146.0 hours. Which end should she plan against, and what single measurement next quarter would narrow the range most?
  2. Sahastra will now maintain 64 forked dimensional tokens. At what number of form factors does the fork become the cheaper system, and what would make it the wrong call?
  3. Neither firm can say whether a visual discrepancy changes anything a user does. Design the cheapest experiment that would tell them, and say what you would stop doing if the answer were "nothing".

13. Going deeper

  • Agile in practice - the handoff happens inside the sprint, so cadence sets how long an unanswered point stays unanswered.
  • Design systems and components - tokens and components are what is handed off, and where the 212 tokens come from.
  • The software development lifecycle - places the handoff among the other stage transitions that behave alike.
  • Kanban and flow - a sign-off gate is a queue, and flow prices it.
  • The execution rhythm - walkthroughs and critiques need a reliable slot.
  • Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing - an estimate made before the decision points are enumerated estimates different work.
  • Backlog management and refinement - where the 16 engineering-fact questions can be answered.
  • Definition of done - where a sign-off either acquires a criterion or becomes a checkbox.
exp20v2-agile.tech.leadership.partnershi:
Operating with a tech lead and architect

Delivery & Technology / Engineering collaboration. The question this page answers: which technical decisions should a product manager be in the room for?

1. A promise with a date on it

On Monday 7 September 2026, Yashada Ghate, product manager for shipment tracking at Mandovi Freight Systems in Pune, sat down with two colleagues. Mandovi sells freight-visibility software to manufacturers and retailers; annual recurring revenue stood at ₹48 crore across 140 customers. A national retailer had offered ₹3.6 crore a year, 7.5 per cent of that base, if Mandovi could show live arrival estimates for its shipments from Tuesday 15 December, in time for the winter peak. The retailer would add 22,000 active shipments to the 38,000 the platform already tracked.

Ghate had a plan. The existing pipeline polled carrier systems every 15 minutes and wrote results to one primary database. An estimate calculation on top would take four engineers four weeks. She expected to say yes that afternoon. Yuktesh Gandhe, tech lead of the tracking team, thought the four weeks honest. Yajat Gadiyar, a principal architect responsible for the design of four teams' systems, said only that he wanted to look at one graph before anyone wrote to the customer.

More than one deal was at stake. If Ghate committed and the database could not carry the load, the failure would arrive in December, in front of the retailer and of every existing customer. If she let the architect stretch the project into a rebuild, she would lose the contract. The decision turned on which technical questions were hers, which were not, and which became hers only after learning what the others already knew.

Mandovi, its people and every figure in this case (the 5,000,000 ceiling, the four engineers, the 16-week rebuild, the revenue and shipment counts) are invented for teaching. Only Brooks, Conway, Nygard and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act are real references.

2. The idea

A tech lead is the engineer accountable for how one team builds: code structure, testing, sequencing, and whether the team's estimates are honest. An architect is accountable for how several systems fit together over years: where data lives, which components may call which, and what the whole can bear. Both answer for something the product manager does not: whether the system still works at three in the morning, and whether it can still be changed next year.

The role exists because of a problem Frederick Brooks described in The Mythical Man-Month (1975): a system with many builders loses conceptual integrity unless someone holds the whole design in mind. Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that systems come to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them, so design and organisation cannot be separated. In 2011 Michael Nygard proposed the architecture decision record, a short dated note stating a decision, its context and its consequences, so the reasoning survives staff turnover.

An architectural decision is one that is expensive to reverse and sets the cost of later work. Not every technical choice qualifies. Ghate could repeat one sentence in a meeting without sounding glib: "I decide which problem and how fast it must be solved, you decide what the system can bear, and anything that changes the price of the next ten features gets decided in the same room."

3. How it actually works

There are five steps, two usually left implicit. First, the product manager brings the decision to the technical leaders before a date is promised outside the company. Second, the group classifies it: is it about the problem, the build or the structure? Third, whoever holds a constraint states it as a number; "this is risky" cannot be planned around, whereas "the database tolerates five million reads a day" can. Fourth, options are priced in customer terms: weeks, rupees, and what the customer sees. Fifth, the person holding the decision right decides, and it is written down with a date to revisit.

The implicit steps are the second and the fifth. Nobody announces the classification; it happens silently and the loudest voice wins it. And an unrecorded decision is relitigated next quarter by someone who was absent. Table 1 fixes the usual allocation of rights. Its rows are different classes of decision, not rephrasings of one.

Class of decisionDecidesConsultedInformed
Which problem, for whom, by whenProduct managerTech lead, architectEngineering
Customer-visible targets (freshness, uptime)Product managerArchitect confirms feasibilitySales, support
System shape: data stores, boundaries, protocolsArchitectProduct manager, tech leadAffected teams
How the team builds: structure, tests, sequenceTech leadArchitect, where standards applyProduct manager
Hard to reverse: public API contracts, customer-data modelProduct manager and engineering director, on the architect's recommendationLegal, tech leadCustomers, as contracts require
Deliberate technical debtProduct manager and tech lead jointlyArchitectEngineering
Security, data-protection and capacity floorsArchitect with securityProduct managerLeadership
 Table 1. A starting allocation. The tracking team adapted it; no allocation is universal.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

The graph Gadiyar wanted was the database's read load. Each active shipment is polled every 15 minutes, which is 96 polls a day (24 hours times four). Today's load is 38,000 shipments times 96, or 3,648,000 reads a day. For this case the primary database is assumed to have been load-tested to a ceiling of 5,000,000 reads a day, so the platform already used 73.0 per cent of it. Each poll is taken to cost one read before its write; dashboard traffic and the estimate calculation's own reads are ignored for this illustration. Adding the retailer gives 60,000 shipments, and 60,000 times 96 is 5,760,000 reads, or 115.2 per cent of the ceiling. The four-week plan, delivered perfectly, would take the platform down.

Gadiyar's remedy was an event-streaming rebuild, in which carriers push updates instead of Mandovi pulling them. That would take 16 weeks, starting 14 September and ending 4 January 2027, twenty days after the customer date. His objection was correct. His remedy carried a price in rupees that only Ghate could weigh.

Now change one input. Ghate asked the retailer's logistics head how the estimates would be used. The answer was that its dispatch desk reviewed exceptions on a 30-minute rhythm. The pipeline has one global polling interval, so the change would move all 60,000 shipments to 30 minutes, existing customers included. Ghate was therefore trading their freshness for the retailer's contract. She checked with account managers: every existing contract promised a refresh at least hourly, so none was breached, and she arranged for those customers to be told. That meant 48 polls a day, not 96, and the same four-week build.

ScenarioActive shipmentsPolls a dayReads a dayShare of 5,000,000 ceiling
Today, 15-minute polling38,000963,648,00073.0%
With retailer, 15-minute polling60,000965,760,000115.2%
With retailer, 30-minute polling60,000482,880,00057.6%
 Table 2. Reads equal shipments times polls. Percentages are reads divided by 5,000,000.

The architectural constraint did not move; the product input did. With everyone at 30 minutes the ceiling supports about 104,000 shipments (5,000,000 divided by 48), against about 52,000 at 15 minutes. That is the pattern worth noticing: the architect supplied the constraint, the product manager supplied the freshness requirement, and neither could have found the answer alone.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

The tech lead and the architect are different jobs

The tech lead knows one team's code in depth and answers for its delivery. The architect knows the breadth and answers for coherence. In a company of twelve engineers one person holds both titles; in a larger one they disagree, and a tech lead's "no" about a build approach is not an architect's "no" about structure. Ask which hat the person is wearing.

The three-question test for "is this a product decision?"

Ask: does it change what the customer experiences? Does it change what the next ten features cost? Can it be undone within a sprint? If the first two answers are yes, or the third is no, the product manager belongs in the room. The refresh interval passed the first test directly, which is why it belonged to Ghate.

Voice is not veto

A technical objection that cites a number about data loss, security, legal exposure or a capacity ceiling should win; Gadiyar's graph did. An objection resting on taste, such as a preferred framework, deserves a hearing and a recorded reason, not a veto. The product manager's discipline is to ask which kind of objection is on the table. Floors of this kind include customer-data integrity, security, regulatory duties such as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and tested capacity limits. There the architect's objection simply wins, and the product manager's task is to re-plan, not to argue.

Each side holds information the other cannot see

The architect knows incident history, other teams' plans and vendor contract dates. The product manager knows what customers will pay for, how fast, and what competitors have promised. Neither can see the other's half, so each owes the other disclosure early.

Technical debt is a loan, not a sin

Shipping on the existing pipeline is a loan with an interest rate (extra effort on every later change) and a repayment date. Taken deliberately, with a named trigger, it is a tool. Taken silently, it is how a platform arrives at 115.2 per cent of its ceiling.

This is not agile mechanics

Stand-ups, sprints and backlogs do not create the partnership. A product manager can run flawless ceremonies for a year and never learn the database ceiling. Equally, negotiating estimates downward is not partnership; it trains engineers to pad.

What the relationship cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether the customer wants the product, and it does not remove the duty to decide on incomplete information. Before relying on any technical view, ask what evidence would change the person's mind, and what they would gain if you accepted it.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; small and large firms

Product typeDecisions that biteWhere the architect usually wins
ConsumerPeak load, latency, experiment toolingCapacity before a launch or festival peak
B2BIntegrations, tenant isolation, per-customer variationRefusing one-off forks that multiply maintenance
MarketplaceTwo-sided data model, payments ledger, trust and safetyLedger correctness and dispute trails
 Table 3. Where the partnership is tested in each product type. The right-hand column is the author's judgement, not a measured pattern.

Mandovi is a B2B business, and its pressure came from a single large customer asking for something bespoke. A consumer firm meets the same tension as a spike on a known date; a marketplace meets it where money moves and an error is a legal matter, not a bug. Stage matters too. In a firm of twelve engineers the tech lead is the architect and the conversation is a daily one. In a firm of four hundred, architects sit across teams, decisions are recorded, and the product manager must book time with people who are scarce.

7. Common mistakes

Inviting the architect after the commitment. The symptom is an estimate that balloons the day after sales promises a date. The misunderstanding is treating architecture as a review gate rather than an input. The cheapest diagnostic: list the decisions this quarter that engineering learned about after the date was set.

Refereeing a technical dispute by picking a side. The symptom is two designs trading places every fortnight. The misunderstanding is that a decisive product manager must have a technical opinion. The diagnostic: ask each person what evidence would change their mind; if neither can say, the dispute is about taste.

Abdicating to the architect. The symptom is a roadmap reordered by elegance, with customer commitments slipping unexplained. The misunderstanding is that deference is partnership. The diagnostic: can the product manager state, in weeks and rupees, the customer cost of each technical item on the roadmap?

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the 7 September meeting would have found the arithmetic already done. Ghate would have sent Gandhe and Gadiyar the retailer's request and the draft date before the meeting, so the read-load graph existed beforehand and Gadiyar arrived with a proposal, not a warning. She would have said which constraint she cared about (freshness) and which she did not (the build method). The decision would have been recorded: 30-minute refresh at launch, four weeks, and a stated trigger for rebuilding. Gandhe would have committed his team to a date he believed, and nobody would have been surprised in December.

9. Closing

Ghate chose the 30-minute refresh. She wrote to the retailer that day, and asked Gadiyar to set the rebuild trigger at 80 per cent of the ceiling, which is 4,000,000 reads, or about 83,000 shipments at 48 polls a day. She chose it because the number made the choice, not the seniority of anyone speaking. She also scheduled the stream rebuild, with a date, so that the deferral was a loan with a repayment day.

The next thing to learn is how to hold a system design conversation, because the partnership is built there: it teaches the questions to ask and the answers worth distrusting. Two questions to sit with. First, think of a technical decision your team made last quarter: which class in Table 1 was it, and who actually decided? Second, when did you last accept a technical objection that cost you something you wanted, and what would make you do it again?
exp40v2-agile.tech.leadership.partnershi:
Operating with a tech lead and architect

Delivery & Technology / Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration. Which technical decisions a product manager should be in the room for, and which she should lose.

1. Two meetings, two clocks

On Thursday 12 November 2026, Anuprita Hingmire, director of product at Nirveda Learning in Bengaluru, expected a forty-minute meeting. Nirveda's study app for Classes 9 to 12 has 6,20,000 monthly active students, of whom 92,000 pay ₹299 a month: ₹2.75 crore a month, ₹33.01 crore annualised, a paying share of 14.8 per cent. Ask Nirveda, the feature on the table, let a student photograph a problem and receive a worked explanation, and it needed a call to an external language-model vendor inside the request path. A telecom operator's winter catalogue set the clock. It closed on Friday 15 January 2027, and the same placement a year earlier had produced 19,400 paid subscribers in eight weeks, 21.1 per cent of today's paying base.

Aboli Hatolkar, tech lead of the learning platform, called the fast build honest work, ready on Tuesday 12 January. Adhiraj Hanmante, the principal architect, would not sign it, and gave a number whose importance Hingmire grasped only after drawing it out.

Archit Haldule, a product manager, was losing a different argument in Pune. Nabhas Instruments builds battery-powered cold-chain loggers and the cloud service that reads them: FY26 revenue of ₹62 crore, being ₹41 crore of hardware and ₹21 crore of software subscriptions, with 46,000 loggers across 310 distributors on five-year batteries. A pharmaceutical distributor's tender worth ₹9.4 crore over three years wanted per-carton excursion records carrying location, which meant a new field in the on-device record format. Chief architect Akhilesh Hambardikar wanted a version byte so old and new formats could coexist, adding three weeks to a nine-week plan. The demonstration fell on Monday 15 February 2027. Nine weeks from Monday 7 December 2026 ends on Friday 5 February; twelve weeks ends on Friday 26 February, eleven days late.

Both look like schedule arguments. Neither is. In each the product manager held a commercial fact her technical leaders could not see, and they a structural fact she could not — and in only one should the architect simply have won.

2. What the idea is, and whose problem it solved

A tech lead is accountable for how one team builds and delivers. An architect is accountable for how several systems fit together over a horizon longer than any roadmap: where state lives, which components may call which, what the whole bears at three in the morning, and what the next decade of changes costs. The two produce different kinds of "no".

The lineage is older than agile. Melvin Conway argued in 1968 that a system's structure mirrors the communication structure of the organisation designing it. Brooks, in The Mythical Man-Month (1975), named conceptual integrity the first quality of a system and argued it survives scale only where a small group of agreeing minds holds the whole. Parnas supplied the mechanism in 1972: a module should hide the decision most likely to change, which makes architecture the business of deciding what to protect from revision. Cunningham's 1992 debt metaphor priced the failure to do so, and Baldwin and Clark's Design Rules (2000) made it formal: a module is a real option whose value rises with the variance of what you might learn. Nygard's architecture decision record (2011) made the reasoning durable; error budgets and the language of one-way doors made it tradeable.

They do not agree. The quarrel is not whether architecture matters but who holds it.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Conceptual integrity (Brooks; enterprise architecture)Beyond a few teams, coherence must be a named person's job.That the architect decides how a team sequences its code.
Team-owned and emergent (XP; "you build it, you run it")Design authority belongs to whoever carries the pager.That anyone off the rota answers for operability.
Socio-technical (Conway; Team Topologies)If the architecture is wrong, move the team boundary.That a review board holds a boundary the org chart contradicts.
Options and economics (Parnas; Baldwin and Clark)Buy reversibility in proportion to the variance of what you may learn.That reversibility is always worth buying.
 Table 1. Four live traditions. Someone who cannot name the one a colleague argues from mistakes a school for a personality.

3. Mechanics: the three arithmetics an expert runs

Expert practice is not a meeting cadence. It is three computations run before anyone's date is public, and the last two are the ones product managers skip.

First, the reversibility test. "Hard to change" is too loose to act on; everything is, the week you ship it. The usable test is sharper: a decision is architectural when the cost of undoing it does not fall as you learn more. Undoing Nirveda's vendor-in-the-path costs six engineer-weeks plus ₹4.20 lakh to re-grade a 9,000-item regression bank at two graders and four minutes an item — 1,200 grader-hours at ₹350 an hour — but that cost is fixed, and falls once a second integration exists. Nabhas's record format differs in kind. A logger in a cold box cannot be recalled; whatever it writes, it writes for the rest of its battery life, and the cost of error never declines because the population is beyond reach. One is an expensive two-way door; the other a one-way door with a tail.

Second, composite availability, which multiplies. Product managers reason additively about features and keep doing so about reliability, a common structural blind spot in the role. A request traversing a chain succeeds only if every link does, so composite availability is the product of the links. Nirveda's path crosses three internal services, each measured at 99.95 per cent over the previous twelve months: 0.9995 cubed is 0.99850, or 99.850 per cent, which across a 30-day month of 43,200 minutes is 64.8 minutes of unavailability. Put the vendor, whose contractual commitment is 99.5 per cent, in series, and the composite becomes 0.99850 multiplied by 0.995, or 0.99351 — 99.351 per cent, 280.4 minutes a month. The feature adds about 216 minutes of darkness a month — 280.4 less 64.8 — to a path carrying every other function in the app.

Third, carrying cost and payback. Deliberate debt is a loan with a rate. Skipping the version byte obliges the Nabhas firmware team to special-case untagged records in every later release: 2.5 engineer-days per release across 9 releases a year is 22.5 engineer-days, at a loaded ₹14,000 per engineer-day, or ₹3.15 lakh a year. Paying now costs three weeks of four engineers — 60 engineer-days, ₹8.40 lakh. Payback is 8.40 divided by 3.15, or 2.67 years — inside the five-year battery life and inside the tender's three-year term, but outside the 24-month rule Nabhas applies to internal work. On that rule alone the architect loses, and an expert notices before he does.

The implicit fourth step is deciding which arithmetic is load-bearing. At Nirveda availability was tradeable against ₹2.75 crore a month; at Nabhas the carrying cost failed the 24-month rule and was not the argument that mattered.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

The partnership is not free: it costs senior attention and slows the first week of every initiative. State its preconditions as claims that can fail.

ClaimAt NirvedaAt Nabhas
Reversal cost must exceed the cost of the conversation, roughly one engineer-week.Holds: six engineer-weeks plus ₹4.20 lakh.Holds: 2,760 loggers cannot be recalled at any price.
The constraint must be statable as a number.Holds: about 216 minutes a month.Holds as a count, fails as a cost: 2,760 loggers and 38,640 consignments, but no rupee figure.
The product manager must carry a consequence.Holds: she owns the vendor line.Holds: he owns the tender and the fleet.
The architect must be exposed to the commercial result.Fails: Hanmante is not measured on subscribers.Holds: a lost tender is visible in the plant.
 Table 2. Four preconditions. Where a row fails, the structure degrades predictably.

Row two is the subtle one: a floor is a number you cannot trade against a price, so stating it as a count changes nothing about who decides. The frame itself misleads twice over. In a pre-fit team of five whose whole system is three weeks of work, everything is a two-way door. And where the architect has no exposure to the commercial result — row four, which fails at Nirveda — the table becomes deference, because a person with no downside from refusing refuses more often.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulation, hardware and AI

The clean cases are not where money is lost. What follows is what mature organisations do at the seams, rarely what their handbook says.

SettingWhat changesWhat mature firms actually do
Multi-product portfolioA shared service has no owner; its roadmap is the residue of four others.Give the platform its own product manager and budget.
Two-sided marketplaceMoney movement makes a data-model error a legal matter.Remove ledger and dispute trails from product discretion.
RegulatedDPDP Act 2023 and CERT-In six-hour reporting set floors no commercial case clears.Enumerate the floors, so the veto is a checklist.
Hardware plus softwareThe field population cannot be upgraded on command; door tails run to battery life.Version every wire and storage format from the first unit.
AI-nativeUnit cost is vendor-set and quality not deterministic, so regression becomes evaluation.Put model spend on the roadmap as a line the PM owns.
Organisational seamThe decision sits between teams with different directors and quarters.Escalate on the date, not the merits; the merits never converge.
 Table 3. Edge cases and observed practice. The last row is the one most often denied in public.

Nabhas sits in two rows at once. Its loggers ship into a pharmaceutical cold chain, so CDSCO expectations and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules may bear on what the device writes, and 46,000 field units cannot be addressed at will. A firmware push over 2G reaches 94 per cent of the fleet within 90 days, leaving 2,760 devices writing the old format for the rest of a five-year battery.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert

The first objection stated is rarely the one being defended

Hanmante led with availability, a number he could prove; what he feared was vendor coupling, which he could not price. The tell is proportion — about 216 minutes a month against ₹2.75 crore of monthly revenue, and he still would not sign. He is not territorial; he is offering the only part of his concern the meeting's currency admits.

"Hard to change" is the wrong test

Everything is hard to change the week after launch. The question is whether six more months of evidence make undoing it cheaper. The tell is an engineer who says "we can change it later" and cannot name what makes later cheaper.

Decision rights without decision sequence achieve nothing

A right exercised after a date is public produces a correct decision and a broken promise. The tell is an architect whose objections surface in review rather than planning. Teams then make review a formality, closing the last place it could land.

The architect's horizon outlives the product manager's tenure

Nabhas commits its roadmap two quarters out. Haldule has been on the product 1.9 years; Abhiroop Honavar, the firmware tech lead, has held his system 3.1 years; Hambardikar designs on a five-year view because the loggers live five years. The interval is set by the job, not the person.

Debt without a trigger in the PM's own units is not deliberate

A record that defers work behind a trigger in an engineering metric is a record nobody reads. The tell is a latency or queue depth, owned by nobody, on a dashboard the product manager never opens. When it fails, the obvious reading is poor monitoring; it is almost always a units failure.

Estimates and constraints fail in opposite directions

A tech lead is punished for lateness, so estimates tend to drift up. An architect is punished for incidents, so stated limits tend to drift down, their margin undisclosed. Ask the tech lead what would have to go wrong to miss; ask the architect what measurement produced the limit.

A veto exercised is a failure of the preceding six weeks

Where floors are enumerated in advance — data integrity, security, statutory duty, a tested capacity limit — no plan breaching one reaches the room. A veto that feels dramatic means the list is being invented under pressure.

A PM who can price a technical item is consulted; one who cannot is told

This is not technical literacy. It is whether she can say, for every technical item on the roadmap, what it buys in weeks, rupees or risk. The tell is direction — whether engineering brings her the problem or the conclusion.

7. Across product types and company stages

Most writing on this topic exaggerates the variation. The allocation of decision rights barely changes between a consumer app and an industrial device business. What changes is which class of decision is load-bearing, and how fast the doors shut.

ContextWhere the one-way doors are, and how fast they shut
ConsumerPeak capacity and client-side data models; shut at the pace of app adoption.
B2B and enterpriseTenant isolation and per-customer forks; shut at signature, for the term.
Platform and marketplaceLedger shape and dispute trails; effectively shut on first money movement.
Hardware and physical goodsWire and storage formats; shut when the unit leaves the factory.
AI productsVendor coupling and the evaluation set; stay ajar, but unit economics move.
 Table 4. The real variation is in door speed, not in who decides.

Stage changes the conversation more than product type does. Below about fifteen engineers the tech lead is the architect and the exchange is continuous; the failure mode is ceremony, not absence. Between fifty and three hundred a separate architecture function appears and the characteristic failure is the review gate. Above that, architects are scarce and the binding constraint is calendar access, which is why mature firms move the conversation earlier.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Nirveda, where the real objection was commercial. Hingmire asked what would worry him if availability were free. The answer was price. At 18 per cent of monthly actives using the feature nine times a month, Nirveda sends 6,20,000 times 0.18 times 9, or 10,04,400 requests a month; at ₹2.10 a request that is ₹21.09 lakh a month and ₹2.53 crore a year, 7.7 per cent of a ₹33.01 crore revenue line, committed to one supplier. Hanmante had been making a procurement argument he had no standing to make, which is why it emerged as availability. Hingmire took the fallback build, shipping on Thursday 28 January, missed the catalogue, and put the vendor spend on her own roadmap with a trigger at ₹25 lakh a month — 18.5 per cent above today's ₹21.09 lakh — at which point a second-vendor router is committed.

Nabhas, where the cost case lost and the floor case won. Haldule had the payback in front of him: ₹8.40 lakh now against ₹3.15 lakh a year, 2.67 years against a 24-month rule. On that, and on three weeks of schedule against a ₹9.4 crore tender, the version byte did not clear. What decided it was different in kind. Without a version marker, a parser meeting records from the 2,760 un-upgraded loggers would decode them against the new field offsets and report a temperature never measured — across the 38,640 consignments a month those loggers accompany, at 14 apiece, in a vaccine cold chain. That is a floor, not a cost. Haldule accepted it and changed what had to be demonstrated: the version byte went in, dual-parser and backfill moved to a committed phase running to Friday 26 March 2027, and the 15 February demonstration ran on 400 factory-flashed loggers.

Nutana Spaces, where the partnership was run correctly and still failed. Nutana matches homeowners with interior contractors in Hyderabad: 2,400 projects a month and ₹18 crore of contractor payouts, averaging ₹75,000 a project. In July 2026 Anjaneya Halgekar and platform architect Aradhya Hulyalkar did everything this page recommends: money stayed in one ledger service, the decision was recorded, and it carried a revisit trigger — p95 ledger write latency above 400 milliseconds. In January 2027 the business moved to milestone escrow, four instalments a project instead of one, taking ledger writes per project from 3 to 12 and monthly writes from 7,200 to 28,800. The trigger never fired: p95 latency sat at 160 milliseconds. What broke was the nightly reconciliation. Modelling the work as linear in instalments for the 92 per cent of projects without a dispute, a factor of 4, and pairwise for the 8 per cent with one, a factor of 16, the weighted factor is 0.92 times 4 plus 0.08 times 16, or 4.96: the 40-minute job is modelled at 198.4 minutes against the 180-minute window between its 02:30 start and the 05:30 filing deadline. Escrow migrated in cohorts and reached the whole book only in the last week of February, which is why January broke nothing. Once past that line the job overran by 18.4 minutes every night, and the whole of March 2027's ₹18 crore of payouts went a working day late. Of 3,400 active contractors, 212 escalated and 34 stopped accepting work.

The recovery was not a rebuild, which is the instructive part. Reconciliation moved to incremental, returning the job to 34 minutes, and every live decision record had its trigger rewritten in a quantity Halgekar already tracked weekly — instalments per project — with her name against it. Seven engineer-weeks, finished Friday 30 April 2027. The decision had been right; the trigger was in the wrong units and owned by nobody.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should an architect hold a veto? The case for is that a floor commercial pressure can override is not a floor; its evidence is statutory duties — DPDP obligations, CERT-In's six-hour reporting directive — that do not bend to a tender. For this to be wrong, the genuine floors would have to be few enough to enumerate in advance, in which case what is wanted is a checklist, not a veto. The case against is sharper than it looks: almost any commercial risk can be redescribed as a technical floor, and a veto rewards whoever translates best. Nirveda is the exhibit. Hanmante raised two objections that both sounded technical; one was a tradeable cost, the other a procurement argument about ₹2.53 crore a year. A veto would have passed both.

Is a standalone architect role justified at all? The team-ownership school holds that a designer who does not carry the pager cannot answer for operability, and that the role is a symptom of teams not trusted with their systems. The conceptual-integrity school replies that cross-system coherence is nobody's incentive by default, and that the firms cited for the first position employ many architects under other titles. What would settle it is evidence that change cost per feature does not rise with team count where no cross-cutting authority exists. None exists.

Named roadmap items, or a fixed share of capacity? Naming technical work makes the trade explicit and forces the product manager to learn the system. A fixed share — the familiar twenty per cent — avoids asking her to adjudicate what she cannot evaluate and is not renegotiated each quarter. The share is right precisely when the value of technical work is uniform and her ability to discriminate is near zero. How often that holds is disputed.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this runs the meeting. Someone who has internalised it changes what happens before it. She sends the request and the draft date to the tech lead and the architect a week early, so the capacity graph exists before anyone is defending a position, and she names the constraint she cares about. She asks what measurement produced the architect's limit, then what would worry him if it were free — the question that surfaced ₹21.09 lakh a month. She never adjudicates between two designs; she asks each side what evidence would change its mind. When she defers work, the trigger sits in her own units and carries her name.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Hingmire shipped the fallback build on Thursday 28 January 2027, losing a placement worth 19,400 subscribers, and bought back what the fast build would have cost permanently: the ability to change supplier. Haldule conceded the version byte and demonstrated on 400 factory-flashed loggers. Each gave ground on a different axis, and only after someone put a number on the table the other could not have produced.

  1. Hanmante's availability objection was worth about 216 minutes a month against ₹2.75 crore of monthly revenue; his coupling objection ₹2.53 crore a year. He raised the first, not the second. What made that rational for him, and what would change it?
  2. Hambardikar's version byte misses Nabhas's 24-month payback rule and was still the right call. Which decisions in your product fail a cost test and pass a floor test, and who may tell the difference?
  3. Nutana's practice was textbook and its trigger still failed. If every deferred decision on your roadmap carried a trigger in a quantity you already track weekly, how many could you express that way?

13. Going deeper

  • PM–engineering working agreement — the team-level version of this; it fixes who is told what and when, which is how sequence is beaten.
  • Having a system design conversation — the skill that lets you go past an architect's first answer.
  • The software development lifecycle — where each class of decision closes, and what shuts a door.
  • Agile in practice — why ceremonies alone never produce the partnership.
  • Kanban and flow — how deferred technical work behaves as inventory with a carrying cost.
  • The execution rhythm — the cadence that gets the architect in before the date is public.
  • Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing — why an estimate and a limit need opposite questions.
  • Backlog management and refinement — where a deferred decision and its trigger live, so somebody sees them.
